Variance at the Seams of Emergency Care

A Stochastic Model of Delay Propagation Across the Interfaces of a Time-Critical Pathway, with Application to Severe Paracetamol Poisoning · interactive simulator

By Maisie Mary Cu · Berlin School of Economics and Law, Germany

How delay at the handovers between teams decides who gets the paracetamol antidote in time. About

Applied science research on a time-critical care pathway, using operational research and simulation. Queueing, Monte Carlo simulation, decision rules and Six Sigma, applied to arrival, decisions, hospital buildings and cities worldwide. Every value is illustrative, not an estimate for any hospital. Anyone can use it.

In plain words

This is the main experiment of the paper. Change one setting at a time and see what happens to the share of patients who get the antidote too late.

Start with the three presets: independent steps, a busy hospital that slows everyone, and a busy hospital where delays also pass from step to step.

How to read it

  • The five boxes at the top are the headline numbers; red changes are worse than the pinned comparison.
  • Pin as comparison freezes the current result in grey, so you can change something and compare.
  • Orange in Where the minutes go is waiting at the seams, blue is actual work.

Time from arrival to NAC

Cumulative share of patients. Ticks mark the median and 90th percentile.

Explain this graph

What is shown: A cumulative distribution. Across: minutes from arrival to the antidote. Up: share of patients treated by that time. Solid blue is your scenario; dashed grey is the pinned comparison.

What to look for: Curves further left mean faster care. A curve that is less steep has more spread. The gap between the two curves at the top, around the 90th percentile (P90), is often larger than at the middle (median).

Why it matters: Two pathways can have similar medians but very different slow tails. The slow tail decides who misses the window.

Missed windows by arrival time

Share missing W, by hours from ingestion to arrival. Averages hide where the misses sit.

Explain this graph

What is shown: Across: how many hours after ingestion the patient arrived. Up: share of those patients who missed the window. Blue is your scenario, grey the comparison.

What to look for: Patients who arrive early almost never miss. Patients who arrive 4–6 hours after ingestion miss very often. Compare the bars for early arrivals between scenarios: amplifying pathways fail early arrivals more.

Why it matters: A single overall miss rate hides who is at risk. Performance should be judged by time since ingestion, as Section 4.3 of the paper argues.

Where the minutes go

Median within-step work and interface waiting per stage, current scenario.

Explain this graph

What is shown: One bar per step. Blue is the median time spent doing the step (work); orange is the median time waiting at the handover after it (interface waiting).

What to look for: Orange is longer than blue at most steps. The sentence underneath gives process cycle efficiency: work divided by total time.

Why it matters: Most of the time to treatment is spent waiting at the seams, not working. Improving the seams therefore offers more than making each team faster.

Correlation between stage times

Uniform values point to common shocks; values that fade with distance point to propagation.

Explain this graph

What is shown: A correlation matrix: each square shows how strongly two steps' times move together, from 0 (unrelated) to 1 (always together). Darker means stronger.

What to look for: The pattern. Roughly equal values everywhere point to a common shock (a busy hospital slowing all steps). Values strongest next to the diagonal and fading further away point to direct propagation (lateness passed from step to step).

Why it matters: The two patterns call for different fixes: capacity for common shocks, buffers at specific handovers for propagation. This contrast is how the empirical study tells them apart (hypothesis H2).

Occupancy curve

Missed-window share as mean occupancy rises, both policies, with the other settings as set.

Explain this graph

What is shown: Across: mean occupancy, how full the receiving units are. Up: share missing the window. Blue: wait for results. Green: treat first.

What to look for: The blue curve stays flat, then bends sharply upward above about 80% occupancy. The green curve sits lower and bends later.

Why it matters: Delay grows slowly and then explodes as a hospital fills up (Proposition 4), so the last few percent of occupancy are the most costly. Treat first works as a buffer but cannot make the pathway immune to crowding.

Four declared inputs give the threshold that minimises expected loss, L(α) = (1 − π)·C·α + π·(1 − power).
Statistical decision theory · from “Testing the Test” (Cu, 2026)

Choosing the significance threshold by its consequences

Every decision in this simulator that rests on a test (is the day out of control? is coupling real? did the improvement work?) commits two kinds of error. A fixed p < .05 ignores sample size, effect size, how often real effects occur and what each error costs. Following Cu's paper Testing the Test: Calibrating Statistical Significance Under Asymmetric Error Costs, the threshold here is the one that minimises expected loss. Power uses the normal approximation to the two-sided test (as in the paper's companion workbook), so values can differ slightly from the exact t-test in small samples.

Expected loss against the threshold

Total expected loss (dark) is the false-positive part (rising) plus the false-negative part (falling). The calibrated α* is the lowest point; .05 and .005 are marked for comparison. Logarithmic α axis.

Calibrated threshold over prevalence and cost

Colour is α* for the current n and δ. Solid outline: cells where α* is close to .05. Click any cell to use that prevalence and cost ratio.

The cost ratio that .05 silently assumes

C at which .05 is loss-minimising, against the non-centrality λ = δ√(n/2), at the current prevalence. At π = .5 it never exceeds about 3.41 (the paper's bound).

In plain words

Before collecting real hospital data, it helps to know how many patients are needed to see linked delays, if they exist.

This also shows a trap. If staff rush sicker-looking patients at every step, the data can show a link that is not really there.

How to read it

  • Solid line: how often a study of that size finds the real link. Above the amber 80% line is the usual target.
  • Dashed red line: how often a study wrongly finds a link that does not exist. It should stay near 5%.
  • Raise unobserved urgency to see the dashed line climb. That is the trap.

Power to detect coupling at S1 → S2

Solid: share of studies that detect the true β. Dashed: share that "detect" coupling when the true β is 0, the false-positive rate.

Explain this graph

What is shown: Across: number of patients in a future real study (log scale). Up: share of simulated studies that find coupling. Solid blue: when coupling really exists. Dashed red: when it does not (false positives).

What to look for: Where the blue line crosses the orange 80% line: the sample size needed. Then raise 'unobserved urgency' and watch the red line climb above 5%.

Why it matters: It tells the empirical study how big it must be, and warns that a hidden factor can fake the very effect the study is looking for.

Estimates by cohort size

Mean estimated β̂ across replications. Bias appears when urgency is unobserved.

What the reference run found

With occupancy controlled and no hidden urgency, β = 0.3 is detected in 95% of studies at about 100 patients, and β = 0.15 in 84% at 200 and 96% at 400. The test holds its false-positive rate near 5%.

An unobserved urgency factor with log-sd 0.3, staff moving faster at every stage for patients who look sicker, adds about +0.13 to β̂. With true β = 0, the test then "finds" coupling in 63% of studies at 200 patients and 99% at 800. A larger cohort makes this worse, not better. This is the case for the negative-control test and the shift-handover check in Section 5.5.

Section 4.3 check resolves [CHECK]

Two pathways rescaled to the same mean in-hospital time of 200 minutes.

Calibration against Bailey et al. (2016) inconclusive

Each bag-change delay was fitted as log-normal from its published median and IQR (25 [10–60] and 50 [15–104] minutes), and the two were joined with a correlation r chosen to reproduce the cumulative delay of 90 [50–163] minutes.

No value of r fits. The median matches at about r = 0.5, but the modelled upper quartile stays between 197 and 214 minutes against 163 published. The published summaries are consistent with C close to 1, and they cannot show whether delay propagates between bag changes. Only patient-level timestamps can, which is the case for the empirical design.

Try the equation live

Move the sliders to see how one stage's waiting time hᵢ and stage time Xᵢ respond. The curve is the crowding multiplier g(ρ); the dot is your setting.

Reading it: g(ρ) barely moves until the hospital is about 80% busy, then climbs steeply; that is why a little extra crowding hurts so much. β×hᵢ₋₁ is the part of the previous stage's delay that is carried into this one.

Model

Each patient passes stages S1 to S4. Stage time is within-step work plus interface delay, and delay passes forward with coupling β while a shared occupancy load slows every stage at once.

Xᵢ = dᵢ + hᵢ, hᵢ = g(ρ)·Vᵢ + β·hᵢ₋₁, g(ρ) = 1 + k·ρ/(1 − ρ)

A patient misses the window when pre-hospital time plus in-hospital time exceeds W. The containment ratio compares the variance of the total with the sum of stage variances.

miss ⇔ A + ΣXᵢ > W, C = Var(ΣXᵢ) / Σ Var(Xᵢ)

Treat first removes S2 and S3 from the clock and adds a preparation step after recognition (Proposition 7). Occupancy is drawn per patient from a Beta distribution; durations and delays are log-normal.

Equations explained

Every equation used on this page, in the order a simulated patient meets them. Each has a plain reading, its symbols and a worked example.

T = X₁ + X₂ + X₃ + X₄

In words: time in hospital is the sum of the time at each step.

Symbols: T = minutes from arrival to the antidote; Xᵢ = minutes spent at step i (S1 recognition, S2 sample, S3 laboratory, S4a start of antidote).

Example: 28 + 31 + 73 + 49 = 181 minutes.

Xᵢ = dᵢ + hᵢ (also Xᵢ = Lᵢ + Rᵢ)

In words: each step is the work itself plus the waiting at the handover after it. The paper also splits it into waiting for information to exist (L) and waiting for someone to act on it (R).

Symbols: dᵢ = work time; hᵢ = interface waiting; Lᵢ = information latency; Rᵢ = reaction time.

Example: the lab takes 40 minutes to run the test (work) and the result waits 33 minutes before anyone acts (waiting).

hᵢ = g(ρ) · Vᵢ + β · hᵢ₋₁

In words: waiting at a handover is a random delay, made longer when the hospital is full, plus a share of the waiting at the previous handover.

Symbols: Vᵢ = random base delay (log-normal); g(ρ) = load factor; β = coupling, the share of earlier waiting passed on; hᵢ₋₁ = waiting at the previous step.

Example: base delay 10 min × load factor 2.4 = 24 min, plus 0.3 × 20 min carried over = 30 min.

g(ρ) = 1 + k · ρ / (1 − ρ)

In words: the load factor. It barely changes when the hospital is half full, then shoots up as it approaches full. This comes from queueing theory (Kingman's formula).

Symbols: ρ = occupancy, 0 to 1; k = load sensitivity, how strongly waiting reacts to load.

Example: with k = 0.25, at ρ = 0.70 the factor is 1.6; at 0.85 it is 2.4; at 0.95 it is 5.75.

time = median × exp(σ · Z)

In words: how each random time is drawn. Z is a bell-curve random number; exp() turns it into a lopsided log-normal time, mostly short with a few very long.

Symbols: median = the typical time; σ = spread (log-sd); Z = standard normal random number.

Example: median 10 min, σ = 0.6: Z = 0 gives 10 min, Z = 1 gives 18 min, Z = 2 gives 33 min.

miss ⇔ A + T > W

In words: the patient misses the window if time before arrival plus time in hospital is longer than the window.

Symbols: A = pre-hospital time; T = in-hospital time; W = treatment window (8 hours here).

Example: arrives 2 h after ingestion and takes 5 h 30 in hospital: 7 h 30 < 8 h, treated in time.

C = Var(T) / Σ Var(Xᵢ)

In words: the containment ratio compares how unpredictable the total is with how unpredictable it would be if the steps were unrelated.

Symbols: Var = variance, a measure of spread; Σ = add up over all steps.

Example: C = 1.85 means the total is 85% more variable than independent steps would make it: delays pile up together.

P(miss) ≈ 1 − Φ( (W − μ) / √(σ²_A + C · Σσᵢ²) )

In words: a shortcut formula for the miss rate (equation 8 of the paper). The further the average sits inside the window, in units of spread, the fewer misses; a higher C widens the spread and raises misses.

Symbols: Φ = the bell-curve cumulative probability; μ = average total time since ingestion; σ²_A = spread of pre-hospital time; σᵢ² = spread of each step.

Example: if the margin is 2 spreads, misses are about 2% at C = 1 and about 7% at C = 1.85.

SE = √( p (1 − p) / n ), 95% interval = p ± 1.96 · SE

In words: the Monte Carlo error, how much the estimated miss rate would wobble if the simulation were rerun.

Symbols: p = estimated miss share; n = number of simulated patients; 1.96 = the multiplier for 95%.

Example: p = 0.116, n = 200,000: SE = 0.0007, so 11.6% ± 0.14 points.

p* = c_U / (c_U + E[c_D(Δ)])

In words: the treat-first threshold (Proposition 6). Start the antidote before results if the chance the patient needs it is above p*. The slower and less predictable the lab, the lower p*, so earlier treatment becomes worthwhile.

Symbols: c_U = cost of unnecessary treatment; c_D(Δ) = cost of delaying needed treatment by Δ; E[ ] = expected value.

β(ρ) = β₀ + γ · (ρ − 0.85)

In words: an extension on the Coupling tab. Coupling grows when the hospital is fuller, so handovers leak more when busy.

Symbols: β₀ = coupling at 85% occupancy; γ = how fast coupling rises with load.

Example: β₀ = 0.3, γ = 3: at ρ = 0.93 coupling is 0.54.

delayⱼ = base · exp(σ · Z) · m + β_b · delayⱼ₋₁

In words: the delay at each bag change on the Infusion tab: a random delay, multiplied by m if the change falls near a shift handover or ward transfer, plus a share of the previous bag's delay.

Symbols: m = handover multiplier (1 if no collision); β_b = coupling between bag changes; j = bag change number.

effect = miss(linked) − miss(independent)

In words: the amplification effect on the PSA tab: extra percentage points of missed windows caused by linked delays, using the same random patients in both runs.

h₂ = a + β̂ · h₁ + c · g(ρ) + error

In words: the regression a real study would run (equation 13), used on the H2 power tab. It asks whether waiting at the first handover predicts waiting at the second, after allowing for how busy the hospital was.

Symbols: β̂ = estimated coupling; a, c = other fitted numbers; error = what the model cannot explain.

Variance at the Seams of Emergency Care: A Stochastic Model of Delay Propagation Across the Interfaces of a Time-Critical Pathway, with Application to Severe Paracetamol Poisoning

Research paper

Maisie Mary Cu

Berlin School of Economics and Law, Germany

“He will wipe every tear from their eyes. There will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain (Revelation 21:4).

After all it came back to you. All I ever wanted was one more childhood sleepover, shooting rubber bands at the glow-in-the-dark stars on your ceiling. You’re with God now. The pain is over. Goodnight, angel.”

Abstract

Time-critical care pathways are serial service systems of interdependent stages that must complete before a deadline, yet their performance is usually reported as mean intervals at individual stages, which cannot show where delay arises or how it spreads. Severe paracetamol poisoning is a demanding instance: it is often clinically silent at first, treatment is time-critical, and care spans several teams. This paper asks how the interfaces of a time-critical pathway contain or transmit delay, and how this affects the probability of missing the treatment window. The pathway is modelled as a chain of interfaces, each split into information latency, the time until the signal to act exists, and reaction time, the time until the system acts on it. The probability of missing the window then depends not only on mean pathway time but also on stage variability and on a containment ratio C, the variance of total time relative to the sum of stage variances, which measures how far the interfaces pass delay on rather than absorb it. Seven propositions follow. At a fixed mean, propagation raises the miss probability, and it has two distinct sources: direct coupling between successive interfaces and shared occupancy that slows them all at once. Interface delay is convex in occupancy, so a fuller unit loses time ever faster. The threshold for treating before laboratory results depends on how the laboratory performs, and treat-first rules buffer delay by removing coupling. A Monte Carlo simulation with illustrative parameters shows these mechanisms at work. Occupancy and coupling raised C from 1.00 to 1.85 and the share of patients missing the window from 6.3% to 11.6%, while a treat-first rule kept misses below 6% up to 90% mean occupancy, against 28% without it. Because these parameters are assumed rather than estimated, the paper then specifies a retrospective cohort study, to be pre-registered, that uses routine hospital timestamps to estimate propagation at each interface, to separate it from common shocks and to test whether bag changes that coincide with shift handovers wait longer; its results are pending. The results imply that time-critical pathways for hidden dangers should be designed and evaluated at their interfaces, and judged on their variability as well as their average. More generally, the containment ratio offers a tractable design measure for serial service systems that must meet a deadline.

Keywords: OR in health services, stochastic modelling, queueing, simulation, patient flow, variability propagation, containment ratio, interface delay, occupancy, treatment window, paracetamol poisoning

1. Introduction

Some emergencies are dangerous before they appear so. When early clinical signals are weak and treatment is most effective early, outcomes depend on coordination across interfaces more than on the speed of any single team. Severe paracetamol (acetaminophen) poisoning illustrates this problem: patients may initially appear well, the antidote works best when started early (Chiew et al., 2020; Commission on Human Medicines/MHRA, 2012; Smilkstein et al., 1988), and care may cross emergency medicine, laboratory, pharmacy, intensive care, toxicology, hepatology, mental health services and a transplant centre. Each crossing can lose time. Two features of such pathways matter. First, the pathway is a race against a clinical window: the patient benefits only if the antidote starts before it closes. Second, performance is measured mainly by mean or median intervals at individual steps (e.g., Bailey et al., 2016; Bradley et al., 2006; Royal College of Emergency Medicine, 2014). Such averages hide propagation. If delay at one interface increases delay at the next, variability compounds (Hopp & Spearman, 2008), so a pathway can miss the window often despite an acceptable mean. Average intervals therefore cannot show whether interfaces contain or transmit delay.

1.1. Time-critical pathways with hidden danger

▶ Explore this in the simulator: Arrival & liver clock →

Pathways for stroke, myocardial infarction and sepsis have been redesigned around explicit interval targets, and much of their improvement has come from coordination rather than from new treatments (Bradley et al., 2006). These conditions, however, usually announce themselves at presentation. Paracetamol poisoning tests the harder case, in which the system must act on history, timing and laboratory results before the patient appears unwell. Where danger is hidden, the system cannot rely on visible deterioration to prompt action; it must act through procedure, and the reliability of each handover determines whether treatment arrives in time.

1.2. The problem of average-based measurement

▶ Explore this in the simulator: Monte Carlo →

A mean interval alone does not describe a pathway's risk of missing a deadline, because that risk depends on the whole distribution of total time and in particular on its upper tail; even independent stages with different distributions carry different tail risks at the same mean. Dependence between stages makes the problem worse. When stage times co-move, whether because delay passes forward from one team to the next or because a crowded hospital slows every team at once, the variance of total time exceeds the sum of the stage variances (Hopp & Spearman, 2008), and the tail of the distribution, which is where patients miss the window, grows faster than the mean. Two pathways with the same average can then carry very different risks, and a performance target set on the mean will rank them incorrectly. These consequences are structural rather than incidental: they follow from the arithmetic of sums of dependent random variables, and they apply to any pathway in which a treatment window is fixed and care crosses several teams.

1.3. Research question

▶ Explore this in the simulator: Research design →

This paper accordingly asks: how do the interfaces of a time-critical emergency pathway contain or transmit delay, and how does this affect the probability that patients miss the treatment window? The study is a contribution to operational research in healthcare: it models the pathway as a serial stochastic system with a deadline and derives analytical and simulation results for its design. It draws on health services research and is not a clinical toxicology study. It measures delay at each interface in minutes, separating the time until the signal to act exists from the time the system takes to act on it. It takes clinical guidance as given and analyses how the system executes and coordinates it; it makes no claim about which clinical decisions are correct.

1.4. Contribution

▶ Explore this in the simulator: Research design →

The paper makes five contributions to operational research on time-critical service systems. It formalises a care pathway as a chain of interfaces, linking step durations, propagation between steps, occupancy and a treatment window, and derives a closed-form expression for the probability of missing the window in terms of mean time, stage variability and a containment ratio C; it also decomposes each interface time into information latency and reaction time, so that delay can be attributed to the information system or to coordination. It establishes seven propositions showing that, for a fixed mean, propagation alone raises the miss probability; that direct coupling and shared occupancy are distinct sources of propagation; that interface delay rises convexly with occupancy; and that rules for treating before laboratory results act as buffers by removing coupling at the laboratory interface. It synthesises the published timing evidence to locate where delay is documented along the pathway and where it is not (Section 2.4). It reports a simulation study that illustrates the size of these effects under stated, illustrative parameters, together with a counterfactual analysis of which interface to improve first. Finally, it specifies a mixed-methods empirical design, to be pre-registered, for testing the resulting hypotheses with routinely recorded hospital timestamps and staff interviews.

The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. Section 2 reviews the literature on time-critical pathways and on operational research in patient flow, and describes the paracetamol pathway as a system of interfaces. Section 3 sets out the model, its propositions, the hypotheses that follow from it and the design of the simulation. Section 4 reports the simulation findings. Section 5 specifies the empirical study design. Section 6 discusses the implications for practice and theory, states the limitations and concludes. Appendix A records the selection of cases, the published timing benchmarks and the mapping of each interface to a timestamp source. Figure 1 summarises how these parts fit together and which hypothesis each part tests.

Figure 1. Research process, from question to evidence. The analytical model (Section 3) is illustrated by a Monte Carlo simulation with illustrative parameters (Section 4) and tested in the empirical cases of Section 5, whose identifiers follow Table A1; each part of the design is linked to the hypotheses H1–H5 it tests and to the outputs the study is intended to deliver. The sub-hypothesis H3a (Section 3.8) is not shown separately.

2. Literature review

Three literatures frame the study: the redesign of time-critical pathways, operational research on patient flow, and the clinical pathway for paracetamol poisoning described as a system. Read together, they establish that coordination is the principal lever in time-critical care, that hospital delay is governed by occupancy and variability rather than by averages (Armony et al., 2015; Hopp & Spearman, 2008), and that the paracetamol pathway is a demanding test of both claims because its danger is hidden at presentation.

2.1. Time-critical pathways and coordination

Several emergencies are managed as time-critical pathways with explicit interval targets. Stroke thrombolysis (door-to-needle), primary angioplasty for myocardial infarction (door-to-balloon) and antibiotics in sepsis are the best-known examples (Bradley et al., 2006; Kumar et al., 2006), and in sepsis each hour of delay to antibiotics has been associated with higher mortality (Seymour et al., 2017). Improvement in these pathways has come largely from coordination rather than from new treatments: pre-hospital alerts, single-call team activation, fixed protocols and direct routing that removes handovers (Bradley et al., 2006). Crowding lengthens time to treatment even where the indication is clear (McCarthy et al., 2009; Pines et al., 2007) and is associated with worse outcomes for admitted patients (Sun et al., 2013).

These pathways share a feature that paracetamol poisoning lacks. Their danger is usually visible at presentation, through sudden neurological deficit, chest pain, an abnormal ECG or physiological instability, and visible danger lets a system trigger action from appearance (Bradley et al., 2006; Kumar et al., 2006). Paracetamol poisoning is the harder case set out in Section 1.1: its danger is hidden at presentation, so action must be triggered by procedure rather than by appearance.

2.2. Operational research on patient flow

Operational research treats hospitals as networks of queues (Armony et al., 2015; Hall, 2006), and two of its results matter here. The first is that waiting time rises non-linearly with utilisation. In Kingman's (1961) heavy-traffic approximation, expected waiting time scales with ρ/(1 − ρ), where ρ is occupancy, multiplied by the variability of arrivals and service (Hopp & Spearman, 2008). Studies of bed management have used this logic to argue that running acute beds at very high average occupancy produces frequent access failures (Bagust et al., 1999), and a conceptual model of emergency department crowding attributes much of it to the flow of patients out of the department (Asplin et al., 2003).

The second is that much of the variability in hospital demand is generated by the hospital itself. Litvak and colleagues distinguish natural variability, arising from patients, from artificial variability, arising from scheduling, and argue that the latter is often the larger driver of crowding (Litvak & Fineberg, 2013; McManus et al., 2003). Empirical studies of hospital operations add that service times themselves respond to load, so that congestion at one unit changes how patients are treated and discharged elsewhere (KC & Terwiesch, 2009, 2012). Process mining, finally, offers a method for reconstructing actual patient paths from timestamped event logs (Rojas et al., 2016; van der Aalst, 2016), although it has rarely been used to measure how delay propagates between steps.

2.3. The paracetamol pathway as a system

▶ Explore this in the simulator: Process map →

The pathway is described here from published guidance and protocols, not from clinical judgement by the author; local protocols differ, and the empirical study uses the protocol of the participating hospital. On arrival and at triage, the time and pattern of ingestion (single or staggered) are recorded, and every later decision is measured from the time of ingestion. A paracetamol concentration is interpretable only after an absorption interval, and liver, kidney and coagulation tests are taken alongside it. The concentration is then compared with a treatment line on a nomogram (Rumack & Matthew, 1975), although protocols specify starting acetylcysteine (NAC) before results in defined circumstances, such as unknown or staggered ingestion or late presentation (Chiew et al., 2020; Commission on Human Medicines/MHRA, 2012). Figure 2 sets out the clinical course that makes the danger hidden: the reserve that protects the liver drains during a latent phase in which many patients appear well, which is why the system must act on history, timing and tests rather than on appearance.

Figure 2. The biological clock after paracetamol overdose and the point at which the care system must act. Schematic of the clinical course described in guidance (stages I–IV), with typical timings that vary between people, shown hour by hour over the first five days (0–120 hours). The body's glutathione reserve drains while many patients still look well, so the front-end interfaces S1–S4 race against a window W taken from the local protocol, and the later interfaces S5–S8 matter for the minority whose liver injury progresses. The rows separate what happens in the body, what staff can see and what information exists, so the gap between the closing of the window and the first visible sign of danger can be read directly. With an illustrative W of 8 hours, the window closes some 64 hours before danger becomes visible at about 72 hours. Kidney injury typically shows on blood tests between 72 and 120 hours, and its signal may arrive only after discharge, which creates a further seam (S5k) (Chiew et al., 2020; Rumack & Matthew, 1975). Educational schematic for systems research; it contains no dosing information and is not clinical advice.

NAC is given either as a traditional three-bag regimen or as a shorter two-bag regimen (Bateman et al., 2014), followed by repeat blood tests; the administration of the infusion is itself prone to error and interruption (Ferner et al., 2001; Hayes et al., 2008). Patients with worsening liver injury are escalated to intensive care, with advice from a poisons service and a liver unit. Prognostic criteria such as the King's College Criteria (O'Grady et al., 1989) inform transplant referral, and patients not at a transplant centre are transferred, although referral patterns are known to vary (Newsome et al., 2001). Kidney injury follows a separate clock. It typically appears on blood tests three to five days after ingestion, peaks around the seventh day, can occur without severe liver injury and rarely requires dialysis (Mazer & Perrone, 2008). By then many patients have completed treatment and been discharged, so the signal may arrive in a setting other than the one that treated them, where no one is designated to act on it. The study treats this as a branch interface, S5k, which runs in parallel with the later interfaces S5 to S8 defined below (Table 1). Because many presentations are intentional, guidance in many countries also requires a mental health assessment; in a US multicentre series of paracetamol-induced acute liver failure, however, about half of cases followed unintentional overdose (Larson et al., 2005). The study treats each handover between these steps as an interface, labelled S1 to S8 in Table 1 and Figure 3, with the kidney branch S5k and two treatment-phase interfaces, S4c and S4m, listed alongside them; the time before arrival, from ingestion to the door, is recorded but treated as outside the hospital's control. Handovers of this kind are recognised points of failure in settings with high consequences for failure (Patterson et al., 2004), and the quality of coordination across professions has been linked to outcomes of care (Gittell et al., 2000).

Table 1. Interfaces of the paracetamol poisoning pathway with the trigger (the signal to act exists) and the action (the system responds) at each, and the routine timestamps that record them. Interfaces are derived from published guidance; the empirical study adapts them to the local protocol.

Interface Trigger → action Timestamps
S1 Arrival with possible paracetamol ingestion → risk recognised and documented Arrival, triage, first documented mention
S2 Recognition → blood sample taken Sample collection time
S3 Sample received in laboratory → result reported (mostly information latency) Result reported
S4a Result reported, or treat-first criteria met → NAC infusion started Prescription, infusion start
S4b Scheduled bag change due → next infusion bag started Administration time of each bag

S5 First abnormal result showing deterioration → ICU referral and admission First abnormal result, ICU admission

Blue tags mark the eight interfaces S1–S8; the dashed path shows the treat-first rule, under which NAC is started before results when protocol criteria are met, bypassing S2 and S3. 2.4. Where the published evidence locates the bottlenecks

▶ Explore this in the simulator: Bottleneck analysis →

Taken together, the operational studies of Section 2.3 and Appendix A locate the bottlenecks of the paracetamol pathway at five points. Some are well documented and others are plausible but not yet measured. Table 2 distinguishes the two, and Figure 4 maps them onto the pathway; the gap between them is part of what this study is designed to fill.

Table 2. Bottlenecks in the paracetamol pathway as located by published evidence, ranked by the strength of that evidence, with the component of interface time each mainly affects.

Interface Bottleneck Evidence Mainly affects
S4 and within the infusion Delay in starting NAC and, above all, between infusion bags Strong. Median delay of 90 min against the intended schedule across three English hospitals, with 68% delayed by more than 1 h and 21% by more than 3 h (Bailey et al., 2016); 19% of infusions interrupted for more than 1 h (Hayes et al., 2008) Reaction time
S1, recognition Risk not recognised, or ingestion time unclear, especially after staggered or accidental overdose Moderate. Accidental or supratherapeutic presentations waited longer (median 170 against 85 min; Bailey et al., 2016); about half of early presenters received NAC within 8 h of ingestion (Royal College of Emergency Medicine, 2014) Reaction time
S2–S3, waiting for the level The concentration cannot be interpreted until the absorption interval has passed, and laboratory turnaround adds to it Moderate, indirect. Treating at-risk patients first raised timely NAC from 12% to 61% (Pettie et al., 2012) Information latency
S5, ICU admission Bed availability when the hospital is full Plausible, not measured for this pathway. Crowding delays time-critical treatment elsewhere (McCarthy et al., 2009; Pines et al., 2007) Common shock (occupancy)
S7–S8, referral and transfer Late discussion with the liver unit; transfer logistics between hospitals Weak or older. Referral patterns vary (Newsome et al., 2001), and guidance stresses early referral Reaction time across organisations

The evidence points to five patterns behind these bottlenecks. First, the largest documented delays occur not at the door but during treatment, at bag changes, which Bailey et al. (2016) associate with handovers between teams and shifts, moves between departments and adverse reactions; patients with anaphylactoid reactions waited a median of 267 minutes. In the terms of the model developed in Section 3, every bag change is a seam, and the older three-bag regimen had more of them. Second, fewer seams meant less delay: the switch to a two-bag regimen cut median cumulative delay from 65 to 35 minutes and delays of more than an hour from 51% to 31% (O'Callaghan et al., 2022), consistent with removing a handover and its coupling. Third, atypical presentations fall outside the protocol. Accidental and staggered overdoses do not match the single acute ingestion around which the protocol is built, so the trigger at S1 is weaker and recognition slower; this is the hidden-danger argument in its sharpest form. Fourth, treat-first rules act as buffers: removing the wait for results from the clock transformed timeliness (Pettie et al., 2012), as Proposition 7 (Section 3.7) formalises. Fifth, occupancy is the most plausible driver of delay at the back end. There is no direct evidence for this pathway, but crowding research makes the ICU admission interface the most likely site of common shocks.

Interpreted through the model of Section 3, the evidence yields expectations that the empirical study can test. Coupling β is likely to be highest from S1 to S4, because late recognition pushes back every later step. Information latency L is largest at S3, which treat-first rules exist to bypass. For early presenters, part of this latency is biological rather than laboratory: the paracetamol level cannot be interpreted until four hours after ingestion, so a patient who arrives earlier must wait for it even if the laboratory is instant (Chiew et al., 2020; see Section 4.2). Reaction time R is largest within S4, at the bag changes, where delay reflects coordination rather than capacity. The ICU admission interface S5 is likely to be the most sensitive to occupancy, and the transfer interface S8 the most fragile, because it crosses two organisations and depends on a retrieval team. These are expectations derived from the literature, not findings.

The documented bottlenecks are therefore mostly front-end reaction times and handovers rather than laboratory capacity, which is consistent with hypotheses H1 and H4 (Section 3.8), while the back end (S5 to S8) is where the evidence is thinnest. The studies come from the United Kingdom, Australia and the United States, mostly before 2020, and each measured a single interval. None measured whether delay at one interface causes delay at the next, which is the question this study addresses.

Figure 4. Bottleneck heat map: where delay is documented along the paracetamol pathway. None of the studies measured propagation between interfaces.

Figure 5 complements this by mapping the gap at each transition rather than only where delay has been documented. For every handover it shows what crosses the seam, how long the wait lasts, who holds responsibility while the patient waits and whether the gap has ever been timed. Published timings exist only for the bag changes during the infusion, where the three-bag regimen loses a median of 25 and then 50 minutes at its two changes against 35 minutes at the single change of the two-bag regimen; the front-end values are illustrative simulation outputs, and no back-end gap has a published timing. The two places where no one is clearly designated to act, the result waiting for a prescriber at S4a and the kidney signal arriving after discharge at S5k, are where the argument of this paper is sharpest.

Figure 5. The gap at each transition of the pathway: what crosses the seam, the waiting time at the seam (median, interquartile range and 90th percentile, log scale), who holds responsibility while the patient waits, and the source of the timing. Front-end gaps are simulated (Section 3.9, illustrative); bag-change gaps are published delays against the intended schedule (Bailey et al., 2016; O'Callaghan et al., 2022); back-end gaps have no published timing. The owner in each gap is the author's reading of the protocol, not a finding, and is to be checked in the staff interviews.

3. Method

The model treats the pathway as a chain of interfaces and derives the probability that a patient misses the treatment window. Seven propositions follow, each with a short proof; the hypotheses for the empirical study and the design of the simulation are derived from them in Sections 3.8 and 3.9.

3.1. Pathway setup

▶ Explore this in the simulator: Process map →

A patient passes through stages i = 1, …, n. Let Xᵢ ≥ 0 be the time spent at stage i, including the handover at its end, so that Xᵢ = dᵢ + hᵢ, where dᵢ is the within-step duration and hᵢ the interface delay. Time from arrival to a milestone m, for example the start of NAC, is then

T = Σᵢ₌₁ᵐ Xᵢ, μ_T = Σᵢ E[Xᵢ], σᵢ² = Var(Xᵢ) (1)

Let A be the pre-hospital time from ingestion to arrival, and W the treatment window specified by the protocol in use. W is an input taken from guidance (Chiew et al., 2020; Commission on Human Medicines/MHRA, 2012), not a quantity estimated here. The patient misses the window if S = A + T > W. Treating W as a fixed threshold is a modelling simplification. The benefit of treatment declines continuously with elapsed time and protocols differ by presentation, so the miss probability P(S > W) is best read as one point on a continuous loss function rather than as a clinical boundary. Likewise, the illustrative value of W used in the simulation (Section 3.9) is not a clinical recommendation. Section 3.7 replaces the threshold with a continuous cost of delay c_D(Δ), and the empirical study repeats its analyses across the range of W that the hospital protocol allows.

Because the empirical study measures delay in minutes from routine timestamps, each interface time is also decomposed by what the timestamps record. A trigger is the moment the information needed to act exists, for example when a laboratory result is reported; an action is the moment the system acts on it, for example when the NAC infusion starts. Table 1 lists the trigger and action at each interface, and Figure 6 shows who acts at each front-end interface and where reaction time and latency are spent. The reaction time at interface i is

Rᵢ = t_action,ᵢ − t_trigger,ᵢ, Xᵢ = Lᵢ + Rᵢ (2)

where the information latency Lᵢ is the time until the trigger exists, such as laboratory turnaround at S3. Latency is a property of the information system; reaction time is a property of coordination, since it measures whether a signal that already exists is seen and acted on. Minutes lost at interface i are reaction time in excess of the target the hospital protocol specifies for that interface. The two decompositions are related but not identical: within-step work that generates the trigger falls in Lᵢ, and waiting after the trigger falls in Rᵢ, so that Lᵢ broadly corresponds to dᵢ and Rᵢ to hᵢ. Propositions 1 to 7 depend only on the covariance structure and the occupancy dependence of the interface times, and they hold for either decomposition; in particular, the propagation model of Section 3.3 applies directly to reaction times, Rᵢ₊₁ = βᵢRᵢ + Uᵢ₊₁. Because the best-documented delays occur during treatment rather than before it (Section 2.4), interface S4 is split into two sub-interfaces: S4a, from the result being reported or the treat-first criteria being met to the start of the infusion, and S4b, from each scheduled bag change to the start of the next bag. Each bag change is a seam in the sense of the model, so a regimen with fewer bags has fewer S4b interfaces. Two further treatment-phase interfaces are recorded but not modelled: S4c, at the end of the infusion, where a second laboratory latency precedes the decision to stop, continue or escalate and is therefore the usual trigger for S5; and S4m, the mental health assessment, which runs in parallel with the infusion and can interrupt it through moves between units or self-discharge. Table 3 shows how the two decompositions line up at each interface and lists the notation used in the rest of the paper.
