3.2. The containment ratio

▶ Explore this in the simulator: Coupling extensions →

The central quantity of the model is the containment ratio, defined as the variance of total time relative to the variance the stages would produce if they were independent:

C = Var(T) / Σᵢ σᵢ² = 1 + 2 Σᵢ<ⱼ Cov(Xᵢ, Xⱼ) / Σᵢ σᵢ² (3)

C = 1 when stage times are uncorrelated. C > 1 when delays at one stage tend to accompany delays at others, so that the interfaces amplify variability, and C < 1 when later stages compensate for earlier delays.

Proposition 1. If Cov(Xᵢ, Xⱼ) ≥ 0 for all i < j, then C ≥ 1, with equality if and only if all covariances are zero.

Immediate from the definition, since the numerator of the second term is a sum of non-negative terms.

Two mechanisms generate positive covariance, and the model separates them because they imply different remedies.

3.3. Mechanism 1: direct propagation

▶ Explore this in the simulator: Pathway →

A delay passes forward when, for example, late recognition leaves a patient deprioritised at the next step, or when information is lost at handover (Arora et al., 2005). This is modelled as

Xᵢ₊₁ = βᵢ Xᵢ + Uᵢ₊₁, βᵢ ≥ 0 (4)

where Uᵢ₊₁ is new delay arising at stage i + 1, independent of all earlier stage times, and βᵢ is the coupling at interface i.

Proposition 2. Under direct propagation, for i < j, Cov(Xᵢ, Xⱼ) = (Πₖ₌ᵢʲ⁻¹ βₖ) σᵢ² ≥ 0. Hence C ≥ 1, strictly so if any βᵢ > 0 and the corresponding σᵢ² > 0.

By induction on j. For j = i the covariance is σᵢ². Assume the result holds for j. Then Cov(Xᵢ, Xⱼ₊₁) = Cov(Xᵢ, βⱼXⱼ + Uⱼ₊₁) = βⱼ Cov(Xᵢ, Xⱼ), because Uⱼ₊₁ is independent of Xᵢ. Substituting the induction hypothesis gives the product form. Non-negativity follows from βₖ ≥ 0, and strictness from Proposition 1.

The covariance between distant stages decays with the product of the couplings between them. A single interface with β close to zero therefore cuts propagation for every stage downstream of it, which is the formal sense in which one buffer can protect an entire pathway; in the terms of the theory of complex systems, a weakly coupled interface makes the pathway nearly decomposable (Perrow, 1984; Simon, 1962).

3.4. Mechanism 2: common shocks from shared occupancy

▶ Explore this in the simulator: Pathway →

Stages also slow down together when the hospital is busy, even if no delay passes directly between them (Asplin et al., 2003; McManus et al., 2003). Let ρ be occupancy at the time of the patient's stay, and let

Xᵢ = gᵢ(ρ) Vᵢ (5)

where each gᵢ is non-decreasing and the Vᵢ are mutually independent, independent of ρ, and have mean vᵢ > 0.

Proposition 3. Under common shocks, Cov(Xᵢ, Xⱼ) = vᵢvⱼ Cov(gᵢ(ρ), gⱼ(ρ)) ≥ 0, so that C ≥ 1 even without direct propagation.

By independence, E[XᵢXⱼ] = vᵢvⱼ E[gᵢ(ρ)gⱼ(ρ)] and E[Xᵢ] = vᵢ E[gᵢ(ρ)]. Hence Cov(Xᵢ, Xⱼ) = vᵢvⱼ Cov(gᵢ(ρ), gⱼ(ρ)). Two non-decreasing functions of the same random variable have non-negative covariance by Chebyshev's association inequality (Grimmett & Stirzaker, 2001).

The distinction matters for identification. A positive correlation between stage times does not by itself show that delay passes between teams; it may instead reflect a busy hospital slowing every team at once. Figure 7 sets the two mechanisms side by side, and Section 5.5 sets out how the empirical design separates them.

3.5. Occupancy and interface delay

▶ Explore this in the simulator: Scenario lab →

Following Kingman's (1961) heavy-traffic approximation, the expected delay at interface i given occupancy ρ is approximated by

E[hᵢ | ρ] ≈ κᵢ · ρ / (1 − ρ), κᵢ = [(c²ₐ,ᵢ + c²ₛ,ᵢ) / 2] · τᵢ (6)

where cₐ and cₛ are the coefficients of variation of arrivals and service at the receiving unit and τᵢ is its mean service time. The receiving unit differs by interface, from the emergency department at S1 and S2 to the laboratory at S3 and the ICU at S5; Section 5.4 identifies it at each interface and gives the measure of occupancy used in the empirical study.

Figure 7. Anatomy of an interface. Panel A splits one handover, here from sample to NAC (S3–S4), into information latency L, the time until the result exists, and reaction time R, the time from the result to action; minutes lost are reaction time in excess of the protocol target. Panel B shows the two ways delay spreads: direct propagation through the coupling βᵢ between successive reaction times (Section 3.3), and common shocks from shared occupancy ρ, which slow every interface at once (Section 3.4). Conceptual illustration of the model; no data are shown.

Proposition 4. Expected interface delay is increasing and strictly convex in occupancy. Consequently, (a) a given rise in occupancy costs more delay the fuller the unit already is, and (b) fluctuating occupancy produces a higher mean delay than constant occupancy at the same average.

The first derivative is κᵢ/(1 − ρ)² > 0 and the second is 2κᵢ/(1 − ρ)³ > 0 on 0 ≤ ρ < 1. Part (b) follows from Jensen's inequality applied to a convex function (Grimmett & Stirzaker, 2001).

The model therefore predicts not a sharp discontinuity but a rapidly steepening curve that behaves like a tipping point in data, as simulation models of bed occupancy suggest (Bagust et al., 1999).

3.6. The race against the window

▶ Explore this in the simulator: Arrival & liver clock →

The probability of missing the window is P(S > W). Assuming that A is independent of in-hospital time T,

σ²_S = σ²_A + C · Σᵢ σᵢ², μ_S = μ_A + μ_T (7)

and, under a normal approximation,

P(miss) ≈ 1 − Φ[(W − μ_S) / √(σ²_A + C · Σᵢ σᵢ²)] (8)

Stage times are typically right-skewed, so the normal form is a device for reasoning rather than an estimator. A distribution-free counterpart follows from Cantelli's inequality (Grimmett & Stirzaker, 2001): for W > μ_S,

P(miss) ≤ σ²_S / [σ²_S + (W − μ_S)²] (9)

Proposition 5. Holding μ_S and the stage variances fixed, (a) if μ_S < W, the approximate miss probability and the Cantelli bound are both strictly increasing in C; and (b) if μ_S > W, the approximate miss probability is strictly decreasing in C.

σ_S is strictly increasing in C. In (a) the argument (W − μ_S)/σ_S is positive and decreasing in σ_S, so that 1 − Φ of it increases; the Cantelli bound σ²/(σ² + t²) is increasing in σ² for fixed t > 0. In (b) the argument is negative and rises towards zero as σ_S grows, so that 1 − Φ of it decreases.

Part (a) is the practically relevant case: a pathway whose average meets the window can still miss it for many patients if its interfaces amplify variability. Two pathways with the same mean can therefore have different miss rates, and mean-based performance targets will misrank them. Part (b) is a qualification: when the average is already too slow, variability is not the main problem.

Figure 8 plots both expressions. With σ²_A set to zero, a pathway whose mean leaves a margin of two independent-stage standard deviations misses the window for about 2% of patients when stages are independent (C = 1) but for about 7% at C = 1.85, the value in the main simulation, while the Cantelli bound rises from 20% to about 32%. The reversal in part (b) appears only when the margin is negative. Setting σ²_A to zero isolates the contribution of the interfaces: a non-zero σ²_A raises the miss probability at any positive margin and dilutes the effect of C on σ_S, because C then scales only part of the total variance.

Figure 8. Probability of missing the window as a function of the containment ratio C, from equations (8) and (9). Solid curves show the normal approximation for safety margins m = (W − μ_S) / √(Σᵢ σᵢ²), in units of the independent-stage standard deviation, with σ²_A set to zero so that P(miss) ≈ 1 − Φ(m / √C); the dashed curve is the Cantelli bound for m = 2.0, C / (C + m²). For positive margins the miss probability rises with C (Proposition 5(a)); for m = −0.5, where μ_S > W, it falls (Proposition 5(b)). The dotted line marks C = 1.85, the value in the main simulation (Section 4.1). Analytic illustration of the model; no data are shown.

3.7. The weak-signal decision and the treat-first rule

▶ Explore this in the simulator: Decisions at each pause →

At recognition, staff must often decide whether to start NAC before laboratory results are available, and the hospital protocol specifies the circumstances in which this is done (Chiew et al., 2020). Let p be the probability, given the information available, that treatment is needed; let c_U be the cost of treatment that turns out to be unnecessary, and c_D(Δ) the cost of delaying needed treatment by Δ, with c_D increasing. Waiting adds Δ = X₂ + X₃, the sampling and laboratory interval, whose turnaround is itself variable and is commonly monitored by its 90th-percentile completion time (Hawkins, 2007).

Proposition 6. Treating before results minimises expected cost if and only if

p > p* = c_U / (c_U + E[c_D(Δ)]) (10)

and, if c_D is convex, p* falls when Δ undergoes a mean-preserving spread (Rothschild & Stiglitz, 1970).

Treating now costs (1 − p)c_U in expectation, and waiting costs p · E[c_D(Δ)]. Rearranging p · E[c_D(Δ)] > (1 − p)c_U gives the threshold. For convex c_D, a mean-preserving spread of Δ raises E[c_D(Δ)] by Jensen's inequality, which lowers p*.

The decision threshold is therefore not purely clinical: it depends on how well the laboratory interface performs, and slow or unreliable interfaces justify treating earlier on weaker evidence. This connects the model to the calibration of decision thresholds under asymmetric error costs (Cu, 2026; Pauker & Kassirer, 1980).

Figure 9 illustrates Proposition 6 with arbitrary cost units, setting c_U = 1 and a convex cost of delay proportional to Δ². For a predictable laboratory, with a coefficient of variation of 0.3, the threshold probability p* above which treating first minimises expected cost falls from about 0.88 at a mean wait of 30 minutes to about 0.10 at 240 minutes. For a variable laboratory with the same mean wait and a coefficient of variation of 0.9, which is a mean-preserving spread of Δ, p* is lower at every mean wait. The figure is a conceptual illustration of the decision structure, not a clinical threshold.

Figure 9. Threshold probability p* above which treating before laboratory results minimises expected cost, as a function of the mean wait for the laboratory result, for a predictable laboratory (coefficient of variation 0.3) and a variable laboratory (0.9) with the same mean. Conceptual illustration with arbitrary cost units (c_U = 1, c_D(Δ) ∝ Δ²); not a clinical threshold. The structure parallels the calibration of decision thresholds under asymmetric error costs (Cu, 2026; Pauker & Kassirer, 1980).

Proposition 7. For an eligible patient, a treat-first rule replaces time to NAC, X₁ + X₂ + X₃ + X₄, by X₁ + X̃₄, where X̃₄ is a preparation time independent of the laboratory. The variance removed equals

Var(X₂ + X₃) + 2Cov(X₁, X₂ + X₃) + 2Cov(X₂ + X₃, X₄) + [Var(X₄) − Var(X̃₄)] + 2[Cov(X₁, X₄) − Cov(X₁, X̃₄)] (11)

Expand Var(X₁ + X₂ + X₃ + X₄) − Var(X₁ + X̃₄) and collect terms, noting that Var(X₂ + X₃) = Var(X₂) + Var(X₃) + 2Cov(X₂, X₃), so that the covariance between the sampling and laboratory stages is included in the first term.

When propagation runs through the laboratory interface, the treat-first rule removes not only that interface's own variance but also the covariance terms that carry delay through it. It is a designed buffer that sets the effective coupling at that interface to zero, in the sense in which buffers protect flow lines from upstream variability (Hopp & Spearman, 2008).

3.8. Model summary and hypotheses

▶ Explore this in the simulator: Research design: hypotheses tested live →

Table 4 summarises how each element of the model maps to a measurable quantity and a testable implication. Five primary hypotheses follow, each paired with the quantity that tests it, together with a sub-hypothesis, H3a, that refines H3 at the bag-change interface S4b. Each is stated as a directional alternative to a null of no effect (for H2, H₀: βᵢ = 0 against H₁: βᵢ > 0, conditional on occupancy), and its test and decision quantity are fixed in the pre-registered analysis plan before data are examined (Nosek et al., 2018). H1 to H5 are the primary hypotheses; H3a and the subgroup, root-cause and outcome analyses of Section 5.5 are secondary and are reported as exploratory. Because several hypotheses are tested on the same data, inference emphasises effect sizes with clustered bootstrap intervals rather than a fixed significance threshold (Cu, 2026; Efron & Tibshirani, 1993).

Table 4. Elements of the model, the quantity each introduces and its testable implication.

Model element Quantity Testable implication
Pathway clock Xᵢ = dᵢ + hᵢ Interface delays hᵢ are a large share of T
Latency and reaction Lᵢ, Rᵢ, minutes lost Reaction time accounts for more minutes lost than latency
Direct propagation βᵢ Delay at one interface predicts delay at the next, conditional on occupancy
Common shocks gᵢ(ρ) Stage times co-move with occupancy
Occupancy ρ/(1 − ρ) Interface delay steepens at high occupancy
Seam collision S4b reaction time × shift or transfer overlap Bag changes that coincide with a shift handover or a transfer wait longer (H3a)
Race C, σ_S, P(miss) Variability explains misses beyond the mean
Weak-signal decision p*, treat-first Treat-first weakens propagation from early delays

H1 (interfaces dominate). Interface delays hᵢ account for a larger share of the variance of in-hospital time T than within-step durations dᵢ, and reaction time Rᵢ accounts for more minutes lost than information latency Lᵢ. Test: a variance decomposition of T into its d and h components, and a decomposition of minutes lost into Lᵢ and Rᵢ at each interface.

H2 (early interfaces propagate). Conditional on occupancy, delay at the recognition interface S1 predicts delay at subsequent interfaces, with coupling β₁ > 0, and coupling at later interfaces is smaller. Test: lagged regressions of hᵢ₊₁ on hᵢ with occupancy controls (Proposition 2 against Proposition 3).

H3 (occupancy and conditions steepen delay). Interface delays and reaction times rise convexly with the occupancy of the receiving unit, are longer at night, at weekends and near shift changes, and rise most sharply at the ICU admission interface S5, where congestion is known to alter admission and discharge decisions (KC & Terwiesch, 2012). Test: spline or ρ/(1 − ρ) terms for occupancy, with time-of-day and weekday terms (Proposition 4).

H3a (seam collisions at S4b). A bag change whose scheduled time coincides with a shift handover or with a transfer between units is a compound seam, at which two interfaces fall at once, and its reaction time is longer than that of a bag change that coincides with neither, and longest when both coincide. This sharpens the association that Bailey et al. (2016) report between bag-change delays, handovers between teams and shifts, and moves between departments. Test: reaction time at each S4b interface regressed on indicators for a shift collision, a transfer collision and both, conditional on the occupancy of the unit where the patient is at the bag change.

H4 (treat-first buffers). For patients eligible for treatment before results, the association between early delay and time to NAC is weaker than for patients treated after results. Test: an interaction between treat-first status and S1 delay in models of time to NAC (Propositions 6 and 7). A second test uses S4b: a change from a three-bag to a two-bag regimen removes one bag-change interface, and the model predicts that cumulative delay during the infusion falls accordingly, as the before-and-after evidence suggests (O'Callaghan et al., 2022); Section 5.5 shows how removing a bag change also reduces exposure to shift-handover collisions.

H5 (variability explains misses beyond the mean). A model using μ_S alone under-predicts the observed proportion of patients who miss the window, and adding σ_S, C and the 90th percentile of reaction times improves prediction beyond the median. Test: predicted against observed miss proportions under nested models (Proposition 5).

H2 and H3 jointly address the identification problem of Section 3.4. Propagation (H2) predicts that delay passes between interfaces even at fixed occupancy, whereas common shocks predict that the association disappears once occupancy is controlled.

3.9. Simulation design

▶ Explore this in the simulator: Code & equations →

The simulation follows the front end of the pathway, from arrival to the start of NAC, through four stages corresponding to interfaces S1 to S4. Each stage time is a within-step duration plus an interface delay:

Xᵢ = dᵢ + g(ρ) Vᵢ + β hᵢ₋₁, g(ρ) = 1 + k · ρ / (1 − ρ) (12)

This combines both mechanisms of the model: a shared occupancy load g(ρ), which generates common shocks (Proposition 3), and a direct coupling β, which generates propagation (Proposition 2). Durations are log-normal, reflecting the right skew typical of hospital service times (Armony et al., 2015; Brown et al., 2005). The treat-first policy removes stages 2 and 3 from the clock and adds a preparation stage after recognition (Proposition 7); it is applied to all patients as a bounding case, although in practice only eligible patients are treated first. Table 5 lists the parameters. They are chosen to be plausible in shape and are not estimates of any real hospital. The specification of the simulation's aims, data-generating mechanism and Monte Carlo error follows general guidance on simulation studies (Morris et al., 2019).

A counterfactual analysis asks which interface to improve first. Holding all other parameters fixed, one feature at a time is changed: the delay at a single interface is halved, coupling is set to zero, mean occupancy is lowered, or the treat-first rule is applied, and the resulting fall in the share of patients missing the window is recorded. Ranking the interfaces by this fall identifies the binding constraint of the pathway, in the sense of the theory of constraints, and the ranking is reported as a tornado chart (Section 4.5).

Table 5. Simulation parameters. All values are illustrative; the empirical study takes the treatment window and stage distributions from the participating hospital.

Parameter Value Note
Patients per scenario 120,000 to 300,000 Monte Carlo draws
Window W 480 minutes Illustrative; the empirical study takes W from the local protocol
Pre-hospital time A Log-normal, median 120 min 1.0% of patients arrive after W
Within-step medians dᵢ 8, 8, 40, 12 min Stage 3 is laboratory processing
Interface delay medians Vᵢ 8, 6, 10, 10 min Log-normal, σ = 0.6
Occupancy ρ Beta, mean 0.70 to 0.94, sd 0.05 Drawn per patient
Load sensitivity k 0.25 Kingman-type load factor
Coupling β 0, 0.15 to 0.6 0.3 in the main scenario

4. Simulation results

The simulation yields three main results. First, shared occupancy and direct coupling are separable sources of amplification, and together they nearly double the share of patients who miss the window while the mean rises far less. Second, the treat-first rule shifts the whole occupancy curve down and to the right. Third, two pathways with the same mean time can carry very different risks depending on when patients arrive, so that average-based metrics misrank them. The simulation illustrates the propositions; its parameters are not estimates of any real hospital.

4.1. Mechanisms of amplification

▶ Explore this in the simulator: Coupling extensions →

At a mean occupancy of 0.85, the three scenarios of Table 6 and Figure 10 differ markedly. Shared occupancy alone raises C to 1.37, confirming Proposition 3: stages can co-move without any delay passing between them. Adding direct coupling raises C to 1.85 and the 90th percentile by more than an hour relative to independent stages. The miss rate nearly doubles, from 6.3% to 11.6%, while the mean rises by only 36 minutes: variability, and not only the average, drives misses.

Table 6. Containment ratio, in-hospital time and missed-window rate under three mechanisms of amplification, at mean occupancy 0.85 (200,000 patients per scenario).

Scenario C Mean T (min) SD T (min) 90th pct. (min) Missed window
Independent stages, fixed occupancy 1.00 171 36 217 6.3%
Shared occupancy (common shocks) 1.37 179 50 242 7.9%
Shared occupancy and coupling β = 0.3 1.85 207 63 284 11.6%

Figure 10. Two mechanisms of amplification at a mean occupancy of 0.85. Shared occupancy alone (common shocks) raises the containment ratio C above 1, and adding direct coupling (β = 0.3) raises it further and nearly doubles the share of patients missing the window. Illustrative Monte Carlo simulation, 200,000 patients per scenario.

The two mechanisms leave different signatures in the correlations between interface times (Figure 11). With independent stages every off-diagonal correlation is zero. Shared occupancy produces small and nearly uniform correlations, between 0.12 and 0.14 for every pair, because a busy hospital slows all stages alike (Proposition 3). Adding direct coupling produces a different pattern: correlations are highest between adjacent interfaces (0.47 between S1 and S2, 0.32 between S2 and S3, 0.39 between S3 and S4) and decline with distance (0.20 between S1 and S3, 0.19 between S1 and S4), as the product form of Proposition 2 implies. A uniform pattern points to common shocks and a pattern that decays with distance points to propagation, which is the contrast the empirical test of H2 exploits.

Figure 11. Correlations between interface times S1–S4 under independent stages, shared occupancy alone, and shared occupancy with coupling β = 0.3. The off-diagonal values are what the containment ratio C sums. Illustrative Monte Carlo simulation, mean occupancy 0.85 (parameters of Table 5); the figure shows mechanism, not estimates for any hospital.

Varying the coupling shows how amplification scales (Figure 12). As β rises from 0 to 0.8 at a mean occupancy of 0.85, the containment ratio rises almost linearly, from 1.37 to 2.64, while the share of patients missing the window rises convexly, from 7.6% to 27.0%. Each further increment of coupling therefore costs more missed windows than the last, because the tail of total time grows faster than its variance, which is the behaviour Proposition 5 predicts for a pathway whose mean lies inside the window.

Figure 12. Containment ratio C and share of patients missing the window as functions of the coupling β between interfaces, at a mean occupancy of 0.85. Illustrative Monte Carlo simulation (parameters of Table 5); the figure shows mechanism, not estimates for any hospital. The sweep is a separate simulation run from Table 6 and Figure 10, so values at β = 0 and β = 0.3 differ slightly from those reported there (7.6% against 7.9%, and about 11.3% against 11.6%) because of Monte Carlo variation.

4.2. Occupancy and the treat-first buffer

▶ Explore this in the simulator: Scenario lab →

Under the wait-for-results policy, the miss rate rises slowly up to an occupancy of about 0.80 and then steepens sharply, as Proposition 4 predicts (Figure 13) and as earlier models of bed occupancy suggest (Bagust et al., 1999). The containment ratio rises with it, from 1.37 at 0.70 to 2.66 at 0.92, because high occupancy both slows every stage and strengthens their co-movement.

The treat-first policy shifts the whole curve down and to the right. It removes the laboratory interface from the clock, and with it both that interface's variance and the covariance it carried (Proposition 7); its containment ratio stays between 1.21 and 1.55, and it holds the miss rate below 6% up to 90% mean occupancy, against 28% without it. The direction of this effect is consistent with before-and-after evidence that redesigning an interface shortens delays (O'Callaghan et al., 2022; Pettie et al., 2012), although that evidence does not isolate the mechanism. The buffer does not make the pathway immune to crowding, however: at 0.94 occupancy it still misses 21.6% of patients.

Figure 13. Share of patients missing the treatment window as a function of the mean occupancy of receiving units, under the wait-for-results and treat-first policies (coupling β = 0.3). Missed windows climb steeply above 80% occupancy; treat-first shifts the whole curve down and to the right but does not make the pathway immune to crowding. Illustrative Monte Carlo simulation, 120,000 patients per point (parameters of Table 5).

The treat-first rule changes the shape of the distribution as well as its centre (Figure 14). At a mean occupancy of 0.85, time from arrival to the start of NAC has a median of 195 minutes and a 90th percentile of 283 minutes under the wait-for-results policy, against 78 and 131 minutes under treat-first. The rule therefore shortens the median by 117 minutes but the 90th percentile by 152 minutes, and narrows the gap between the two from 88 to 53 minutes. It compresses the upper tail, where windows are missed, more than the centre, which is why the median alone understates its value and why H5 is tested on the 90th percentile.

Figure 14. Cumulative distribution of time from arrival to the start of NAC under the wait-for-results and treat-first policies, with the median and 90th percentile marked. A median hides the slowest tenth of patients, which is where treatment windows are missed. Illustrative Monte Carlo simulation, mean occupancy 0.85 (parameters of Table 5); the figure shows mechanism, not estimates for any hospital.

Figure 15 shows what the two policies mean for an individual patient, using the median stage times of Table 5 for an early presenter (pre-hospital time A = 2 hours) and a late presenter (A = 6 hours). Waiting for results leaves the early presenter about 1.7 hours after recognition before the paracetamol level can be interpreted at 4 hours. This wait is set by the biology rather than by the laboratory, so it is information latency that would remain even with instant laboratory turnaround. The late presenter who waits for results starts NAC at 7 hours 42 minutes, 18 minutes inside an illustrative 8-hour window; at median timings almost no slack remains, so any delay in the tail produces a miss. Under treat-first, NAC starts about 40 minutes after arrival in both cases, and bloods are still taken but no longer hold up treatment.

Figure 15. The front end hour by hour for an early presenter (A = 2 hours) and a late presenter (A = 6 hours), under the wait-for-results and treat-first policies. For the early presenter, waiting for results includes a wait for the 4-hour level that comes from the biology, not the laboratory; the late presenter who waits starts NAC 18 minutes inside the illustrative window. Under treat-first, bloods are still taken but no longer hold up treatment. Deterministic illustration built from the median stage times of Table 5 rather than from the simulation, so its times need not match the simulated distributions of Figure 14; W = 8 hours is illustrative and not a clinical recommendation.

4.3. When variability matters

▶ Explore this in the simulator: Uncertainty →

To isolate the effect of amplification from the effect of speed, two pathways were rescaled to the same mean in-hospital time of 200 minutes. One has independent stages (C = 1.00, SD 42 minutes); the other has shared occupancy and coupling β = 0.6 (C = 2.36, SD 65 minutes). Their overall miss rates are similar, at 9.2% and 10.8%, but their miss rates by arrival time are not (Figure 16).

For patients who arrive early enough that the remaining time exceeds the mean pathway time, the amplifying pathway misses the window more often in every band: 12.0% against 6.4% for arrivals three to four hours after ingestion, and 4.0% against 1.0% for arrivals two to three hours after. For patients who arrive too late for the average pathway to succeed, the ranking reverses, because variability gives some of them a chance. The crossover falls close to where the remaining time equals the mean in-hospital time, as Proposition 5 predicts; the small offset reflects the skew of stage times, which the normal approximation ignores. An aggregate miss rate or average door-to-NAC time, of the kind reported in national audit (Royal College of Emergency Medicine, 2014), therefore cannot distinguish the two pathways, and performance must be assessed conditional on time since ingestion, which the empirical design does.

Figure 16. Share of patients missing the window by time from ingestion to arrival for two pathways with the same mean in-hospital time of 200 minutes, one with independent stages (C = 1.00) and one with amplifying interfaces (C = 2.36). The dotted line marks where remaining time equals mean pathway time. Illustrative Monte Carlo simulation, 300,000 patients per pathway, mean occupancy 0.85.

4.4. What the simulation does and does not show

▶ Explore this in the simulator: Validation →

The simulation confirms that the propositions hold for skewed, realistically shaped distributions, and it gives a sense of the magnitudes involved. It supports H3, H4 and H5 in principle, and it shows why H2 requires conditioning on occupancy. It does not estimate any real effect: the parameters are illustrative, the treat-first rule is applied universally, the stages are not split into information latency and reaction time, and the back end of the pathway, from ICU admission to transfer, is not simulated. Section 5 sets out how each hypothesis is tested with data.

Figure 17 tests whether the main result depends on the illustrative values of Table 5. Varying one parameter at a time across a plausible range, the amplification effect, the extra share of patients missing the window under shared occupancy and coupling compared with independent stages, stays positive throughout, between 2.1 and 17.6 percentage points around a baseline of 5.3. Mean occupancy moves the effect most, followed by load sensitivity and the interface delay medians, while the within-step spread barely moves it at all, which is consistent with the claim that the seams, not the steps, carry the risk.

Figure 17. Sensitivity of the amplification effect to the simulation parameters. The effect is the share of patients missing the window under shared occupancy and coupling (β = 0.3) minus the share under independent stages at fixed occupancy, in percentage points (baseline 5.0). Each bar varies one parameter between the values shown, holding the others at Table 5. The effect remains positive across every range tested. Illustrative Monte Carlo simulation, 150,000 patients per scenario.

4.5. Counterfactual analysis: prioritising interfaces for improvement

▶ Explore this in the simulator: Bottleneck analysis →

The counterfactual analysis of Section 3.9 changes one feature of the baseline pathway at a time and records the fall in the share of patients missing the window, from a baseline of 11.6% (Figure 18). The treat-first rule, which bypasses S2 and S3, has by far the largest effect, reducing the missed-window share by 8.8 percentage points to 2.7%. Lowering mean occupancy from 0.85 to 0.75 reduces it by 5.6 points (to 6.0%), halving laboratory processing and waiting at S3 by 4.6 points (to 7.0%), and removing coupling between interfaces (β = 0) by 3.6 points (to 7.9%). Halving the delay at a single front-end interface has smaller effects: 2.4 points at S1 (to 9.1%), 2.1 points at S4 (to 9.4%) and 1.8 points at S2 (to 9.8%). Among the single-interface changes, the early recognition interface S1 ranks above the later interfaces S4 and S2, as Proposition 2 implies, but the largest gains come from removing an interface from the clock or from reducing the load on the whole system rather than from speeding up any one step. The ranking illustrates the logic of identifying the binding constraint; with illustrative parameters it is not an estimate for any hospital.

Figure 18. Counterfactual simulation: reduction in the share of patients missing the window when one feature of the baseline pathway (mean occupancy 0.85, coupling β = 0.3; baseline 11.6%) is changed at a time, in percentage points, with the resulting missed-window share in parentheses. Illustrative Monte Carlo simulation, 200,000 patients per scenario; the figure shows mechanism and ranking logic, not estimates for any hospital.

4.6. Work and waiting: process cycle efficiency

▶ Explore this in the simulator: Operations →

Splitting each stage of the simulated front end into within-step work dᵢ and interface delay hᵢ shows where the minutes go (Figure 19). For the median patient at a mean occupancy of 0.85 and coupling of 0.3, the stages from arrival to NAC take 28 minutes at S1, 31 at S2, 73 at S3 and 49 at S4. Work within steps accounts for 68 minutes and waiting at interfaces for 113 minutes, a process cycle efficiency of about 38% (George, 2002). Waiting exceeds work at every interface except S3, where laboratory processing is itself the dominant step, so that in the simulation most of the time to treatment is spent at the seams rather than within the steps, as H1 predicts. Because medians are taken stage by stage, they do not sum exactly to the median total.

Figure 19. Where the minutes go for the median simulated patient from arrival to NAC: within-step work (blue) and waiting at interfaces (orange) at S1–S4, medians per stage summed. Process cycle efficiency is work divided by total time. Illustrative Monte Carlo simulation, mean occupancy 0.85, coupling 0.3.

5. Empirical study design

▶ Explore this in the simulator: Research design: field study →

The hypotheses are tested with a retrospective cohort built from routinely recorded hospital timestamps and analysed with pre-registered models (Nosek et al., 2018). The design is specified in advance so that results cannot shape the analysis.

5.1. Design and setting

The study is a retrospective cohort, framed as an embedded single-case design (Yin, 2018), in one or more hospitals with an emergency department and an intensive care unit, ideally including one hospital that must transfer patients to a transplant centre and one with transplant services on site. Analysis plans are pre-registered before data extraction, and the study is reported following RECORD for routinely collected data (Benchimol et al., 2015), an extension of STROBE (von Elm et al., 2007), STRESS for the simulation (Monks et al., 2019) and COREQ for the interviews (Tong et al., 2007). A clinical co-investigator in emergency medicine or clinical toxicology validates the pathway definition, the local protocol and the interpretation of timestamps. Clinical judgements remain theirs; the study analyses the system's execution of the protocol.

5.2. Population

Two nested cohorts are used, because the front and back ends of the pathway differ greatly in size. The front-end cohort comprises all adult presentations with paracetamol ingestion recorded at triage or in the first clinical note, and it is used to test H1 to H5 on interfaces S1 to S4. The severe cohort is the subset meeting a pre-specified definition agreed with the clinical co-investigator, such as ICU admission for liver injury or meeting local criteria for liver-unit referral (O'Grady et al., 1989), and it is used for interfaces S5 to S8. The definition of severity is fixed before extraction, because it determines which patients enter the back-end analysis.

5.3. Data sources and timestamps

Each timestamp is defined precisely in a data dictionary prepared with the clinical co-investigator, and Table 7 lists the sources from which they are drawn; in the primary case these are the linked tables of MIMIC-IV and MIMIC-IV-ED (Johnson et al., 2023, 2024), as set out in Appendix A. The pre-hospital interval A is computed from the reported ingestion time and recorded separately, with a flag for uncertain or staggered ingestion. Each source is rated for timestamp reliability before analysis (Table A3); electronic system timestamps are preferred over times transcribed into notes, and any trigger or action recorded only by hand is flagged.

Table 7. Routine data sources and the timestamps and variables drawn from each.

Source Timestamps and variables
ED information system Arrival, triage, clinician assessment, disposition
Clinical notes Reported time and pattern of ingestion, first mention of paracetamol
Laboratory information system Sample collected, received, result reported
Pharmacy and medication administration records NAC prescribed, infusion started, regimen
ICU and bed management systems ICU referral, admission; hourly occupancy of ED, wards and ICU
Referral and transfer logs Specialist contact, referral accepted, departure, arrival

5.4. Measures

Eight measures are constructed. Stage and interface times are the Xᵢ, split into dᵢ and hᵢ where the records allow. Each interface time is also split into information latency Lᵢ and reaction time Rᵢ using the trigger and action timestamps of Table 1, and minutes lost are computed against the target the hospital protocol specifies for each interface; all are summarised by their median and 90th percentile rather than their mean. The containment ratio C is estimated from the covariance matrix of stage times, with bootstrap confidence intervals clustered by calendar day (Efron & Tibshirani, 1993; Harrell, 2015). Occupancy ρ is that of the receiving unit at the moment of each handover; Table 8 defines the receiving unit at each interface and the measure of its occupancy or load. Treat-first status records whether NAC started before the first paracetamol result and whether the patient met the protocol's criteria for doing so. A missed window is S > W, with W taken from the local protocol. Two further measures place the pathway in operations terms. A value-stream view splits total time into value-adding time, in assessment and treatment, and waiting time, and reports process cycle efficiency, the ratio of value-adding time to total time (George, 2002). Resource utilisation is estimated for the laboratory, pharmacy, nursing staff and ICU beds from hourly workload and occupancy, because the heavy-traffic logic of Section 3.5 implies that delay rises most steeply at the most heavily utilised resource (Kingman, 1961), which links H3 to specific resources; the proxy for each resource is the occupancy measure of Table 8.

Table 8. Receiving unit and occupancy measure at each interface, with the primary-case source and the resource it proxies.

S5 ICU ICU beds occupied relative to available beds icu.icustays; hosp.transfers ICU beds

Where the capacity of the receiving unit is not recorded, as for the laboratory and pharmacy, load is expressed relative to the unit's own hourly distribution over the study period, so ρ is a relative rather than an absolute utilisation; ICU occupancy uses the number of staffed ICU beds at the participating hospital as the denominator. At S5k and S6–S8, fᵢ(ρ) in equation (13) is replaced by an availability indicator. Field names to be confirmed against the current MIMIC-IV documentation.

5.5. Estimation by hypothesis

H1. Var(T) is decomposed into within-step, interface and covariance components, and minutes lost at each interface are decomposed into latency and reaction; the shares are reported with clustered bootstrap intervals. Median and 90th-percentile Lᵢ and Rᵢ at S1 to S4 will be reported in minutes.

H2 (propagation against common shocks). For each interface i, the model estimated is

hᵢ₊₁,ₖ = αᵢ + βᵢ hᵢ,ₖ + fᵢ(ρᵢ₊₁,ₖ) + λ_hour + λ_day + Zₖ′θ + εᵢ,ₖ (13)

where k indexes patients, fᵢ is a flexible function of occupancy at the receiving unit, the λ are time fixed effects and Z are patient characteristics. Under Proposition 3 alone, βᵢ should be close to zero once occupancy is controlled; under Proposition 2, βᵢ > 0. Conditioning on occupancy does not by itself identify direct propagation, however, because patient severity, staffing decisions and prioritisation can each affect several interfaces at once. Estimates of βᵢ are therefore reported as conditional associations, and are interpreted as propagation only to the extent that the assumptions set out below can be defended. The main threat is unobserved urgency: staff may move faster at every stage for patients who seem sicker, which biases βᵢ in an unknown direction; the power simulation of Section 5.7 shows that it can produce spurious coupling that grows more likely with cohort size. Two strategies address it. The first conditions on recorded severity markers and triage category. The second is a quasi-experimental check using arrivals shortly before a shift handover, which plausibly delays recognition at S1 for reasons unrelated to the patient, in the same spirit as studies that use time of admission as a source of variation in staffing (Bell & Redelmeier, 2001); its exclusion restriction, that shift timing affects later stages only through S1 delay, is examined by testing whether shift timing predicts later delays among patients recognised promptly. This restriction is demanding, because a shift change can also affect later stages directly, for example through the handover of the whole workload, so the check is treated as supporting evidence rather than as identification. It is complemented by a negative-control test: delay at S1 should not predict delay at interfaces it cannot plausibly reach, such as laboratory processing within S3, once occupancy is controlled.

Compensation, load-dependent coupling and sites. Three extensions make the test of H2 fairer. First, propagation has a rival: staff who see that a patient is running late may speed up, so that later stages catch up and C falls below one. Compensation predicts βᵢ < 0, and the test of equation (13) is therefore two-sided, with a negative estimate reported as evidence of compensation rather than discarded. Second, coupling may itself depend on load, because handovers plausibly become leakier when the receiving unit is crowded; an interaction term, replacing βᵢ with βᵢ + γᵢ(ρᵢ₊₁ − ρ̄), tests whether γᵢ > 0, that is, whether the two mechanisms of Sections 3.3 and 3.4 reinforce each other. Third, where data are pooled across hospitals, equation (13) is estimated as a multilevel model with random intercepts and random coupling slopes by site, because hospitals running the same protocol can differ markedly in delay (Bailey et al., 2016), and site differences left in the error term would inflate the apparent propagation.

H3. Each interface delay is modelled against receiving-unit occupancy with restricted cubic splines (Harrell, 2015), and convexity is tested. A breakpoint is estimated by segmented regression (Muggeo, 2003) and its confidence interval is bootstrapped.

H3a. Each scheduled bag change, the previous bag start plus its intended duration (Table A3), is placed on a timeline against the shift handover times in the participating hospital's rota, and against the patient's moves between units recorded in hosp.transfers. A bag change is classified as a shift collision or a transfer collision if its scheduled time falls within a collision window, fixed in the pre-registered analysis plan, of a handover or of a transfer, as both if it falls within that window of each, and as clear otherwise. Reaction time at S4b is modelled on these indicators with the occupancy of the unit where the patient is at the bag change (Table 8), the time fixed effects of equation (13) and standard errors clustered by patient, since a three-bag regimen contributes two bag changes per infusion. Because the bag schedule is fixed by the start of the infusion and the regimen rather than by the state of the ward, whether a bag change falls on a shift handover is plausibly unrelated to the patient's urgency, which makes the shift contrast one of the better identified comparisons in the study. Transfers, by contrast, may be timed around the infusion, so the transfer contrast is reported as an association. The timeline of bag changes against shifts and transfers is also reported descriptively, and sensitivity to the collision window is examined.

Figure 20 shows why the regimen matters for H3a and for the second test of H4. If start times are spread evenly over the day, a bag change falls within 30 minutes of a 12-hour shift handover in about 17% of three-bag infusions but 8% of two-bag infusions, and with 8-hour shifts in 25% and 13%. Removing one bag change roughly halves the exposure to handover collisions, which offers one mechanism consistent with the fall in delays of more than an hour reported after the regimen change (O'Callaghan et al., 2022); the two quantities are not the same measure, and the empirical study tests the mechanism directly.

Figure 20. Exposure of each regimen to shift-handover collisions at S4b. Left: clock times at which starting NAC places a bag change within ±30 minutes of a 12-hour shift handover (orange), for the three-bag (1 h + 4 h + 16 h) and two-bag (4 h + 16 h) regimens. Right: share of infusions with at least one such collision, assuming start times uniform over the day, for 12-hour (08:00 and 20:00) and 8-hour (07:00, 15:00 and 23:00) shift patterns. Handover times, the ±30-minute margin and the uniform start-time distribution are assumptions, to be replaced with the shift handover times in the participating hospital's rota and the observed distribution of start times; the two-bag regimen follows the Australian protocol studied by O'Callaghan et al. (2022). Deterministic illustration; no patient data are shown.

H4. The association between S1 delay and time to NAC is estimated with an interaction for treat-first status. Because eligibility for treat-first correlates with presentation features, the main specification is restricted to patients who met the protocol's treat-first criteria and compares those who were and were not treated first. Where a hospital changed its protocol during the study period, a difference-in-differences comparison before and after the change (Angrist & Pischke, 2009) provides a second estimate, as the regimen change studied by O'Callaghan et al. (2022) and the integrated care pathway evaluated by Pettie et al. (2012) illustrate.

H5. Time to NAC is modelled as a time-to-event outcome with ingestion time as the origin (Cox, 1972). Nested models predicting the missed window (mean only; mean and variance; mean, variance and C) are compared using calibration and Brier scores (Brier, 1950; Harrell, 2015), overall and by arrival band, to test the crossover reported in Section 4.3.

Process reconstruction. Process mining of the event log (Rojas et al., 2016; van der Aalst, 2016) maps the paths patients actually took, including loops such as repeat sampling and skipped steps, and compares them with the protocol's intended pathway.

Root causes. For each interface at which minutes are lost, the missing interface invariant is identified from the process map, the protocol and the event log: time (no fixed point at which the handover happens), format (information that does not travel), capacity (no reserved slack), authority (no one designated to act) or meaning (no shared definition). Bag-change delays at S4b, for example, would point to missing authority, if no one is designated to restart the infusion after a shift change, and to missing time, if there is no fixed check; these are hypotheses to be tested against the records, not findings. This keeps the analysis on coordination rather than on clinical decisions. Figure 21 sets out the candidate causes at each invariant.

Figure 21. Root causes of interface delay organised by the five interface invariants (fishbone diagram). Each branch is an invariant and each bone a documented or plausible cause. Causes marked ¹ are reported as contributing causes by Bailey et al. (2016); the others are plausible causes drawn from the pathway and operations literature, to be tested in the interviews and the event log. The diagram is used to code the interviews and to trace each bottleneck to what is missing at the seam.

Figure 22. Interface × invariant matrix: which of the five interface invariants is likely to be missing at each interface, including the kidney branch S5k. Rows are the interfaces of Table 1 and columns the invariants of Figure 21. Dark red cells mark contributing causes reported by Bailey et al. (2016), both at the bag-change interface S4b; all other cells are hypotheses drawn from the pathway and operations literature, graded as the main hypothesis, possible or not expected, and are to be tested against the event log and the staff interviews. Where the fishbone organises candidate causes by invariant, the matrix assigns them to interfaces, and it serves as the interview guide and coding frame. Conceptual illustration; no data are shown.

Staff interviews. To explain the bottlenecks that the timestamps reveal, semi-structured interviews are held with about 10 to 15 staff across the emergency department, pharmacy, laboratory and ICU, sampled to cover each interface and each shift pattern. Interviews follow the five interface invariants defined under Root causes above, using the matrix of Figure 22 as the interview guide, and ask at each handover when it happens, what information travels, what slack is reserved, who decides and how terms are defined, and they are analysed thematically against the quantitative results. The design is therefore mixed methods: the event log locates where minutes are lost, and the interviews explain why (Braun & Clarke, 2006; Creswell & Plano Clark, 2018).

Link from delay to outcome (exploratory). With the clinical co-investigator, the study examines whether longer time from ingestion to NAC is associated with ICU admission or with rising liver tests. Because this is a clinical question, the outcome definitions, the adjustment for severity at presentation and the interpretation of any association are the co-investigator's, and the analysis is reported as exploratory and associational. It is included only to indicate whether the minutes the study measures plausibly matter for patients, not to make a clinical claim.

Subgroups. Reaction times and propagation are compared between intentional and accidental or supratherapeutic overdose, single and staggered ingestion, arrival at night or at weekends and on weekdays, and arrival near a shift change. Published evidence already shows that atypical presentations wait longer (Bailey et al., 2016), and these are the patients for whom the danger is most hidden.

Equity and the patient as a seam. Hidden danger is likely to fall hardest on patients who cannot give a clear history, including those with limited English, those who are intoxicated or homeless, and older adults with accidental overdose. Reaction times at S1 to S4 are therefore also compared by insurance type and preferred language, recorded in hosp.admissions, as proxies for deprivation and communication barriers, and referral patterns at S6 and S7 are compared in the same way, extending the association with deprivation reported by Newsome et al. (2001). The patient can also be a seam: leaving before the infusion is complete, often around the mental health assessment, ends the pathway at an interface (S4m in Table 1). Self-discharge before the last scheduled bag, identified from discharge against medical advice and the infusion record, is reported by interface and presentation type as a descriptive outcome, since it lies outside the model of Section 3.

Figure 23 shows why these subgroups are expected to differ. Each type of presentation puts a different set of interfaces on the clock to the start of NAC: early single ingestions wait for the four-hour level, late, staggered and unknown-time presentations are treated before results so that S2 and S3 come off the clock (Proposition 7), and accidental and staggered presentations weaken the trigger at S1. Subgroup contrasts therefore test whether propagation and reaction time differ where the protocol routes patients differently.

Figure 23. Interfaces on the clock to the start of NAC by type of presentation. Early single ingestions wait for the four-hour level; late, staggered and unknown-time presentations are treated before results, taking S2 and S3 off the clock (Proposition 7); accidental and staggered presentations weaken the trigger at S1. Routes are from published guidance (Chiew et al., 2020; Commission on Human Medicines/MHRA, 2012) and follow the local protocol in the empirical study.

Sensitivity analyses. Key results are re-estimated under alternative definitions of the severe cohort, alternative values of the window W within the range the hospital protocol allows, and with presentations of uncertain or staggered ingestion time excluded, so that conclusions do not rest on any single analytic choice.

Calibration against published benchmarks. As a face-validity check on the simulation, the simulated distribution of cumulative delay during the infusion is compared with the distribution reported by Bailey et al. (2016) (Table A2) before the empirical results are interpreted. Fitting each bag-change delay as log-normal from its published median and interquartile range and joining them with a correlation r, no value of r reproduces the published cumulative delay: the median matches at r ≈ 0.5, but the modelled upper quartile remains between 197 and 214 minutes against 163 minutes reported. The published summaries are therefore consistent with C close to 1 and cannot identify propagation between bag changes; only patient-level timestamps can. The simulation parameters are then re-estimated from the cohort, and Section 4 is re-run with the estimated values.

5.6. Data quality and missing data

Timestamps are checked for impossible orderings, implausible intervals and default times such as midnight entries. Missing timestamps are handled by multiple imputation under a missing-at-random assumption (Harrell, 2015; Sterne et al., 2009), with sensitivity analyses that exclude imputed records. Reported ingestion times are uncertain by nature, so analyses using A are repeated with uncertainty bands. The share of missing, implausible and default timestamps is reported for each interface, so that readers can judge where measurement is weakest.

5.7. Sample size

▶ Explore this in the simulator: H2 power →

Front-end analyses can draw on several years of presentations. The severe cohort is much smaller, so back-end analyses are planned as descriptive and estimation-focused, reporting effect sizes with intervals rather than relying on significance tests, whose fixed thresholds are poorly suited to small samples with asymmetric error costs (Cu, 2026). For the front end, the required size was estimated by simulation (Figure 24). Cohorts of size N were generated from the model of Section 3.9 with the parameters of Table 5, equation (13) was fitted with occupancy controlled, and the share of studies in which β was detected was recorded. Without unobserved confounding, about 100 patients detect a coupling of β = 0.3 and 200 to 400 detect β = 0.15, while the false-positive rate stays near the nominal 5%. The same simulation shows why the identification checks of Section 5.5 are needed: an unobserved urgency factor that speeds every stage for sicker-seeming patients produces apparent coupling where none exists, and larger cohorts make this spurious result more, not less, likely. Precision alone therefore does not secure H2; the negative-control and shift-handover checks do. Pooling across hospitals or years remains the route to adequate precision for the back end.

Figure 24. Power to detect coupling between the recognition and sampling interfaces (H2), by cohort size, from equation (13) with occupancy controlled. Panel A: with no unobserved confounding, β = 0.3 is detected in about 95% of studies at 100 patients and β = 0.15 in 84% at 200, while the false-positive rate stays near 5%. Panel B: an unobserved urgency factor (log-sd 0.3) biases β̂ upward by about 0.13, so that with no true coupling the test rejects β = 0 in 63% of studies at 200 patients and 99% at 800. One-sided test at 5%, 1,000 replications per point, timestamp noise sd 2 minutes. Illustrative simulation; parameters as in Table 5.

5.8. Ethics and data governance

The study requires ethics approval and data-governance agreements at each site. Data are extracted and de-identified by the hospital before analysis, with dates shifted where required, and no patients are contacted. Because many presentations involve intentional overdose (Bailey et al., 2016), results are reported only in aggregate and small cells are suppressed. Interview participants give written informed consent, are not identified in any output, and may withdraw at any time.

6. Discussion and conclusions

The central implication is that a time-critical pathway should be managed for its variability and its interfaces, not only for its average speed. If the hypotheses hold, the same mean door-to-treatment time can conceal very different risks of missing the window, and the risk is concentrated among exactly those patients for whom the average pathway would have been fast enough.

Figure 25 summarises the status of each hypothesis. All five follow from the propositions of Section 3, and the simulation of Section 4 illustrates their mechanisms within the limits set out in Section 4.4. Published evidence is strong only for H4, through the before-and-after evaluations of the treat-first pathway and the regimen change (O'Callaghan et al., 2022; Pettie et al., 2012). It is partial for H1, indirect for H5, and drawn from other time-critical pathways for H3. For H2, the propagation of delay between interfaces, there is no published evidence for this pathway, which is the central gap the empirical study is designed to fill.

Figure 25. Hypotheses H1–H5 and the evidence behind each: the proposition from which each follows, whether the simulation reproduces it, the strength of published support, and where each will be tested empirically. Green denotes strong published support, amber partial or indirect support, and grey no evidence yet (a research gap); blue denotes results shown in the model and simulation. The sub-hypothesis H3a (Section 3.8) is not shown separately.

6.1. Implications for practice

▶ Explore this in the simulator: Risk management →

The model points to five levers, each acting on a specific term. The first is to cut coupling at early interfaces. Because covariance decays with the product of couplings (Proposition 2), one well-buffered early interface protects every later stage; treat-before-results rules, pre-filled order sets triggered at triage and default escalation when ingestion time is uncertain all reduce β at the front of the pathway, as the integrated care pathway evaluated by Pettie et al. (2012) did. The second is to manage occupancy at receiving units. Interface delay is convex in occupancy (Proposition 4), so reserved capacity in intensive care and fast access to laboratory processing do most good exactly when the hospital is busiest (Bagust et al., 1999; Litvak & Fineberg, 2013).

The third lever is to measure variability conditional on time since ingestion. Averages misrank pathways (Proposition 5), and reporting the 90th percentile of time to NAC and the minutes lost at each interface, together with miss rates by arrival band, would reveal amplification that averages hide. The fourth is to fix interface invariants. Each handover can be specified by five invariants: time (when it happens), format (what information travels), capacity (what slack is reserved), authority (who decides on escalation) and meaning (shared definitions, such as of severity), and coordination failures can be traced to the invariant that is missing (Arora et al., 2005; Gittell et al., 2000; Patterson et al., 2004). The fifth is to align decision thresholds with interface performance. The optimal threshold for treating before results depends on how slow and variable the laboratory interface is (Proposition 6; Pauker & Kassirer, 1980), and protocols could make this dependence explicit, for example by widening treat-first criteria where laboratory turnaround is known to be long.

The levers can also be read economically, although only qualitatively in the absence of cost data. A minute saved early in the pathway is worth more than a minute saved late, because early delay is carried forward by coupling and spends the part of the window in which treatment works best. The costs that follow from delay include intensive-care days, repeat blood tests, additional infusion bags and transfers between hospitals, while the costs of the levers are mainly staff time, reserved capacity and the treatments started before results that turn out to be unnecessary, which is the trade-off Proposition 6 formalises. Where cost data become available, the counterfactual analysis of Section 4.5 can be extended to rank interfaces by expected cost saved rather than by minutes saved, and the cost per minute of delay at each interface reported.

6.2. Implications for theory

The study tests a general claim: that interconnected systems fail less from variability within their parts than from the transmission of variability across their interfaces (Perrow, 1984; Simon, 1962). The paracetamol pathway is a demanding test of that claim because the danger is hidden, so that the system cannot rely on visible deterioration to prompt action and must act through procedure, with the defences against error that procedures provide (Reason, 2000). The model also separates two sources of systemic variance, direct propagation and common shocks, which call for different remedies: propagation calls for buffers at specific interfaces, and common shocks call for capacity management across the whole hospital. Most studies of pathway delay do not distinguish them. Separating information latency from reaction time sharpens the claim further: if reaction time, and not latency, accounts for most minutes lost (H1), variance at the seams is generated by coordination rather than by the information systems that feed it.

The framework builds on, and must be distinguished from, three established bodies of models. Tandem-queue and factory-physics models describe how variability propagates through serial production lines and how buffers protect flow (Hopp & Spearman, 2008; Kingman, 1961); hospital patient-flow models apply the same logic to beds and units (Armony et al., 2015; Hall, 2006); and reliability models of series systems treat a pathway as failing when any component fails. The present framework differs in four respects: its outcome is a deadline whose clinical meaning is hidden at presentation, rather than throughput or mean waiting time; it separates direct propagation from common shocks and specifies how the two are to be told apart empirically; it decomposes each interface into information latency and reaction time; and it treats decision rules such as treat-first as designable buffers whose value can be derived. Table 9 sets out which of the framework's claims are inherited from these models and which are new. Two are inherited: convexity of delay in occupancy follows directly from heavy-traffic queueing (Kingman, 1961) and is well documented for hospital beds (Bagust et al., 1999), and the statement that positive dependence between stages makes C exceed one restates a standard variance identity. The contribution lies in the other four claims, which recombine known elements around a hidden-danger deadline. The closest analogue to the separation of propagation from common shocks is the distinction between independent and common-cause failures in reliability analysis, but that distinction has not, to the author's knowledge, been given an empirical test in patient-flow data. The assignments in Table 9 are the author's reading of these literatures and are to be checked against them. Figure 26 summarises the same comparison over eight claims, adding the containment ratio C as a summary measure and the treatment of the deadline as the outcome.

Table 9. Claims of the framework compared with three established bodies of models: inherited, partly addressed, not addressed, or new.

Claim Tandem queues and factory physics Hospital patient-flow models Series reliability This paper
Positive dependence between stages makes C > 1 and widens the spread of total time Inherited: variability propagates down a line through departure processes Partly: correlated stays and boarding are documented, rarely as a variance ratio Not addressed: outcome is failure, not time Inherited identity, reframed as one ratio linked to the deadline (Propositions 1–3)
Interface delay is convex in occupancy Inherited (Kingman approximation) Inherited (bed-occupancy and crowding models) Not addressed Inherited; applied interface by interface with a receiving unit for each (Table 8)
A buffer protects the deadline Inherited: inventory and capacity buffers protect throughput Partly: reserved beds and capacity slack Partly: redundancy protects a series system New in form: a decision rule (treat-first) as a buffer whose threshold p* is derived (Propositions 6–7)
Each interface splits into information latency and reaction time Partly: process time against queue time Partly: service time against waiting time Not addressed New as a timestamp-based decomposition at each handover (equation 2)
The outcome is a deadline whose meaning is hidden at presentation Partly: due-date performance, with visible jobs Partly: time targets such as door-to-needle Partly: mission time Extended: miss probability as a function of C, including the reversal when the mean is too slow (Proposition 5)
Direct propagation is separated from common shocks Partly: blocking and starvation against a shared bottleneck Partly: crowding effects on several stages at once Partly: independent against common-cause failures New: an empirical strategy to tell the two apart in routine data (H2, H3)

Tandem-queue and factory-physics models (Hopp & Spearman, 2008; Kingman, 1961), hospital patient-flow models (Armony et al., 2015; Hall, 2006; KC & Terwiesch, 2009) and series reliability models are compared on eight claims. 6.3. Transferability

▶ Explore this in the simulator: Hospital design →

The framework applies to any time-critical pathway with a treatment window and multiple handovers. It is most informative where danger is hidden early, as in sepsis and some poisonings (Kumar et al., 2006), because those pathways depend most on procedural triggers. It is least novel where danger is visible and pathways have already been redesigned around a single activation call, as in stroke and myocardial infarction (Bradley et al., 2006); those pathways can instead serve as benchmarks for what disciplined interfaces achieve. The pathway also has seams before the door. Calls to a poison centre and ambulance pre-alerts are interfaces between the community and the hospital, and pre-alerts were the main lever that shortened door-to-treatment times in stroke and myocardial infarction; extending the model to these pre-hospital interfaces, so that A is partly within the system's control, is a natural next step. Table 10 lays four other pathways onto the same template.

Table 10. Transferability of the framework: other time-critical pathways mapped onto the same interface template.

Pathway Danger at presentation Main seams Treat-first equivalent Expected main mechanism
Severe paracetamol poisoning (this paper) Hidden: patient often looks well Recognition, sampling, laboratory, NAC start, bag changes, ICU, liver unit, transfer Yes: NAC before results when criteria are met Propagation from S1; common shocks at ICU
Sepsis Partly hidden: early signs non-specific Triage, lactate and cultures, antibiotic prescribing and administration, ICU Yes: empirical antibiotics within a fixed time bundle Propagation from recognition; occupancy at ICU
Acute ischaemic stroke Visible but subtype hidden until imaging Pre-alert, triage, imaging, thrombolysis decision, transfer for thrombectomy Partly: pre-alert and direct-to-scanner routes; no treatment before imaging Latency at imaging; transfer between organisations
STEMI Visible: diagnostic ECG ECG, catheter-laboratory activation, transfer Yes: pre-hospital ECG with direct activation Few seams; reaction time at activation
Toxic alcohol poisoning Hidden: delayed acidosis Recognition, specialist levels, antidote, dialysis Yes: antidote before levels on suspicion Laboratory latency, as at S3

Note. Characterisations are illustrative, drawn from the general clinical literature rather than a systematic review, and are offered as hypotheses for the wider Variance at the Seams programme.

6.4. Limitations

The findings are subject to limitations in both the model and the empirical design. The propagation model is linear, the occupancy model rests on a heavy-traffic approximation (Kingman, 1961), and the normal form of the miss probability ignores skew, which the Cantelli bound and the simulation address only in part. The model assumes that pre-hospital time is independent of in-hospital time, an assumption that would fail if late presenters were recognised differently. The simulation is illustrative: its parameters were chosen to be plausible in shape rather than estimated, the treat-first rule was applied to all patients, and only the front end of the pathway was simulated.

The empirical design faces further constraints. Staff respond to how ill patients appear, which can create correlations between stage times unrelated to interface design; Section 5.5 sets out partial remedies, but residual confounding is likely. Routine timestamps may be recorded late, in batches or by default, and reported ingestion times are often uncertain; earlier audits drew partly on handwritten records for this reason (Bailey et al., 2016). Reaction times at fast interfaces may last only a few minutes, so timestamp precision at the level of the minute bounds what can be detected there. Back-end interfaces involve few patients per hospital, which limits precision without pooling. Treating W as a single protocol value simplifies a clinical reality in which benefit declines gradually with time, and the continuous cost of delay c_D(Δ) introduced in Section 3.7 is the natural extension. Finally, the study analyses coordination, not clinical appropriateness, and cannot say whether any individual decision was medically correct. The model treats the patient as passing through every interface and does not represent self-discharge, which is analysed only descriptively. The kidney branch S5k is analysed descriptively only, because signals that arrive after discharge are largely unobserved in hospital records.

6.5. Conclusion

Whether a patient with severe paracetamol poisoning is treated in time depends not only on how fast each team works but on whether the pathway's interfaces absorb or transmit delay. This paper has formalised that claim. It has shown that, for a fixed mean, propagation between stages raises the probability of missing the treatment window; that shared occupancy and direct coupling are distinct sources of this propagation; that interface delay rises convexly with occupancy; and that treating before results acts as a buffer by cutting the coupling at the laboratory interface. By separating information latency from reaction time, it has also made it possible to ask whether delay at each seam is generated by the information systems that feed it or by the coordination that acts on it. A simulation illustrated these effects and showed that average-based metrics can misrank pathways.

The empirical design specified here can test these claims with routine hospital data. If they hold, emergency care for hidden, time-critical conditions should be designed and measured at its interfaces: buffered early, protected from crowding, and judged by its variability as well as its average. Beyond this pathway, the analysis treats a care pathway as a serial service system with a deadline and gives operational research a measure, the containment ratio, for asking whether such a system absorbs delay or passes it on.

Data and code availability

The simulation code and the code used to generate Tables 5 and 6 and Figures 2, 5, 8, 10 to 20, 22 to 24, 26 and A1 will be deposited in a public repository on acceptance. The empirical analysis plan will be pre-registered on the Open Science Framework before data extraction. No patient-level data are shared with this paper. MIMIC-IV, MIMIC-IV-ED and MC-MED are available to credentialed researchers through PhysioNet under a data use agreement, and the ALFSG data are available on request from the NIDDK Central Repository.

Appendix A. Data sources and case selection

This appendix records how the cases for the empirical study in Section 5 are selected, which published evidence is used as a benchmark, and how each trigger and action is mapped to a timestamp source. It contains no patient-level data. Patient records require credentialed access or ethics approval in the author's name, and every patient-level quantity therefore remains a placeholder.

A.1. Case-selection logic

The design is an embedded single-case study (Yin, 2018) with contrast cases chosen by theoretical sampling. The pathway is the case and each interface S1 to S8 is an embedded unit of analysis, because the theory concerns how delay moves between steps. Seven candidate cases were scored from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent) on seven criteria, with weights of 0.25 for minute-level timestamps, 0.20 for interface coverage, 0.20 for access feasibility, 0.10 each for sample size, protocol contrast and cost and time, and 0.05 for novelty of setting. The scores are initial judgements by the author, to be revised as access is confirmed. Table A1 reports the weighted scores and the role each case is proposed to play.

Table A1. Candidate cases, weighted selection scores (1–5) and proposed roles.

ID Candidate case Interfaces Score Rank Proposed role
C1 MIMIC-IV and MIMIC-IV-ED (Beth Israel Deaconess, Boston) S1–S6 3.95 1 Primary quantitative case
C5 Australian ED network (Monash / Austin toxicology) S1–S6 3.30 2 Natural-experiment contrast
C2 MC-MED (Stanford ED) S1–S4 3.20 3 Replication of the front end
C4 UK clinical toxicology units (London, Newcastle, York) S1–S6 3.00 4 Contrast or replication
C6 Scottish integrated-care-pathway sites S1–S4 2.90 5 Interface-design contrast
C3 US Acute Liver Failure Study Group registry (NIDDK) S5–S8 2.80 6 Back-end (severe) case
C7 Poison centre data (NPDS, ToxIC, TOXBASE) None directly 2.00 7 Context only

Note. Weights: minute-level timestamps 0.25; interface coverage 0.20; access feasibility 0.20; sample size 0.10; protocol contrast 0.10; cost and time 0.10; novelty of setting 0.05. Dataset sources: MIMIC-IV (Johnson et al., 2024), MIMIC-IV-ED (Johnson et al., 2023), MC-MED (Kansal et al., 2025) and the ALFSG Adult Acute Liver Failure Study (Lee, 2024).

The selection follows from the scores and from the theory. C1, MIMIC-IV and MIMIC-IV-ED (Johnson et al., 2023, 2024), is the primary case: it has the highest weighted score and is the only option with minute-level, linked emergency department, laboratory, medication-administration and ICU timestamps that can be accessed without a partner hospital, so it is used to build and test the full analysis pipeline. Its limitations are that it is a single US centre, that the size of its paracetamol cohort is unknown until access is granted, and that medication-administration records are incomplete in early years, because the electronic medicine administration record was deployed across the hospital between 2014 and 2016 (Johnson et al., 2024); the primary analysis of S4 is therefore restricted to stays from 2016 onward. Because severe cases are rare in any single hospital, C3 supplies the back-end case for interfaces S5 to S8, accepting that its timing is mostly recorded at the level of the day.

A contrast case is chosen where an interface changed, so that H4 can be tested as a before-and-after comparison: either C5, where a switch from a three-bag to a two-bag regimen in 2014 provides a natural experiment (O'Callaghan et al., 2022), or C6, where an integrated care pathway records the time and initials at each step (Pettie et al., 2012). C2 is a replication of the front-end findings in a second hospital and period. Its structured records include orders, medication administrations and laboratory results alongside visit timestamps (Kansal et al., 2025), so it can in principle cover interfaces S2 to S4 as well as S1, which makes it a stronger replication case than its initial score suggests; the coverage of paracetamol-specific orders and acetylcysteine administrations is confirmed on access. C7 is excluded from the analysis because poison centre data contain no hospital timestamps and cannot measure reaction times; it is used only to describe incidence and context.

Figure A1 shows what each candidate case can observe at each interface and at what time resolution. Minute-level electronic timestamps are concentrated at the front end, S1 to S4b, which is where H1 to H5 are tested. At the back end coverage thins quickly: S6 is visible mainly through clinical notes, and only the ALFSG registry (C3) observes the full run from S5 to S8, and then only by the day. This is why a separate back-end case is needed and why those interfaces are analysed descriptively.

Figure A1. Coverage of each interface by each candidate case (Table A1), by timestamp resolution. Shading distinguishes minute-level electronic timestamps, minute-level proxies or handwritten records, day-level timing, clinical notes only and no observation; hatched cells are expected coverage still to be confirmed on access. The dotted line separates the front-end interfaces S1 to S4b, which support the inferential tests of H1 to H5, from the back-end interfaces S5 to S8 and the kidney branch S5k, which are analysed descriptively. Assignments are the author's assessment from the dataset documentation cited in Table A1 and are revised once access is granted.

Approximate volumes indicate feasibility. MIMIC-IV-ED (Johnson et al., 2023) covers about 425,000 emergency department stays of all causes between 2011 and 2019, MC-MED (Kansal et al., 2025) 118,385 adult emergency department visits between September 2020 and September 2022, and the ALFSG registry (Lee, 2024) 1,195 participants with paracetamol-caused acute liver failure enrolled at North American academic centres between 1998 and 2019; the number of contributing centres differs between study-group and repository descriptions and is reported from the data on access. Among published operational cohorts, O'Callaghan et al. (2022) analysed 869 patients treated with intravenous acetylcysteine in three Australian emergency departments, Bailey et al. (2016) identified 263 cases in three English teaching hospitals, of which 198 were analysed, and an earlier ALFSG series found that 275 of 662 patients with acute liver failure (42%) had paracetamol-induced injury (Larson et al., 2005). The number of paracetamol presentations in the primary case will be reported once access is granted.

A.2. Published timing benchmarks

No published study measures reaction time separately from latency at each interface, but several report delays at S4 or across the front end that serve as benchmarks for the scale and dispersion the empirical study should expect. Table A2 collects them. They are aggregate values from the cited sources, not data from the study.
