Three features of the benchmarks bear on the hypotheses. First, delays within a single interface are long relative to their intended durations and widely dispersed: in the largest UK cohort, the median delay across the infusion was 90 minutes, and about one patient in five was delayed by more than three hours (Bailey et al., 2016). This is the tail on which H5 rests. Second, the same protocol produced different delays at different sites, with medians ranging from 75 minutes in Newcastle to 140 minutes in London, which is compatible with, although it does not establish, delay being a property of local coordination rather than of the protocol alone. Third, changes to interface design were followed by shorter delays: the switch to a two-bag regimen coincided with a fall in median cumulative delay from 65 to 35 minutes (O'Callaghan et al., 2022), and an integrated care pathway with a rise from 12% to 61% in timely starts (Pettie et al., 2012). Both are before-and-after comparisons and do not by themselves establish cause, but they identify the natural experiments that the contrast cases in Table A1 are chosen to exploit. Figure A2 plots the infusion delays.

Figure A2. Published delays to the acetylcysteine infusion against the intended schedule, median and interquartile range, in UK (Bailey et al., 2016) and Australian (O'Callaghan et al., 2022) emergency departments. The dotted line marks one hour. Atypical presentations and anaphylactoid reactions wait longest, and the two-bag regimen, with one fewer bag change, shows the shortest delay. Published aggregates, not study data.

The share of infusions delayed or interrupted by more than one hour varies widely by setting and by definition (Figure A3): 68% across three English hospitals (Bailey et al., 2016), 51% under the three-bag and 31% under the two-bag regimen in three Australian emergency departments (O'Callaghan et al., 2022), and 19% and 5.5% for infusions interrupted by more than one hour in the United States (Hayes et al., 2008) and Malaysia (Au & Zakaria, 2014, as reported in Bailey et al., 2016). Because the definitions differ, the values are not directly comparable across studies; the within-study contrast between regimens, which nearly halves the share, is the more informative comparison.

Figure A3. Share of acetylcysteine infusions delayed or interrupted by more than one hour in published studies. Sources: Bailey et al. (2016); O'Callaghan et al. (2022); Hayes et al. (2008) and Au & Zakaria (2014), as reported in Bailey et al. (2016). Definitions differ between studies; published aggregates, not study data.

The reliability ratings determine how each interface is analysed. The front-end interfaces S2 to S4 have electronic timestamps and support the inferential analyses of H1 to H5. S1 is rated medium because recognition is observed only indirectly, so its reaction time is estimated with a sensitivity analysis that substitutes triage time. S6 to S8 are rated low in the primary case and are analysed descriptively from the registry and partner data. Figure A4 maps every step of the pathway to the role that performs it and to the timestamp source from which it is measured.

Figure A4. End-to-end process map of severe paracetamol poisoning, from ingestion to the transplant centre. Roles are shown in swimlanes and decisions in diamonds; interfaces S1–S8 are tagged with their reaction time (R) or information latency (L), and the timestamp source used to measure each step is given beneath it. The panel on the right summarises what is measured at every interface. Steps are taken from published guidance and are to be confirmed against the local protocol; the map describes how the system coordinates care and contains no clinical recommendation or dosing information.

A.4. Cohort definition and extraction

The cohort rules are drafts to be agreed with the clinical co-investigator before extraction. The front-end cohort includes every adult (aged 18 or over) emergency department presentation with paracetamol ingestion, identified by diagnosis codes (ICD-10 T39.1 or ICD-9 965.4) or by a paracetamol concentration being ordered. The severe cohort adds the condition of ICU admission for liver injury or referral to a liver unit, under a definition still to be agreed. Presentations with no recorded arrival time or no paracetamol-related order are excluded, as are transfers from another hospital in the front-end analysis. Unknown or staggered ingestion times are flagged rather than excluded and are examined in sensitivity analyses.

A patient-level extraction template records, for each presentation, the reported ingestion time, arrival, recognition, sample, result and NAC start times, the scheduled and actual start of each NAC bag, treat-first status, receiving-unit occupancy at each interface (Table 8) and whether a shift change fell within 30 minutes of arrival. From these it computes pre-hospital time A, the reaction times R₁, R₂ and R₄, the laboratory latency L₃, time from arrival and from ingestion to NAC, and whether the window W was missed, and it summarises each as a median and 90th percentile. The template currently holds a single synthetic example row, which is to be deleted before use; the window is set to a placeholder until the value the hospital protocol specifies is entered. Results from the extraction will be reported against the measures of Section 5.4, including the median and 90th-percentile Lᵢ and Rᵢ at S1 to S4.

Appendix B. A worked patient journey

▶ Explore this in the simulator: Patient journey, step by step →

This appendix follows one composite patient through the pathway to make the framework concrete. The patient is fictional, the timings are the illustrative medians of Table 5 and Figure 14 rather than observations, and nothing here is clinical advice.

Before the door (A). A 34-year-old takes a single large ingestion at 18:00 and tells no one. At midnight, six hours later, a flatmate brings them to the emergency department. The pre-hospital interval A is six hours, already three quarters of an illustrative eight-hour window, and it lies outside the hospital's control.

S1, arrival to recognition. At triage the patient reports nausea and looks well. The ingestion is mentioned once, in passing, and the time is uncertain. Recognition depends on whether the triage nurse asks the right question; there is no fixed point at which the risk must be documented, the missing time invariant of Figure 21. The risk is recorded about 20 minutes after arrival, the simulated median at S1 (Figure 5).

S2 and S3, sample to result. Under a wait-for-results policy, bloods are taken, the sample travels to the laboratory and the level is reported. Each step is short, but the steps are in series and each waits on the one before.

S4a, result to NAC. The result appears in the electronic record at about 01:20. Nobody is alerted; the prescriber sees it when they next check, and NAC starts at 01:42, ingestion plus 7 hours 42 minutes. The patient is inside the window by 18 minutes, which leaves no slack for any tail delay (Figure 14). Under a treat-first rule the same patient would have started NAC at about 00:38, an hour earlier, with bloods still taken in parallel.

S4b, the bag changes. The first bag is due to end at 05:42. The night shift hands over at 07:00 and the patient is moved to the short-stay ward at 05:30, so the bag change falls between a transfer and a handover, the compound seam of H3a. The next bag starts 50 minutes late. No one was designated to restart the infusion after the move, the missing authority invariant.

S4c and S4m, end of infusion. Repeat bloods at the end of the infusion are taken on time but reported during the morning ward round, a second laboratory latency. The mental health assessment is booked for the afternoon; the patient, feeling well, considers leaving before it.

S5 and S5k, the late signals. In this composite case the liver tests stay normal and the patient is discharged on day 2. On day 4 a routine creatinine taken at the general practice is mildly raised. The result has no route back to the team that treated the poisoning and no one is designated to act on it, the kidney seam S5k.

What the journey shows. No single step in this journey was slow, and each would pass a mean-based audit. The risk lay in the seams: a recognition that depended on a question, a result that waited to be seen, a bag change that fell between a move and a handover, and a late signal with no owner. That is the claim of this paper in one patient.

Appendix C. Glossary

▶ Explore this in the simulator: Glossary →

The paper draws on clinical toxicology and operational research. The glossary in Table C1 defines the terms most likely to be unfamiliar to readers from one side or the other.

Table C1. Glossary of clinical and operational-research terms.

Term Field Meaning in this paper
NAC (acetylcysteine) Clinical The antidote to paracetamol poisoning, given as an intravenous infusion in two or three bags
Nomogram Clinical A chart that relates the paracetamol level to time since ingestion; it can be read only from four hours after a single ingestion
Staggered ingestion Clinical Ingestion spread over more than about an hour, for which the nomogram cannot be used
Treat-first rule Clinical A protocol rule that starts NAC before the level is known when criteria are met
Window W Clinical The time from ingestion within which treatment is most effective, taken from the local protocol
Interface (seam) Operations A handover between two steps or teams, S1 to S8 and the branches S4c, S4m and S5k
Information latency L Operations Time until the signal to act exists, for example laboratory turnaround
Reaction time R Operations Time from the signal existing to the system acting on it
Containment ratio C Operations Variance of total time divided by the sum of stage variances; C > 1 means interfaces pass delay on
Coupling β Operations How much delay at one interface carries into the next
Common shock Operations A shared cause, such as high occupancy, that slows several interfaces at once
Occupancy ρ Operations The utilisation of the receiving unit at a handover (Table 8)
Heavy-traffic approximation Operations Kingman's result that waiting rises roughly as ρ/(1 − ρ), steeply near full capacity
Interface invariant Operations A property a handover needs to work reliably: time, format, capacity, authority or meaning

Appendix D. Staff interview guide

This guide supports the semi-structured staff interviews described in Section 5.5. It is organised by the five interface invariants and uses the matrix of Figure 22 to choose which interfaces to explore with each participant. Wording is to be piloted with two staff members and adapted to the local protocol before use.

D.1. Before the interview

Consent. The interviewer explains the purpose of the study, that participation is voluntary, that the interview is about how handovers work rather than about any individual's performance, and that no patient or colleague will be identified. Written consent is taken, including consent to audio recording.

Sampling. Participants are sampled to cover each interface and each shift pattern: emergency nurses and doctors (S1–S4b), laboratory staff (S3), pharmacists (S4a), ward nurses (S4b, S4c), mental health liaison (S4m), ICU staff (S5, S6) and, where possible, staff who handle results after discharge (S5k).

Opening question. “Can you walk me through what happens, from your point of view, when a patient with a possible paracetamol overdose arrives, and where you come in?”

D.2. Questions by invariant

Time. When does this handover happen? Is there a fixed point, a rule or a prompt that makes it happen, or does it depend on someone noticing? What happens to it at night, at weekends or at a shift change? Probe: at S2, how is the four-hour sample triggered; at S4b, who checks that the next bag is due.

Format. What information travels across this handover, and how: verbally, on paper, in the electronic record or by alert? What is most often missing or unclear when it reaches you? Probe: at S1, is the ingestion time and pattern recorded; at S4a, how do you learn that a result is back.

Capacity. What happens when you are busy? Is any time, bed or person kept free for this step? Can you remember a time when this patient waited because of workload elsewhere? Probe: laboratory load at S3, ICU beds at S5.

Authority. Who decides at this point, and who is expected to act? Is that written down, or understood? What happens if that person is not available, or the patient has moved? Probe: at S4a, who may start NAC before a result; at S4b, who restarts the infusion after a transfer; at S5k, who acts on a result after discharge.

Meaning. Do the teams on each side of this handover mean the same thing by the key terms, such as overdose, staggered, deterioration or referral criteria? Have you seen a case where a different reading of a term caused a delay? Probe: at S1, whether accidental or staggered ingestions are recognised as overdoses.

D.3. Closing and analysis

Closing questions. “If you could change one thing about how this pathway hands patients on, what would it be?” and “Is there anything about these handovers we have not asked that you think matters?”

Analysis. Transcripts are coded deductively against the five invariants and the interfaces of Table 1, with an inductive code for themes outside that frame, and analysed thematically (Braun & Clarke, 2006). Each coded theme is compared with the cells of Figure 22 to confirm, revise or reject the hypothesised missing invariant, and with the timestamps to see whether the interfaces staff describe as fragile are those where reaction times are longest. Reporting follows COREQ (Tong et al., 2007).

Every idea the paper and simulator use, explained with buses, kitchens and queues. Each card says what it means, gives an everyday example, and where it appears in the study. Three ideas you can play with are first.

Variance: same average, different trouble

Covariance: do delays travel together?

Convex: why crowding explodes

Applied science research · design of the study

From a practical problem to a tested way of fixing it

Applied research starts from a problem in practice, builds and tests theory about its causes, and ends with something practitioners can use and evaluate. This page sets out the study in that form: the problem, the question, the hypotheses and how each is tested here, the methods, the validation, how ready the evidence is, and what a hospital can take away.

How this simulation came about

From a general question to an interactive simulator, in nine steps. Click a step to open where it lives in the simulator.

The practical problem

What goes wrong

About 11 in 100 patients with a paracetamol overdose start the antidote after the 8-hour window, when it protects the liver least.

Why it matters

Liver injury rises from about 6 to 26 in 100 high-risk patients as the start slips from 8 to 16 hours. Most patients who start late arrived in time.

Where it is decided

In the handovers between teams (seams): recognition, sampling, laboratory, prescribing, bag changes and transfers.

Who needs the answer

ED clinical leads, laboratory and pharmacy managers, pathway leads, district hospitals and poison centres.

Research question

How do the interfaces of a time-critical emergency pathway contain or transmit delay, and how does this affect the probability that patients miss the treatment window?

RQ1 · Where

Which seams hold the waiting and the variation?

RQ2 · How

Is delay passed from one seam to the next, or driven by shared crowding?

RQ3 · What works

Which changes (decision rules, layout, stock, staffing) reduce missed windows most?

RQ4 · How to keep it

How should a hospital decide, monitor and manage the risk once a change is made?

Hypotheses, tested live in the simulation

Each hypothesis from the paper is tested here on simulated patients at the current settings. “Supported in simulation” means the model behaves as the hypothesis predicts; confirming it needs real hospital timestamps (section 7).

The applied research cycle

Green stages are complete in this study; red is the next step. Click a stage to open where it is done.

Methods and what each answers

Evidence readiness

A readiness scale adapted from technology readiness levels to service interventions. The treat-first decision rule and the seam measurement are at level 4: validated in simulation against published data, not yet tested in a hospital.

Field study to move from simulation to practice

Design

Stepped-wedge rollout of the treat-first rule and seam timestamps across emergency departments, with a before-and-after comparison inside each.

Primary outcome

Share of patients whose antidote starts more than 8 h after ingestion (the Six Sigma defect).

Secondary outcomes

Door-to-antidote time, time at each seam, unneeded antidote, liver injury, staff time, RPN of the risk register.

Sample size

About 100–400 patients to detect coupling (H2 power tab); the decision threshold is set by expected loss, not fixed at .05 (Calibrated significance tab).

Data

Routine timestamps: arrival, triage, first mention, sample, lab receipt and report, prescription, administration, each bag.

Governance

Service-evaluation or research ethics approval as local rules require; pseudonymised extracts; no change to clinical protocol beyond the rule being evaluated.

Outputs for practice

Limits and validity

  • Internal validity: results follow from the model's assumptions; the simulator reproduces the paper's tables (Validation tab).
  • External validity: parameters are illustrative; hospital, city and rural figures are calibrated to published sources, not local data.
  • Construct validity: the defect (antidote after 8 h) is a process outcome; liver injury is estimated from published risk curves.
  • Statistical conclusion validity: Monte Carlo error is reported; thresholds are calibrated to error costs.
  • Scope: operational, not clinical; contains no dosing information.

How to cite

Cu, M. M. (2026). Variance at the Seams of Emergency Care: A Stochastic Model of Delay Propagation Across the Interfaces of a Time-Critical Pathway, with Application to Severe Paracetamol Poisoning [Research paper]. Berlin School of Economics and Law. Interactive simulator: Cu, M. M. (2026b). Variance at the Seams of Emergency Care: Interactive simulator [Computer software]. https://github.com/maisiecu-web/variance-at-the-seams

Methods and reproducibility

In plain words

These are the main things the simulations show, each with its headline number, what it means, what it means for patients, and the tab where you can see and change it.

All numbers come from reference runs of an illustrative model. They show what the model implies under stated assumptions, not measurements from any hospital.

How to read it

  • The big number is the headline result.
  • For patients translates it into people.
  • The button opens the tab where the result is produced, so you can check it or change the settings.
1

The typical patient is treated in time; the slowest are not

11 in 100 miss the 8-hour window

Median antidote start is about 5 h 28 after ingestion, but the slowest 1 in 10 start after 8 h 12. The miss rate lives in the tail, not the average.

For patients: about 11 of every 100 patients who need the antidote get it after it works best.

2

Most hospital time is waiting at seams

about 113 of 181 minutes are waiting

Work within steps takes about 68 minutes; waiting at handovers about 113. Process cycle efficiency is about 38%.

For patients: the delay patients feel comes from handovers between teams, not from slow care.

3

Linked delays nearly double missed windows

6.3% → 11.6% at the same hospital

Shared crowding and delay passed between steps raise the containment ratio C from 1.00 to 1.85 and the miss rate from 6.3% to 11.6%, while the mean rises only 36 minutes.

For patients: about 5 more patients in 100 are treated late purely because delays pile up together.

4

The finding holds whatever the true hospital numbers

harm in 100% of 500 random hospitals

Drawing all nine settings at random, linked delays added between 0.7 and 21.4 percentage points of misses (median 4.5) and never reduced them. Occupancy matters most.

For patients: the harm to patients is not an artefact of the chosen parameters.

5

Crowding is the tipping point

misses climb steeply above about 85% occupancy

At 94% occupancy, 58% miss when waiting for results and 25% with treat first. In the grid, misses stay under 10% up to about 86% occupancy with perfect handovers, but only up to about 74% with leaky ones.

For patients: in a full hospital, more than half of patients waiting for results would be treated late.

6

Treat first is the single biggest protection

11.3% → 2.6%

Starting the antidote before results removes two seams from the clock. All five improvements together reach 1.9%. A faster laboratory adds nothing once treat first is in place.

For patients: treat first spares about 9 patients in 100 a late antidote.

7

Fewer bags, fewer delays

68% → 24% of infusions over an hour late

With calibrated settings the three-bag regimen loses about 86 minutes to bag changes (Bailey et al.: 90), the two-bag regimen about 27 (O'Callaghan et al.: 35). Every bag change is a seam exposed to shift handovers.

For patients: removing one bag change spares about 44 in 100 patients an hour-long gap in treatment.

8

The hour of arrival changes the risk threefold

21.6% at 19:00 vs 6.6% at 08:00

The half hour before the evening handover is the riskiest time to arrive; night staffing and the evening peak add to it.

For patients: the same patient with the same tablets faces three times the risk depending on the clock.

9

Hidden danger falls hardest on atypical patients

accidental 87%, staggered 42%, early 8%

Accidental and staggered overdoses are recognised late; early arrivals lose about 103 minutes waiting for the 4-hour blood test.

For patients: patients who do not look like a classic overdose are the most likely to be treated late.

10

Deciding at each pause cuts misses by three quarters

11.4% → 2.5% late; 4 per 1,000 spared liver injury

A slack-based rule (speed up when spare time is under 80 minutes, treat now when under 20) acts on a minority of patients: 0.28 speed-ups per patient and 9.7% unneeded treatment. In hospital it saves minutes at the late seams, where patients running late are caught.

For patients: about 9 in 100 patients who need the antidote move from late to on time, and the antidote starts about 25 minutes sooner in hospital. With published injury risks, about 4 in 1,000 are spared liver injury: most patients were already treated in time, so the gain is concentrated in the late tail.

11

A real study is feasible, with safeguards

100–400 patients; false alarms if urgency is hidden

Coupling of 0.3 is detected in 95% of studies of about 100 patients; 0.15 needs 200–400. Unobserved urgency fakes coupling in 63% of studies of 200.

For patients: hospitals can learn which handovers to fix from a few hundred records, if the study guards against false alarms.

12

The numbers are precise enough to trust

± 0.14 points at 200,000 patients

The spread between reruns matches the standard-error formula (0.25 against 0.22 points at 20,000 patients). The model reproduces the paper's Table 6 and counterfactual ranking.

For patients: differences between policies shown here are real effects of the model, not chance.

13

Late arrivals carry most of the risk

5 h 11 vs 2 h 02 before arrival

Patients treated late had spent on average 5 h 11 between ingestion and arrival, against 2 h 02 for those treated in time. A typical arrival time of 1 hour gives 2.0% missed windows; 3 hours gives 26.6%. Starting NAC on arrival for anyone more than 4 h after ingestion cuts missed windows from 11.4% to 5.8%, while treating only 12% of patients before a result.

For patients: about 1 in 100 are past 8 h at the door and cannot be saved by speed alone; about 10 in 100 arrive in time and are treated late, and these are the ones the hospital can still save.

14

The body gives no warning inside the window

0–8 h decision, 24–72 h symptoms

By 8 hours about half of high-risk patients have felt sick and almost none have any liver symptom. Liver injury shows in blood after about a day and peaks at 3–4 days. For a patient arriving 6 h after ingestion, waiting for results starts NAC at about 9 h 15 (risk 9.3 in 100); a late-arrival rule starts it at about 7 h 21 (6.1 in 100).

For patients: feeling well is not a sign of safety. Time since ingestion, and doubt about it, must drive the decision, not symptoms.

15

Match the action to the patient's state at the door

drowsy: 79.5% → 52.7% late

Across six arrival states and four actions, waiting for the result is never the best choice when the history cannot be trusted. For drowsy patients, NAC now (or the optimised rule) cuts late antidote from 79.5% to 52.7% and liver injuries from 102 to 61 per 1,000; for unconscious patients from 124 to 74 per 1,000. For alert patients with a clear history, fast-tracking the seams brings late antidote from 9.7% to 0.1% for about 20 extra staff-minutes, without giving NAC to anyone who does not need it.

For patients: the sickest arrivals, who cannot tell their story, gain most from a decision made at the door.

16

The building is a seam too, and cheap fixes close it

15.0% vs 10.5% late by layout

On a pavilion-plan layout (St Thomas' 1871 and Johns Hopkins 1889 type), 15.0% of patients get the antidote late, against 10.5% on a hot floor: about 45 per 1,000. Half the gap is the blood sample travelling to a distant laboratory (+20 min), and most of the rest is fetching the antidote. Staff walk about 1,470 m per patient against 42 m. A pneumatic tube and antidote stocked in the ED bring the old layout to 10.8%.

For patients: where the laboratory and the antidote are kept changes who is treated in time, and the fix does not need a new hospital.

17

Crowded hospitals lose most, and gain most from treating first

~23–47% late → 4–10% with treat first

Across the hospitals modelled on seven continents, overloaded public hospitals in dense cities (Chợ Rẫy, Bạch Mai, Dhaka, AIIMS, Kenyatta, Baragwanath, São Paulo, Bellevue) give the antidote late to about 23–47% of patients in the model, against 10–13% in purpose-designed hospitals (Karolinska, Rikshospitalet, Humber River). Starting NAC first brings the crowded hospitals down to 4–10%, and roughly halves the energy each pathway uses (Chợ Rẫy: 3.6 → 1.9 kWh, about 1.6 → 0.8 kg CO₂). Tubes and an ED antidote stock help less where crowding is the problem (Chợ Rẫy 33.8% → 26.8%). Patient weight matters for staff effort, not for antidote timing: a 200 kg patient on a bariatric bed needs more force than one person should sustain, but adds under a minute to arrival.

For patients: in the busiest hospitals of the world's densest cities, a decision rule costs nothing to build and protects most; the same pathway emits 20 times more carbon on a coal-heavy grid than a hydro one.

18

The journey to hospital eats the window, most in the densest cities

10 km: ~16 min in Perth, ~45–79 min in Dhaka

Using measured city traffic (TomTom 2025; a GPS study for Dhaka), the same 10 km takes about 16–17 minutes in Perth or Canberra, 32 minutes in Ho Chi Minh City (41 in the evening rush) and 45 minutes in Dhaka (79 when congested). In the model, a patient going to Chợ Rẫy in the rush hour arrives about 8 minutes later and the late-antidote share rises from 35.6% to 37.5%; going to Dhaka Medical College Hospital by ambulance in the rush hour, it reaches about 62%. Ambulances do not always help: where response times are long (Lagos averaged 17 minutes; Rwanda about an hour for whole journeys), the wait for the ambulance can outweigh its faster drive.

For patients: in congested cities the hospital has less time left at the door, so a decision to treat on arrival protects them most.

19

The bottleneck is the wait for the laboratory result, almost everywhere

S3 is the longest seam in 28 of 29 hospitals

Across all modelled hospitals, the laboratory seam (sample to result reaching a doctor) is the longest wait between arrival and antidote; the remote clinic, which cannot measure a level and treats first, is the exception. The building's worst route is the blood sample's trip to the laboratory in 26 hospitals and the antidote fetch in 2. Fixing each hospital's building bottleneck (tube or lab hub; NAC stocked in the ED) lowers late antidote by about 3.4 points on average; a treat-first rule lowers it by about 19 points, and is the bigger lever in 28 of 29 hospitals. In dense-city hospitals the gap is widest: about 24 points from treating first against 4.5 from the building fix.

For patients: the delay that matters is waiting for a result that the decision does not need to wait for. Starting NAC first, and confirming with bloods afterwards, takes the bottleneck off the critical path.

20

In rural areas the bottleneck is between facilities

rural Vietnam: ~92% late on the usual chain → ~4% with NAC at the district

When the district hospital cannot measure the paracetamol level (sent out, results in days) the patient is transferred: assessment, arranging the transfer and a second journey add about 4 hours, so in the rural Vietnam setting about 92% start the antidote late on the usual referral chain and about 43% even when going straight to the referral hospital. If the district stocks NAC and starts it on the history, as poison centres advise when levels are unavailable, late treatment falls to about 4% (and liver injuries from about 130 to 63 per 1,000 high-risk patients). Floods triple travel times; even then starting at the district keeps late treatment near 10%. Where only air retrieval is possible (remote Australia, median 238 min from call to hospital), about half start late.

For patients: stocking NAC at district hospitals and allowing staff to start it on the history alone protects rural patients more than faster roads or bypassing. Distances, speeds and waits are illustrative.

21

When the hospital is far, the first facility decides the outcome

transfer first 64–100% late → start locally 0–15% (arriving 2–6 h, 3 h+ away)

In the scenario matrix, a patient who reaches the first facility 2 hours after ingestion and is 3 hours from the capable hospital starts the antidote late 64% of the time if transferred first, and almost never if NAC starts locally; arriving at 6 hours, 99–100% against 11–15%. Transfer-first stays inside 8 hours only when travel plus transfer is under about 2 h 50 for a patient arriving at 2 hours, and under about 50 minutes for one arriving at 4 hours. Across the four rural settings, the columns with NAC stocked at the district are best everywhere (4–13% late), with or without a level on site; a level on site without NAC does not help.

For patients: the decision point is when the history is taken, in the first 15 minutes, not when results return. Charcoal only within the first hour; bloods before leaving; NAC before the journey when a toxic dose is possible or the time is unknown; red flags mean transfer at once with NAC running.

22

Operations: two-thirds of the time is waiting, and the decision rule beats any single fix

1,000,000 patients: 135 of 207 min waiting · treat first spares 88/1,000

In a million simulated patients, 65% of the time from arrival to antidote is waiting between teams (process cycle efficiency 35%; containment ratio C = 1.82). The prescribe-and-start seam (S4a) is most often the longest wait in patients treated late (41%), while the laboratory step (S3) carries the most variance (35%) and halving its wait spares the most of any single seam (28 per 1,000). Removing coupling spares 36 per 1,000; treating first spares 88. For a hospital with 8 overdose patients a day, about 330 a year would get the antidote late.

For patients: fix the seams in the order of patients spared, but change the decision rule first: it removes two seams from the critical path at once.

What the findings say, and what's usually seen in real hospitals

Left: what this simulation finds (made-up patients, illustrative). Right: what published studies of real hospitals report. They are not measured the same way, so compare the direction and size, not the exact numbers.

What the simulation findsIn plain wordsWhat's usually seen in real hospitals
About 11 in 100 patients get the antidote after the 8-hour windowMost people are treated in time, but a steady minority are notA UK national audit found only about half of patients who arrived within 8 hours got NAC within 8 hours (Royal College of Emergency Medicine, 2014). Real hospitals may do worse than the model.
Most of the time in hospital is waiting between teams, not the work itselfThe blood test isn't slow; waiting for someone to act on it isInfusions ran a median of 90 minutes behind schedule, and 1 in 5 patients were more than 3 hours behind (Bailey et al., 2016).
Delays add up to more than their parts (containment ratio about 1.8, where 1 would mean no build-up)A bad day at one handover tends to come with a bad day at the nextThe same treatment protocol produced median delays of 75 minutes in one city and 140 in another (Bailey et al., 2016), which suggests local coordination matters, not just the rules.
A busy hospital misses far more: roughly 6 in 100 when 75% full, about 30 in 100 when 92% fullCrowding doesn't hurt a little at a time; near full, it hurts a lotCrowded emergency departments are linked to slower treatment, even for the sickest patients (McCarthy et al., 2009; Pines et al., 2007).
Treating first cuts late treatment to about 2.5 in 100Starting the antidote before the blood result removes the biggest waitA care pathway that streamlined these steps raised timely treatment from 12% to 61% (Pettie et al., 2012); a simpler two-bag drip halved delays from 65 to 35 minutes (O'Callaghan et al., 2022).

Real-hospital figures are from the paper's Appendix A.2 (published timing benchmarks). They are before-and-after or audit figures, so they show the size of the problem, not proof of cause.

Finding at each gap

Every seam in the pathway, from before the door to the liver unit: the time spent there, what the simulations found, and the inference (what it means and what to do). Evidence shows how strong each statement is. Use "See it" to open where each is shown.

Before the door (A)Model + published traffic data
Median ~2 h (90 min delay + journey)
Patient decides to come; journey through the city
Finding

Patients treated late had spent 5 h 11 on average before arriving, against 2 h 02 for those treated in time. The same 10 km takes ~16 min in Perth and 45–79 min in Dhaka.

Inference

Most missed windows start before the hospital is involved. Late arrivals must be identified at the door and treated without waiting.

S1 Arrival → recognisedModel (simulated)
29 min (20 of it waiting)
History of ingestion time and amount; weak ownership at triage
Finding

Halving S1 delay lowers missed windows only from 11.6% to 9.1%. Recognition doubles in the half hour before a shift handover; in drowsy or unconscious patients attention goes to airway first and paracetamol is recognised later.

Inference

A triage prompt (any overdose or collapse → paracetamol level and time of ingestion) is cheap and matters most for patients who cannot tell their story.

S2 Recognised → blood sampleModel (simulated)
32 min (23 waiting); early arrivals wait ~103 min for the 4-h level
Blood request; level not interpretable before 4 h
Finding

Halving S2 has the smallest effect of any seam (11.6% → 9.8%). For early arrivals the wait is required by the nomogram, not a failure.

Inference

S2 is a timed wait, harmless when timing is known and early. When timing is uncertain or the patient is late, the wait should be removed by treating first.

S3 Sample → resultModel + layout analysis
77 min (34 waiting, 40 work) — the longest seam
Specimen to laboratory; result back to a doctor; ownership split
Finding

Longest seam in 28 of 29 hospitals. Halving laboratory work and wait lowers misses to 7.0%. The sample's trip is the building bottleneck in 26 hospitals; a tube or lab hub recovers ~3 points.

Inference

The decision does not need to wait for this result. Starting NAC first takes S3 off the critical path; tubes and lab hubs shorten what remains.

S4a Result → NAC startedModel (simulated)
51 min (37 waiting)
Result to prescriber; prescription; preparation; no one designated
Finding

Halving S4 lowers misses to 9.4%. Between Dhaka and Karolinska, S4a holds the largest share (31%) of the gap. Fetching NAC from a central pharmacy is a bottleneck in 2 layouts.

Inference

Give the result an owner: an electronic alert and a standing order, with NAC stocked in the ED.

S4b Bag changesPublished + model
Median delays 25 and 50 min per change (published)
Infusion schedule across nursing handovers
Finding

68% of three-bag cumulative delays exceed 1 hour (model calibrated to Bailey 2016); delays double within ±30 min of a handover. A two-bag regimen: 27 min median, 24% over 1 hour.

Inference

Remove a bag change (two-bag / SNAP-style) and protect changes that fall near shift handovers.

S5 Deterioration → ICUNot measured (inference)
No published timing; model: lift waits add ~13 min in a crowded tower
Abnormal result, bed, transfer
Finding

Not measured in the literature. In the model, transfers depend on lifts and corridors; in Antarctica, air evacuation took about 60 hours end to end.

Inference

Measure it. Agree in advance who calls ICU and on which results (INR, lactate, pH).

S5k Kidney signal → actionNot measured (inference)
No published timing
Creatinine result; no owner
Finding

Kidney injury appears in some patients at 2–5 days, after the antidote decision; no seam owner was identified.

Inference

Include creatinine in the end-of-infusion bloods and name who acts on it.

S6 ICU → liver unit / poisonsNot measured (inference)
No published timing
Telephone referral
Finding

Not measured. Ownership weak in the author's reading.

Inference

Record referral call times; use a structured referral (criteria + numbers) to cut back-and-forth.

S7 Criteria met → referralNot measured (inference)
No published timing
Prognostic criteria; split ownership
Finding

Not measured. Criteria often met hours apart (INR, pH, creatinine, encephalopathy), so recognition can lag.

Inference

Automatic flag when transplant criteria are met.

S8 Accepted → arrival at liver unitInference + traffic data
No published timing; road time from city traffic
Patient, records and team move between hospitals
Finding

Not measured. Inter-hospital transfer uses the same congested roads: 16–79 min per 10 km across the cities modelled.

Inference

Plan transfers outside rush hour where possible; pre-book transport when criteria are approaching.

Across all gaps: couplingModel (simulated)
C rises from 1.00 to ~1.85
Delay passed from one seam to the next; shared crowding
Finding

Linked delays nearly double missed windows (6.3% → 11.6%) while the mean rises only 36 min. In crowded hospitals (occupancy ~0.9) late antidote reaches ~23–47%.

Inference

Fixing one seam in isolation underperforms; rules that bypass seams (treat first, decide at the door) work because they cut the chain.

Rural: between facilitiesModel + published access data
Assessment + arranging transfer + second journey ≈ 4 h (rural Vietnam setting)
Health post → district → referral hospital; transport and transfer ownership split
Finding

Where the district hospital cannot measure the level or give NAC, ~92% start late on the usual chain; starting NAC at the district cuts this to ~4%. 41.6% of people worldwide cannot reach care within an hour on foot.

Inference

Stock NAC at district hospitals and start it on the history; transfer afterwards. Treat the referral itself as a seam with an owner and a target time.

Overall inference: the measured and simulated gaps (before the door, S1–S4b) explain most missed windows, and the largest is S3, the wait for the laboratory result, which the decision does not need. The back-end gaps (S5–S8, S5k) are unmeasured; they matter for the sickest patients and are the first thing a real study should time.

What it all means

Taken together, the simulations tell one story. The patients who are harmed are not those who meet an unusually slow hospital. They are those whose time before arrival, waiting at handovers between teams, and the hour they arrive happen to add up past the window. Each part looks acceptable alone. The harm is in the combination, and in the slow tail that averages hide.

For the system

  • Delay lives at the seams. About 113 of 181 minutes in hospital are waiting between steps, not treatment.
  • Delays are linked. Shared crowding and delay passed from one seam to the next nearly double missed windows (6.3% → 11.6%) while the average rises only 36 minutes.
  • The decision rule is the strongest lever. Starting the antidote on time-since-ingestion rather than on the result removes up to three seams at once: 11.4% → 2.5% missed with the optimised rule, 2.6% if everyone is treated first.
  • Risk depends on when you arrive. Late arrivals, evening hours (21.6% at 19:00 against 6.6% at 08:00) and the half hour before handover concentrate the misses.

For patients

  • About 11 in 100 patients who need the antidote get it after it works best, even though the typical patient is treated well inside the window.
  • The optimised rule moves about 89 in 1,000 patients from late to on-time treatment, and spares about 4 in 1,000 a liver injury.
  • About 1 in 100 arrive too late for any process to help; for them, only treating at once and early escalation matter.
  • Patients cannot feel the window closing. The first liver symptoms come a day or more after it has closed.

What could be better

In the pathway

  • Give the result an owner (S4a). No single person is responsible between "level back" and "NAC prescribed". An automatic alert and a standing order would close the seam with the longest reaction time.
  • Decide on arrival for late or uncertain timing. Start NAC at the door when ingestion was more than about 4 hours ago, staggered, or unknown, and take bloods in parallel.
  • Remove bag changes. The 12-hour two-bag (SNAP-style) regimen removes one of the two bag-change seams, where 68% of three-bag changes run more than an hour late.
  • Protect the handover half hour and the evening peak. A named owner for overdose patients across 08:00 and 20:00, and staffing matched to the late-evening arrival peak.
  • Fix the building's seams cheaply. A pneumatic tube to the laboratory and a stock of NAC in the ED recover most of the gap between old and new layouts.
  • Prioritise crowded hospitals. Where occupancy and shared porters are saturated, treating first gives the largest gain and also cuts pathway energy and carbon.
  • Decide by state at the door. Drowsy, unconscious, staggered and late patients: NAC now and bloods in parallel; alert patients with a clear history: fast-track the seams.
  • Shorten time to arrival. Public and primary-care messages: come to hospital at once after an overdose, even if you feel well.

In the model and the evidence

  • Parameters are illustrative. Step and seam times, occupancy and coupling are plausible values, not fitted to any hospital. Fitting them to real time stamps is the next step.
  • One risk curve. Liver-injury risk uses the 1988 high-risk cohort; it does not change with dose, nomogram line, alcohol use or other risk factors. Lower-risk patients would gain less.
  • Ingestion time treated as known in most tabs. Staggered and modified-release overdoses, and recall error, are covered only in the Scenario lab and the ingestion-time estimate.
  • Harms of treating first are priced, not modelled. Reactions to NAC, bed use and cost enter only as the "unneeded treatment" cost.
  • The back end is thin. ICU, liver unit and kidney seams (S5–S8, S5k) have no published timings, so they are mapped, not simulated.
  • Symptom timings are illustrative, taken from the classic clinical stages rather than measured distributions.

Directions

Next for research

  1. Fit the model to time-stamped records (ED stays, lab events, medication administration) and test hypotheses H1–H5.
  2. Measure seam times by arrival-time band and clock hour, not only as one overall median.
  3. Interview staff at each seam to confirm who owns the patient in the gap.
  4. Make liver risk depend on dose (ratio to the nomogram line) and add the kidney branch.
  5. Measure seam times in high- and low-income hospitals in dense cities (for example Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City, Dhaka, Nairobi, São Paulo) to test whether crowding, not layout, drives the gap.
  6. Add energy and carbon per patient pathway to audits, so time saved and energy saved are reported together.
  7. Test the time-since-ingestion decision rule prospectively, for example in a stepped-wedge trial across sites.

Next for hospitals

  1. Audit "ingestion to NAC" as well as "door to NAC", and report the 90th percentile.
  2. Pilot an on-arrival treatment rule for late, staggered and uncertain-time presentations.
  3. Name an owner for the S4a result-to-prescription seam, backed by an electronic alert.
  4. Move to a two-bag regimen and check bag-change delays at shift handovers.

Beyond paracetamol

  1. Apply the same seam analysis to other time-critical pathways where the danger is hidden at presentation, such as toxic alcohol poisoning and sepsis.
  2. Use the containment ratio C as a routine measure of how well a pathway stops delay spreading.
  3. Compare with pathways that have one-call activation (stroke, heart attack) to learn what makes seams disciplined.

All figures come from an illustrative model under stated assumptions. They show the size and direction of effects to test, not measured outcomes from any hospital.

Who gets the antidote in time, and what decides it

Paracetamol overdose has an antidote (NAC) that works best within about 8 hours of swallowing the tablets. Most patients are treated in time. The ones who are not usually arrive late and then wait at the seams, the handovers between teams, while the clock keeps running. This simulator follows thousands of imaginary patients to show where the time goes and what would save it.

11/100get the antidote late with today's pathway
113 minof 181 in hospital are waiting between teams
2.5%late with the optimised decision rule

About this simulation and model

Author: Maisie Mary Cu, Berlin School of Economics and Law, Germany. Based on her research paper Variance at the Seams of Emergency Care: A Stochastic Model of Delay Propagation Across the Interfaces of a Time-Critical Pathway, with Application to Severe Paracetamol Poisoning.

This is applied science research: it takes a practical problem in emergency care, builds theory and an operational research (OR) and simulation model from the paper Variance at the Seams of Emergency Care. It treats emergency care as a service process: a chain of stages linked by handovers (seams), each with its own queue, shared capacity and decision rules. It follows a patient from swallowing the tablets to the start of the antidote (NAC) and asks one question: how much of the delay comes from the handovers between teams, and what would remove it? It is a study of how the system is organised, not a diagnostic or treatment tool.

Process mapping & swimlanesQueueing: congestion g(ρ)Monte Carlo simulationLittle's lawBottleneck & theory of constraintsDecision rules & optimisationSensitivity & uncertainty (PSA)Six Sigma (DMAIC, SPC)Calibrated significance (expected loss)Risk management (FMEA)Facility layout & energy

What it models

The journey has four handovers, called seams: recognising the overdose (S1), taking the blood sample (S2), getting the lab result (S3) and prescribing and starting the antidote (S4). Each seam has some work (doing the step) and some waiting (the queue before it). A patient is late when arrival time plus time in hospital passes the 8-hour window.

The equation

Time at seam i is Xi = di + hi: work plus waiting. Waiting is hi = g(ρ)·Vi + β·hi−1, where g(ρ) = 1 + kρ/(1−ρ) makes waits grow sharply as the department gets busy (ρ near 1), and β carries part of one wait into the next. All values are set from published data and can be changed on every tab.

The Monte Carlo

The computer invents patients one by one, each with a random arrival time, a random level of crowding and random waits drawn from those ranges, then counts how many are late. Running up to 20 million patients makes the answer precise (about ±0.02 points at 10 million), and every scenario uses the same random patients so differences are real, not noise.

What you can do here

Watch patients move through the seams, run a big simulation with any number of patients, find where the bottleneck is, compare 29 real hospitals across every continent, plan rural journeys and local first care, and test the decision rule that starts the antidote first and checks the result later.

Main result: about 11 in 100 patients get the antidote late with today's pathway, mostly because of waiting at the lab seam; starting treatment first cuts that to about 2.5 in 100, far more than any building change. See how this simulation came about. Hover over any dotted term for a definition, or see How it works and the Glossary.

How this simulator is organised

Seven groups, in the order you would read a study. Each one answers one question. Click any tab name to go there.

The title, word by word

Long title, simple idea. It has three parts: the idea, the method and the example.

Variance at the Seams of Emergency Care: A Stochastic Model of Delay Propagation Across the Interfaces of a Time-Critical Pathway, with Application to Severe Paracetamol Poisoning

1The ideawhat the paper is about
Variance
How much times jump around. Two buses both 10 min late on average: one always 9–11, the other 0–30. The second makes you miss your train.
Seams
The handovers between teams (nurse → doctor → lab → doctor → pharmacy), where things come apart.
Emergency care
Care for people who arrive unplanned and need help fast.
2The methodhow it is studied
Stochastic
Involving chance. The model "rolls dice" for every made-up patient, then counts across thousands. (Opposite: deterministic, like a calculator.)
Model
A simplified copy of reality in rules and equations, tested safely on a computer.
Delay propagation
A delay spreading to the next step, like a traffic jam backing up.
Interfaces
Another word for seams: where one team's work ends and the next begins.
Time-critical pathway
Steps that must finish before a deadline. Here: about 8 hours after the overdose.
3The examplewhere it is tested
With application to
"Tested on this real case." The idea is general; this is the example.
Severe paracetamol poisoning
A large overdose of paracetamol (Tylenol, Panadol). It can destroy the liver if the antidote, NAC, starts too late, and the patient often feels fine at first.

In one sentence: a computer model that uses chance to show how delays spread through the handovers between hospital teams, tested on patients who need the paracetamol antidote in time.

    In plain words

    Paracetamol poisoning is dangerous because it is quiet at first. A patient can feel well for a day while the liver is being damaged, and the antidote works best if it starts within about 8 hours of swallowing the tablets. Every minute lost between teams is a minute taken from that window.

    This tab translates the simulation into people: how many of 100 patients are treated late, what a typical patient's day looks like, and who is most at risk.

    How to read it

    • Each little figure is one patient out of 100. Red figures start the antidote after the window.
    • Times in the day are hours and minutes since the tablets were swallowed.
    • Every tab has a green "What this means for patients" box that updates with its settings.

    Your hospital

    Set your own numbers: everything on this tab re-simulates live and the counts are scaled to a year at your hospital.

    100 patients, five ways of running the pathway

    Each picture is 100 simulated patients who need the antidote, run through the same hospital under a different design.

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: five groups of 100 people. Red people start the antidote after the 8-hour window; grey people are treated in time. "Better handovers" cuts coupling to 0.1; "Less crowding" lowers occupancy to 0.75; "Treat first" starts the antidote before blood results; "All five improvements" combines them with faster recognition and laboratory.

    What to look for: how many red people disappear with each change. Treat first removes the most on its own; combining changes removes almost all.

    Why it matters: percentages are easy to ignore. Counting people makes the stakes visible: each red figure is someone whose treatment started after it works best.

    One typical patient's day

    The median patient, step by step, with the slowest 1 in 10 for comparison. Orange dots are waiting at a seam; each time is when that step starts.

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: a timeline from the moment the tablets are swallowed. Blue dots are steps where something is done; orange dots are waits at handovers; the last dot is the antidote starting (green if inside the window, red if not). The grey times show when the slowest 1 in 10 patients reach the same point.

    What to look for: how much of the day is orange, and how far behind the slowest patients fall by the end.

    Why it matters: from the patient's side, most of the time is spent waiting while feeling fine, and nothing tells them, or staff, that the clock is running.

    Who is most at risk

    100 patients of each kind, same hospital.

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: for five kinds of patient, how many of 100 start the antidote too late. Early arrivals must wait for the 4-hour blood test; staggered and late presenters are treated first; accidental and staggered overdoses are slower to be recognised.

    What to look for: accidental overdoses and late presenters fare worst; early single ingestions best.

    Why it matters: the patients most at risk are those who do not look like a typical overdose: hidden danger at its sharpest. Equity of care depends on recognising them.

    Why the minutes matter

    The antidote, acetylcysteine (NAC), protects the liver best when it starts early. In the national multicentre study cited in the paper, liver injury occurred in about 6 of 100 patients at probable risk when treatment began within 10 hours of ingestion, and about 26 of 100 when it began 10–24 hours after (Smilkstein et al., 1988).

    When treatment is late, danger shows only days later: liver injury peaking on days 3–4, sometimes intensive care, transplant referral, and kidney injury that can appear after the patient has gone home. That is why the simulation counts minutes and missed windows: they are the part of the outcome the hospital controls.

    This page models how a care system coordinates. It does not give clinical advice or dosing information. The "patients saved" figures on the Decisions tab apply published risks to simulated times to show scale only.

    In plain words

    This is the whole journey of a patient with severe paracetamol poisoning, drawn as a process map. Each row is a team or place, and each box is a step. The patient moves left to right, and every time care passes from one row to another there is a handover.

    The numbered circles are the seams the paper studies, S1 to S8 plus the kidney branch S5k. Everything on the map can be selected: circles, boxes and lane names.

    How to read it

    • Rows (swimlanes) are who is responsible: the patient, ED nurses, ED doctors, the laboratory, ICU, the liver unit, and care after discharge.
    • Rectangles are steps; diamonds are decisions.
    • The dashed green arrow is the treat-first shortcut, which skips the wait for blood results.
    • The loop on bag changes repeats once (two-bag) or twice (three-bag).
    • Circle colour shows evidence: blue simulated, dark blue published timings, grey never measured.
    • Route highlights one path through the map; Play a patient sends a randomly simulated patient along it with a running clock.

    Severe paracetamol poisoning: from ingestion to transplant centre

    Steps follow published guidance and are illustrative; a real study uses the local hospital's protocol. Scroll sideways on a small screen.

    Route
    Explain this graph

    What is shown: a swimlane process map. Time runs left to right but is not to scale; position shows order, not minutes. Each crossing between rows is a handover, where responsibility changes hands.

    What to look for: how often the patient changes rows. Each change is a seam where delay can start or be passed on. The front end (S1–S4a) races the treatment window in hours; the back end (S5–S8) and the kidney branch (S5k) play out over days.

    Why it matters: the paper's claim is that delay comes mostly from these crossings, not from the boxes. The map shows where to measure: one timestamp for each trigger and each action.

    Patient journey, step by step

    The hospital pathway for one typical patient, using the median time at each seam from the model. Change the arrival time and the policy; press Play to walk through it, or click any card or dot for detail.

    Time between each stage

    Computed live from 100,000 simulated patients at the baseline settings (occupancy 0.85, coupling 0.3). Front-end times are simulated and illustrative; later stages use published timings where they exist.

    before arrival (A)work within the stepwaiting at the seamwindow W
    Explain this graph

    What is shown: the clock from the moment the tablets were taken, in hours. The top bar is the typical (median) patient; the bottom bar is the slowest tenth of patients (90th percentile). Each bar is split into time before arrival (grey), then for each step the work (blue) and the waiting at the seam after it (orange).

    What to look for: how much of each bar is orange, and how close the end of each bar sits to the red window line. The typical patient finishes well inside the window; the slowest tenth runs close to it or past it.

    Why it matters: it shows where the minutes go, stage by stage. Waiting at the seams is a large share of the total, and it grows faster than work in the slow tail. The tail is where windows are missed.

    Simulated time between movements

    The full spread of waiting between one movement and the next, from 40,000 simulated patients and infusions per panel. Blue: front-end seams (simulated). Orange: bag changes (calibrated to published studies).

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: eight small histograms, one per movement between steps. Across: minutes waited, in 5-minute slots (the last slot holds everything over 175 minutes). Up: share of patients. The dotted black line is the median; the dashed red line is the slowest 1 in 10.

    What to look for: the long right tails. Each gap is usually short, but a minority wait several times longer, and those minority patients are the ones who run out of window. Bag changes have the longest tails, because they collide with shift handovers.

    Why it matters: this is "time between movements" as the patient experiences it. Reporting only the median at each step would hide exactly the waits that matter. Press the button to see that the shape is stable from one simulation to the next.

    Explain this table

    What is shown: a RACI matrix. Rows are the seams of the process map, plus the steps of the rapid decision rule and the audit. Columns are the people and teams involved. Each cell says how that role relates to that row: R does the work, A owns the outcome (exactly one per row), C is asked before acting, I is told afterwards.

    What to look for: rows where the accountable person sits in a different team from the one doing the work. Those are seams where ownership can fall between teams: S4a (result to antidote), S4b (bag changes across shift changes) and S5k (kidney follow-up after discharge). They match the "who owns the patient in the gap" findings on the map.

    Why it matters: in the paper's terms, a missing authority invariant is a seam with no clear A. Writing a RACI makes every seam owned, which is the precondition for the rapid decision rule to work. It is a proposal for discussion, not a description of any real hospital.

    Big run
    Any number from 100 to 20 million, e.g. 250000, 250k or 2.5m.
    Policy
    Scenario

    Changing a setting restarts the run, so every estimate comes from one scenario. Dots show a sample of patients; the counters use every patient simulated.

    In plain words

    The computer invents imaginary patients, one after another. Each gets a random waiting time at every step, drawn from realistic ranges, and we check whether treatment started inside the window.

    One imaginary patient tells you nothing. Thousands tell you how often the system fails. Repeating a random experiment until the answer stops changing is what Monte Carlo means.

    How to read it

    • Dots are patients. They bunch up where waiting is long, and turn red once they pass the window.
    • Missed window is the share that started NAC too late.
    • The shaded band is how unsure the estimate still is. It shrinks as more patients are simulated: wide early, narrow later.
    • The histogram shows when patients got NAC. Red bars are too late.

    Patients moving through the seams

    Each dot is one simulated patient, from ingestion through S1 to S4a. Dots slow where waiting is long and turn red once time since ingestion passes W.

    Speed:
    Explain this graph

    What is shown: Each column is one step of the pathway, from ingestion on the left to the start of the antidote on the right. Each dot is one simulated patient travelling left to right. Columns are equal width whatever the step's length, so a dot moves slowly through a step where it waits long.

    What to look for: Dots crowding in a column, which is where waiting builds up. Dots turning red mid-journey: they passed the treatment window W before treatment started. The right-hand column counts patients treated in time (green) and too late (red).

    Why it matters: It shows the core idea of the paper. Lateness is not a property of one step; it builds up across the seams between steps.

    Running estimate of missed windows

    Estimate with its 95% confidence band as patients accumulate. The band narrows with the square root of the sample.

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: Across: number of patients simulated so far, on a log scale, so each step to the right is ten times more patients. Up: estimated share missing the window. The shaded band is the 95% confidence interval.

    What to look for: Early on the line jumps around and the band is wide. As patients accumulate the line settles and the band narrows. That settling is called convergence. With default settings the line settles near the paper's 11.6% (orange dashed).

    Why it matters: It shows how many simulated patients are needed before a result can be trusted, a reporting requirement for simulation studies (STRESS guideline).

    Time from ingestion to NAC

    Distribution filling as the run proceeds; bars past W are patients who miss the window.

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: Across: hours from swallowing the tablets to the start of the antidote. Up: share of patients in each 15-minute slot. The dashed red line is the window W.

    What to look for: The long tail to the right. Most patients sit in the hump, but a thin tail stretches past W, and those patients (red bars) miss the window.

    Why it matters: The average sits well inside the window, yet a fixed share still misses it. Averages hide the tail; this is why the paper argues for measuring variability, not just the mean.

    Six Sigma · DMAIC · statistical process control

    The antidote pathway as a process with defects

    A defect is a patient whose antidote starts more than 8 hours after ingestion. Six Sigma asks how often that happens per million (DPMO), how capable the process is against the 8-hour limit, which step causes most defects, which change improves the sigma level most, and how a hospital would keep it under control.
