    Risk management · FMEA · ISO 31000 style

    Where the pathway can fail, how badly, and what controls it

    Each risk is a way the antidote can be late. Severity is the harm if it happens, Occurrence how often it happens (from the simulation where the model covers it), Detection how unlikely it is to be noticed in time (10 = invisible). RPN = S × O × D; above 200 needs action.

    Risk matrix: likelihood × impact

    Hollow rings show where each risk was before controls; arrows show where controls move it. Click a risk for detail.

    Risk priority numbers, before and after controls

    Sorted by current RPN; the dashed line is the action threshold (200).

    Risk register (FMEA)

    In plain words

    Four bigger simulation studies, each running many scenarios at once instead of one at a time.

    They answer four questions: where on the map of occupancy and coupling the pathway breaks; which combination of improvements works best; which kinds of patients are most at risk; and how much any result moves by chance alone.

    How to read it

    • Each panel runs on its own; press its button to rerun after changing a setting.
    • Hover over or tap any cell, bar or dot for its exact value.
    • Copy as table copies the results so you can paste them into Excel or Word.

    1 · Full grid: occupancy × coupling

    Every combination of 13 occupancy levels and 9 coupling levels: 117 scenarios, 10,000 patients each.

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: A heatmap. Across: mean occupancy of the receiving units. Down: coupling β, how much lateness passes between steps. Each cell's colour and number is the share of patients missing the window in that scenario.

    What to look for: The outlined cells exceed your acceptable miss rate. The boundary between safe and unsafe cells is a curve: the busier the hospital, the less coupling it can tolerate. Switch to Treat first and watch the safe zone grow.

    Why it matters: It turns two abstract parameters into an operating map. A hospital can locate itself on it and see whether to work on capacity (move left) or on handovers (move up).

    2 · Intervention bundles: all 32 combinations

    Five improvements, tried alone and in every combination, on the same 30,000 patients each time so differences are not luck.

    T treat first O occupancy −0.10 R faster recognition, S1 wait halved L faster laboratory, S3 halved H handover checklist, coupling cut to 0.1
    Explain this graph

    What is shown: One bar per combination, sorted from fewest to most missed windows. The letters name the improvements in the bundle. Darker bars contain more improvements.

    What to look for: Where single improvements rank, and whether two together beat the sum of their parts. Some combinations overlap: a faster laboratory adds almost nothing once treat first has taken the laboratory off the clock.

    Why it matters: Resources are limited. The ranking shows which small bundle gets most of the benefit, and the overlaps show which pairs waste effort.

    3 · Types of presentation

    The same hospital, five kinds of patient. Early arrivals cannot have a meaningful blood level before 4 hours after ingestion, so their sample waits for that mark.

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: For each type of presentation: the share missing the window (bars) and, in the table, time from arrival to the antidote and the minutes spent waiting for the 4-hour mark.

    What to look for: Late presenters miss almost by definition: the window has closed before they arrive, so what matters for them is speed after arrival. Atypical presentations (staggered, accidental) are slowed at recognition, the hidden-danger problem. Early arrivals lose time to the 4-hour rule, not to the hospital.

    Why it matters: One overall miss rate mixes very different patients. Improvements should target the groups where the seams, not the biology, cost the time.

    4 · Replications: how much do results move by chance?

    The baseline scenario rerun many times with fresh random numbers, at three sample sizes.

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: Each dot is the miss rate from one complete rerun of the simulation. The three columns use 1,000, 5,000 and 20,000 patients per run. The box marks the middle half of reruns.

    What to look for: The spread shrinks as runs get bigger: four times the patients halves the spread. The table checks that the observed spread matches the standard-error formula.

    Why it matters: It shows the Monte Carlo error directly and justifies the sample sizes used in the paper. A difference between two scenarios smaller than this spread could be chance.

    At every pause, where the patient waits at a handover, staff can wait, speed the handover up, or start the antidote now. The optimiser searches 400 decision rules for the lowest expected cost.

    Costs (relative units)
    Patients and hospital

    In plain words

    The pathway pauses four times: at each handover the patient waits. At every pause someone could act. They can wait, speed this handover up (a phone call, a fast-track, which costs staff time), or start the antidote now without waiting for results (which costs something if the patient turns out not to need it).

    The rule tested is simple and realistic: work out the slack, the minutes left before the window closes after allowing for the typical remaining time. Act when slack is low. The optimiser tries 400 combinations of two thresholds on the same 20,000 patients and keeps the one with the lowest expected cost.

    How to read it

    • Policy comparison: the optimised rule against doing nothing, always speeding up, and treating everyone first.
    • Cost map: every rule tried; the star is the best.
    • Trade-off chart: fewer missed windows usually needs more actions; the best rules sit on the lower-left edge.
    • One patient's pauses: the decision made at each pause, and why.

    Policy comparison

    All policies are evaluated on the same simulated patients.

    Explain this table

    What is shown: five ways of deciding at each pause, tested on the same simulated patients. Do nothing never acts. Always speed up expedites every handover. Treat everyone first starts the antidote for all patients at the first pause. The Proposition 6 rule treats everyone first only if the share needing treatment p is above the paper's threshold p*. The optimised rule acts only when slack runs low, using the best thresholds found.

    What to look for: the expected cost column, where lower is better, and the average time to the antidote. Missed windows count only patients who needed the antidote; unneeded treatment counts only those who did not.

    Why it matters: acting on everyone is safe but wasteful; doing nothing is cheap but misses windows. The optimised rule shows how much of the benefit can be kept with far fewer actions, and how much faster the average patient gets the antidote.

    Cost map of decision rules

    Across: slack below which a handover is sped up. Down: slack below which the antidote is started now.

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: Each cell is one decision rule, defined by two thresholds. Its colour is the expected cost per patient; darker is cheaper. The star marks the cheapest rule. 'never' means that action is never taken.

    What to look for: A valley of cheap rules rather than a single point. Move the cost sliders: when a missed window costs more, the star moves towards acting earlier (larger thresholds).

    Why it matters: It shows the best rule is not 'always act' or 'never act' but act when slack runs low, and that the right threshold depends on what errors cost.

    Missed windows against actions taken

    Each dot is a rule. Lower-left is better: few misses and few actions.

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: Across: actions per patient (handovers sped up plus unneeded treatments). Up: share of patients who needed the antidote and missed the window. Named policies are labelled.

    What to look for: The lower-left edge of the cloud, the trade-off frontier. Rules above it are wasteful: another rule gets fewer misses for the same effort.

    Why it matters: Decision-makers can pick a point on the frontier that matches their budget, instead of guessing.

    Optimisation tool: test your own rule

    Choose the two slack thresholds yourself. The expected cost is worked out in full beside the optimum, on the same 20,000 simulated patients.

    Explain this calculation

    What is shown: the optimisation's objective worked through with real numbers. Expected cost per patient J = c_M × P(needs antidote and misses the window) + c_U × P(treated but did not need it) + c_E × (handovers sped up per patient). Each term is shown for your rule and for the optimum, with the probabilities counted from the simulated patients.

    What to look for: which term dominates. Acting too rarely leaves the miss term large; acting too often grows the unneeded-treatment and speed-up terms. The optimum balances them. Slide either threshold to the far left ("never") or right ("always") to recover the named policies.

    Why it matters: it makes the optimisation transparent and checkable. Anyone can reproduce the cost of a rule from three probabilities and three prices, and see why the optimum wins.

    Decision matrix: what to do at each seam

    Built on the process map: one row per seam where the patient pauses on the way to the antidote, one column per action. Cells show the slack range that triggers each action under the optimised rule, how many patients fall there, and the minutes saved.

    Explain this table

    What is shown: the optimised rule written as a decision matrix. Read across a row: at that seam, staff look at the slack (spare minutes before the window closes, after allowing for the typical remaining time) and take the action whose slack range it falls in. Each cell gives the share of patients pausing at that seam who fall in it, their average slack, and how many minutes the action saves compared with doing nothing.

    What to look for: most patients sit in the Wait column; the rule acts only for the minority whose slack is short. Treat-now cells usually save the most minutes per patient, because they skip every remaining seam; speeding up saves less each time but is cheaper.

    Why it matters: this is the bedside version of the optimisation, one card per handover, so the policy can be written into the protocol and audited against timestamps.

    Time saved at each seam: rapid optimisation policy

    Average minutes at each seam for patients who need the antidote, if nobody acts against the optimised rule. Stages skipped by starting the antidote early count as zero.

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: for each seam on the process map, two bars: grey is the average time spent there if nobody acts, green is the average under the optimised rule. The green number is minutes saved. The table adds the slowest 1 in 10 and the total from arrival to antidote.

    What to look for: where the savings come from. Early seams save little, because the rule rarely acts while slack is still large; later seams save more, because that is where patients running late are caught. The slowest 1 in 10 gain far more than the average.

    Why it matters: it tells a hospital which handover to target first, and shows that a policy acting on only a minority of patients still cuts the waiting that decides who misses the window.

    Patients saved: usual process against rapid optimisation

    Turns minutes into patients. Each simulated patient who needs the antidote gets a chance of liver injury that depends on when the antidote starts. Default chances come from the national multicentre study cited in the paper (Smilkstein et al., 1988): about 6.1% if treatment starts within 10 hours of ingestion, 26.4% if it starts 10–24 hours after, for patients at probable risk.

    Risk management curve

    The chance of liver injury by time to antidote (red line, left scale), with when patients actually get the antidote: usual process (grey) and rapid optimisation (green).

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: across, hours from swallowing the tablets to the antidote. The red line is the assumed chance of liver injury if treatment starts at that time (left scale). The shaded areas show how simulated patients are spread across that time scale: grey without decisions, green with the rapid policy.

    What to look for: the green area sits further left, earlier, than the grey, especially in its right-hand tail. Expected injuries are the risk curve weighted by these areas, so moving the tail out of the steep part of the curve is what saves patients.

    Why it matters: risk management is about the tail, not the average. Most patients sit on the flat, low part of the curve either way; the gain comes from the minority pulled back from the steep part.

    Rapid decision allocation: where an action saves most

    Each patient's reduction in risk is shared among the actions taken on them. Rows are ordered by patients saved per 100 actions, the best use of staff time first.

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: the expected number of patients with liver injury per 1,000 who need the antidote, under the usual process (nobody acts at the pauses) and under each decision policy. "Saved" is the difference from the usual process. The people pictures show 100 patients: red would be injured, green are saved by the rapid policy. The second table shows which seam and which action produced the savings, per 100 actions taken.

    What to look for: the "patients saved" number and its interval, and the "probability a patient is saved", meaning the chance that the policy turns a given patient from injured into not injured. In the allocation table, actions taken late in the pathway, when slack is shortest, usually save the most patients per action.

    Why it matters: it links the paper's minutes to outcomes patients care about. It is a model, not a measurement. The risk figures come from oral treatment in the 1980s and are applied here only to show scale. Change them with the sliders and the conclusion about which policy is better stays the same, but the size of the benefit changes.

    Decision tree: what happens at each pause

    Under the optimised rule, for patients who need the antidote. Branch thickness shows the share taking it.

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: a decision tree. Each blue box is a pause, where the patient waits at a handover, with the share of patients who reach it. From each pause, branches show what the optimised rule did: treat now (green, start the antidote without waiting for results), speed up (orange, the handover is expedited), or wait (grey). Treat-now branches end the race early; the others carry on to the next pause. The last box is patients who reached the antidote by the normal route.

    What to look for: at which pause the rule mostly acts. Typically it waits at the first pause, then speeds up or treats now at later pauses for patients whose slack has run low. The numbers beside each branch give the average time the antidote started and how many still missed.

    Why it matters: it turns the optimisation into a protocol staff can follow: what to do at each handover, depending on how much time is left. The paper's treat-first rule is one branch of this tree.

    Process maps generated for each route

    Every distinct sequence of decisions taken by simulated patients is a route. The eight most common are drawn here, each as its own small process map.

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: one strip per route. Each strip is a process map from arrival to the antidote. Each box is a stage with what happened at its pause (grey: waited; orange: sped up; green: antidote started now) and the average minutes spent there. The route code spells it out: W wait, S speed up, T treat now, one letter per pause.

    What to look for: how common each route is, how long each stage takes on it, and the average time to the antidote and miss rate at the end of the strip. Routes that end with a red box still miss often; they show where the rule is not enough.

    Why it matters: averages hide that different patients take different routes. Seeing the routes side by side shows where the time goes on each one and which decision changed the outcome.

    One patient's pauses under the optimised rule

    A randomly chosen simulated patient who truly needs the antidote, followed through each pause.

    Explain this table

    What is shown: one simulated patient who needs the antidote, pause by pause. At each pause: the time since the tablets were taken, the typical time the rest of the pathway still takes, the slack (window minus both), and the decision the optimised rule made, with its reason.

    What to look for: slack shrinking from pause to pause. When it drops below a threshold the rule acts. The line underneath compares the same patient with no decisions at all.

    Why it matters: it shows the rule is simple enough to use at the bedside: check how much time is left, and act when it is short.

    How the optimisation works

    slack = W − (time since ingestion) − (typical remaining time)

    Slack is the spare time left if the rest of the pathway runs at its median pace. Negative slack means the patient is on course to miss the window.

    rule: speed up if slack < θ_E; start antidote now if slack < θ_T (only before the result is known)
    expected cost J = c_M · P(needs antidote and misses) + c_U · P(treated but not needed) + c_E · E[handovers sped up]

    The optimiser evaluates J for every pair (θ_E, θ_T) on the same simulated patients (common random numbers) and picks the smallest. This is simulation-based optimisation by sample average approximation. It extends Proposition 6 of the paper, where the treat-first threshold depends on how slow and variable the laboratory is, to a decision at every pause.

    Each draw picks every parameter at random from its range, then simulates the same patients twice: independent stages at fixed occupancy, and shared occupancy with coupling. The difference in missed windows is the amplification effect.

    In plain words

    Nobody knows the true numbers for a real hospital. So the computer guesses them hundreds of times, each guess inside a sensible range, and reruns the whole simulation for every guess.

    The question is simple: does the main finding still hold whatever the true numbers are? The main finding is that linked delays make more patients miss the window.

    How to read it

    • Each bar in the histogram counts guesses. Right of zero means linked delays made things worse in that guess.
    • Effect above zero near 100% means the conclusion does not depend on lucky guesses.
    • In the dot chart, darker dots have stronger coupling.
    • Which parameters drive the effect ranks the inputs that matter most. Long bars matter most.

    Distribution of the amplification effect

    Extra share of patients missing the window, percentage points, one value per parameter draw.

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: A histogram. Across: the amplification effect, the extra percentage points of patients missing the window when steps are linked compared with independent. Up: how many parameter draws gave that effect.

    What to look for: Whether any bars fall left of the red 'no effect' line. The orange line marks the median effect.

    Why it matters: If almost all draws are right of zero, the paper's main conclusion holds whatever the true hospital numbers are. That makes it robust, not a lucky choice of parameters.

    Effect against occupancy

    Each dot is a draw; colour shows its coupling β, from light (0.1) to dark (0.5).

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: Each dot is one parameter draw. Across: the occupancy in that draw. Up: its amplification effect. Darker dots had stronger coupling β.

    What to look for: The cloud rises to the right, and the darkest dots sit highest.

    Why it matters: Linked delays do the most harm in full hospitals with leaky handovers, which is exactly when the system is under most strain.

    Which parameters drive the effect

    Rank correlation between each parameter and the effect across draws. Longer bars mean the parameter matters more; the sign shows direction.

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: Each bar is one input parameter. Its length is the rank correlation between that parameter and the amplification effect, from −1 to 1. Blue bars push the effect up; orange bars push it down.

    What to look for: The longest bars. Occupancy usually leads; a longer window W reduces the effect (orange), because there is more slack.

    Why it matters: It shows which numbers the real study must measure most carefully, because they move the result most.

    Each bag change is a seam (S4b). Its delay is a base delay, multiplied when the scheduled change falls near a shift handover or a ward transfer, plus a share of the previous delay. A late change shifts every later change on the clock.

    Shifts
    Bag-change delay

    In plain words

    The antidote runs as two or three bags, one after another. Every time a bag finishes, someone has to start the next one. That moment is a seam.

    If the moment falls during a shift change or a ward move, it is more likely to be late. A late change also pushes every later change on the clock. Fewer bags means fewer chances to be late.

    How to read it

    • Blue is the older three-bag regimen, green the two-bag regimen.
    • Curves further left mean less delay.
    • Peaks in the clock-time chart are start times whose bag changes land on a handover.
    • The table compares the simulation with two published hospital studies. Close numbers mean the simulation is realistic, not that any hospital behaves this way.

    Cumulative delay during the infusion

    Share of infusions with total bag-change delay up to each value, both regimens.

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: Across: total bag-change delay during the whole infusion, in minutes. Up: share of infusions with at most that much delay. Blue: three-bag regimen; green: two-bag regimen.

    What to look for: The green curve rises much faster. Read off the 1-hour line: the curve height there is the share delayed less than an hour.

    Why it matters: Removing one bag change removes one seam, so there is less delay and less exposure to handovers. This is the mechanism behind the published before-and-after improvement.

    Delay by clock time NAC starts

    Mean cumulative delay by hour the infusion starts. Peaks are start times whose bag changes land on handovers.

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: Across: clock time the infusion started. Up: average total bag-change delay. Dotted lines are shift handovers.

    What to look for: Peaks. A peak at a given start hour means that infusions started then have a bag change that lands on a handover a few hours later.

    Why it matters: The same treatment can be fast or slow depending only on the clock. This is hypothesis H3a: two seams falling at once, a bag change and a shift change, cause the longest delays.

    Against the published benchmarks

    Simulated medians and IQRs beside the published values. Close agreement here is calibration, not evidence about any hospital.

    Occupancy follows a daily cycle. Arrivals in the half hour before a shift handover wait longer for recognition, and night staffing slows every interface.

    In plain words

    Hospitals are busier at some hours, have shift changes at fixed times and fewer staff at night. The same patient can face a very different system depending on when they arrive.

    This tab shows which arrival hours are riskiest, and why an average over the whole day hides them.

    How to read it

    • Each bar is one hour of arrival; the thin line on each bar is the uncertainty.
    • Amber bars are the half hour before a shift handover; grey bars are night.
    • The red line is how full the hospital is at that hour (right scale).
    • In the lower chart, the gap between the median and P90 is the slow tail where windows are missed.

    Missed windows by hour of arrival

    Bars: share missing W with 95% interval. Line: mean occupancy at that hour (right scale). Dotted lines mark shift handovers at 08:00 and 20:00.

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: Bars: share missing the window by hour of arrival, with a thin line for the 95% interval. The red curve is how full the hospital is at that hour (right-hand scale). Dotted lines are shift handovers.

    What to look for: The tallest bars: the half hour before a handover (amber) and the busiest evening hours. Compare with the red occupancy curve.

    Why it matters: Risk is not spread evenly over the day. Staffing and handover design can target the hours where most windows are missed.

    Time from arrival to NAC by hour

    Median and 90th percentile by hour of arrival. The gap between them is the tail that averages hide.

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: Two lines by hour of arrival: the median time from arrival to antidote (blue) and the 90th percentile (red). The shaded area between them is the spread.

    What to look for: Where the red line rises faster than the blue one, the slow tail is growing even if the typical patient is barely affected.

    Why it matters: Hospital reports usually give medians. This shows why the slowest tenth of patients, where windows are missed, needs its own measure.

    Time from swallowing the tablets to arriving at hospital (pre-hospital time, A). The clock for the 8-hour window starts at ingestion, not at the door.

    Arrival delay
    Hospital policy
    Arrival stream

    In plain words

    The antidote works best within about 8 hours of swallowing the tablets. That clock is already running before the patient reaches hospital. Someone who arrives after 2 hours has 6 hours left for the hospital; someone who arrives after 6 hours has only 2.

    This tab simulates when patients arrive: how long after ingestion, and at what time of day. It then follows each patient through the hospital to see who misses the window and why.

    How to read it

    • Grey is time at home or on the way, before arrival. Blue is time in hospital until the antidote. Red marks patients treated after the window.
    • Dashed lines at 4 h and 8 h: the earliest reliable blood level, and the end of the window.
    • Move Typical time to arrive to see what earlier or later arrival does. Switch the policy to see how the hospital can protect late arrivals.
    • Press Play a day to watch one simulated day of arrivals in real time.

    From ingestion to liver damage: the body's clock against the hospital's steps

    One patient, followed from the moment the tablets are swallowed. Top lane: what paracetamol is doing in the body. Middle: the chance of liver injury if the antidote (NAC) starts at that moment. Bottom: the hospital steps for this patient, simulated with the seam model. Hover anything for detail.

    Explain this map

    What is shown: (Press Play the patient's clock, or drag the slider, to move a "now" line through the patient's four days: the body lane, the risk dot and the patient token update live.) A time line from ingestion (0 h) to day 4. The first 24 hours are stretched because that is when decisions matter. Body lane: paracetamol is absorbed in the first hours; the liver turns a small part of it into a toxic by-product (NAPQI), which is made safe by a protective substance called glutathione. In a large overdose glutathione runs out after roughly 8 hours, and NAPQI starts to damage liver cells, often while the patient still feels well. Damage shows in blood tests (ALT) after about a day, and peaks at 3–4 days with jaundice, clotting failure, confusion and sometimes kidney injury. Risk lane: NAC refills glutathione. Started within 8 hours, about 6 in 100 high-risk patients still develop liver injury; started at 16–24 hours, about 26 in 100 (Smilkstein et al., 1988). Hospital lane: each dot is a step for this patient, at its simulated time.

    What to look for: Where the antidote dot falls against the green, amber and red zones. Move Arrives at hospital after to the right and watch how little time the hospital has left by the time the patient walks in.

    Why it matters: The body's clock does not wait for the hospital's steps. Every seam crossed before the antidote moves the patient along the risk curve, and the patient cannot feel it happening.

    Time left at each step

    Explain this table

    What is shown: Each hospital step for this patient, its clock time, hours since the tablets were swallowed, what is happening in the body at that moment, how much of the 8-hour window is left, and the liver-injury risk if the antidote started at that moment.

    What to look for: The row where "time left" turns red: from there on, every further step costs liver cells. Compare the risk at arrival with the risk at the antidote row; the difference is what the steps in between cost.

    Why it matters: This is the calculation a clinician makes at the bedside ("how long ago did you take them?"). Putting the hospital steps next to the body's clock shows which seams the patient can least afford.

    When was it taken, and when will symptoms show?

    Left: estimate the time of ingestion from what the patient says, and see how uncertainty changes the decision. Right: simulated timing of symptoms after a high-risk overdose, against when patients arrive and get the antidote.

    Explain this estimate

    What is shown: The time of ingestion is rarely known exactly. The patient's account gives a best guess; the shaded band is the range it could really be (best guess ± your uncertainty). The bar below shows how much of the 8-hour window is left in the best, likely and worst case.

    What to look for: Whether the band crosses the 4-hour or 8-hour line. If the earliest possible ingestion time puts the patient past 8 hours, or the time is too uncertain to use the nomogram, guidance is to start the antidote straight away rather than wait for a level.

    Why it matters: An uncertain ingestion time is a seam of its own: information that should cross from patient to clinician arrives incomplete. The safe rule is to plan for the earliest possible time, which is the worst case for the liver.

    Matching process map: estimated time since ingestion, expected signs and window left at each step

    Explain this map

    What is shown: The steps this patient goes through, in order, using the typical (median) time for each seam from the model. Each box shows the clock time to the second, the estimated time since ingestion (best guess and the range from your uncertainty), the signs you would expect to see at that point, and how much of the 8-hour window is left: likely, worst case (if taken at the earliest possible time) and best case. The coloured top edge follows the worst case: green more than 2 h left, amber less than 2 h, red none. If the suggested action is "NAC now", the map switches to the treat-first route and bloods run in parallel. Otherwise the blood level is timed 4 hours after the latest possible ingestion, so that it can be read.

    What to look for: The first box whose top edge turns amber or red. That is the seam the patient can least afford. Notice how the expected signs barely change while the window runs out.

    Why it matters: The same patient can look safe on the best guess and be past the window on the worst case. Planning each step against the worst case is how uncertainty about the time is turned into a safe decision.

    When symptoms appear after a high-risk overdose (1,000 simulated patients)

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: The share of patients who have shown each sign by each hour after ingestion. Grey: early sickness (nausea, vomiting, feeling unwell), which many patients never have. Blue dashed: liver injury first detectable in blood (ALT rising). Amber: pain under the right ribs. Red: jaundice or confusion, the signs of severe liver injury. Vertical lines: typical arrival and typical antidote start, from the seam model. Liver injury depends on when the antidote started, using the same risk curve as above.

    What to look for: At the 8-hour line, only the grey curve has risen. Liver signs appear a day or more later, long after the window has closed.

    Why it matters: A patient who feels fine, or only sick, at 8 hours may already be past the point where the antidote works best. The hospital cannot wait for symptoms; the decision has to rest on the history and the clock.

    Timings are illustrative, based on the classic clinical stages of paracetamol poisoning (stage I 0–24 h: none or nausea; stage II 24–72 h: liver injury, right upper pain; stage III 72–96 h: peak injury, jaundice, encephalopathy; stage IV: recovery or failure). Real timings vary with dose and individual risk.

    One simulated day: from ingestion to arrival to antidote

    Each row is one patient. The line starts when the tablets were swallowed (clock time), turns blue at the hospital door and ends when the antidote starts. The red tick is where that patient's 8-hour window closes.

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: Each line is one simulated patient on a 36-hour clock. Patients appear at random, more often around the most common hour of ingestion (a Poisson arrival stream). Grey: from ingestion to arriving at hospital. Blue: from arrival to the antidote. The small red tick is 8 hours after that patient's ingestion. The moving vertical line is the clock.

    What to look for: Patients with a long grey section have little room left once they arrive; their blue section often runs past the red tick. Patients who arrive early almost never do.

    Why it matters: The hospital controls only the blue part. How much blue time it can afford depends on the grey part, which differs for every patient. A single target for "door to antidote" treats them all the same.

    How long after ingestion patients arrive

    Distribution of arrival time A for 100,000 simulated patients, in 15-minute bins. Red: patients from that bin who go on to get the antidote after the window.

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: How many patients arrive at each time after swallowing the tablets (light blue), and how many of them end up treated late (red, drawn over the blue). Arrival time follows a log-normal distribution: most people arrive within a few hours, and a long tail arrive much later.

    What to look for: Left of the 4-hour line almost no one is treated late. Between 4 and 8 hours the red share grows quickly. Past 8 hours every patient is already late at the door.

    Why it matters: Most late treatment comes from a minority of late arrivals. The hospital can find them on arrival, because the time since ingestion is asked for in the history.

    Risk of a missed window by time of arrival

    Share treated late by hour after ingestion at arrival, for the three policies. Hover a point for the number.

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: For patients who arrive 0–1 h, 1–2 h, … after ingestion, the percentage who start the antidote after the window. One line per policy: wait for the blood result (blue), start the antidote on arrival only for late arrivals (amber), or start it on arrival for everyone (green).

    What to look for: All lines are near zero for early arrivals and rise to 100% after 8 hours. The gap between the blue line and the others, between about 4 and 7 hours, is what a rapid "treat on arrival" decision buys.

    Why it matters: Late arrivals are where policy matters. A rule based on time since ingestion targets the antidote at the patients most at risk, without giving it to everyone.

    Where the 8 hours go

    Average time before arrival, average time in hospital, and time left in the window, for patients treated in time and patients treated late.

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: Two bars, each 8 hours wide plus any overrun. Grey: average time from ingestion to arrival. Blue: average time from arrival to antidote. Green: time left in the window. Red: time past the window.

    What to look for: Compare the grey parts. Patients treated late arrived much later on average; their hospital time is only somewhat longer.

    Why it matters: A missed window is usually a late arrival combined with an ordinary or slow hospital stay. Both parts count, so both the public (coming in early) and the hospital (acting fast on late arrivals) can change it.

    What if patients arrived sooner or later?

    Share treated late as the typical arrival time changes, for each policy. The dashed line is your current setting.

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: Each line reruns the simulation (20,000 patients per point) for a typical arrival time from 30 minutes to 6 hours. The vertical line is the current setting.

    What to look for: How steeply the lines rise. Arriving one hour later on average adds more missed windows than most changes inside the hospital remove. The green and amber lines rise less steeply because they start the antidote at the door.

    Why it matters: Public messages ("come in straight away, even if you feel fine") and hospital policy work on the same outcome. When arrival is late, only an on-arrival decision protects the patient.

    When in the day patients arrive

    Arrivals per 1,000 patients by clock hour of arrival (bars, red = treated late) and ingestions by clock hour (line). Dotted lines: shift handovers at 08:00 and 20:00.

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: The line is when patients swallow the tablets, peaking at the chosen hour. The bars are when they arrive at hospital: the same pattern, shifted later and spread out by the time it takes to arrive. Red is the part of each bar treated late.

    What to look for: The arrival peak sits a few hours after the ingestion peak, often late at night, and often close to the 20:00 handover or the night shift.

    Why it matters: The busiest arrival hours are when staffing is thinnest. The Time of day tab shows how handovers and night staffing add to the delay at exactly these hours.

    How this simulation works

    Each simulated patient gets three random parts. 1. Ingestion time of day: drawn from a daily pattern, λ(h) ∝ 1 + 0.6·cos(2π(h − peak)/24), so ingestions are three to four times as common at the peak hour as twelve hours later. Patients per day follow a Poisson count with the chosen mean. 2. Time to arrive: A = median × eσZ, where Z is a standard normal draw and σ = ln(ratio)/2.326, so 1 in 100 patients arrive later than "ratio × median". 3. Time in hospital: T from the same seam model as the rest of the page (eq. 12), with shared occupancy and coupling β = 0.3.

    The patient misses the window when A + T > 8 h. Under "Treat late arrivals" the antidote starts on arrival (after a 12-minute preparation step and recognition) whenever A is above the threshold; otherwise the hospital waits for the blood result. With the 4-hour option on, a patient who arrives early cannot have the decisive blood level before 4 hours after ingestion, so the sample step waits until then.

    Arrival delay settings are illustrative. The paper's base case uses a median of 2 hours and a 1-in-100 tail of 8 hours. Real distributions should come from ingestion times recorded in clinical notes.

    An operational planning tool for routes, seams, time and staff effort. It does not diagnose, and does not replace local protocols or poisons advice.

    Patient state at arrival
    Timing
    Optimisation weights

    In plain words

    Patients arrive in different states: some alert with a clear story, some vomiting, some drowsy, some unconscious with froth at the mouth (which can mean a seizure, inhaled vomit, other drugs taken as well, or a very large overdose). Each state sends the patient down a different route through the department, with different seams, bottlenecks and staff effort.

    This tab asks an operational question: for each state, which route gets the antidote in time at the lowest total cost (late antidote, antidote given when not needed, and staff time)? It then turns the best route into a timed plan, to the second.

    How to read it

    • Pick the patient state and the reported time since ingestion.
    • The decision matrix compares four actions for all six states; the best cell in each row is outlined.
    • The bottleneck map shows where time is lost on each route.
    • The trajectory shows the patient's path against the window.
    • The do-now plan gives each step a time budget and a deadline. Press Start the clock when the patient arrives and tick steps off.

    Route for this state

    Where these routes come from

    Routes follow published guidance in outline: the paracetamol level is not interpretable before 4 hours after ingestion; for staggered ingestion, doubt about timing, serious poisoning or an unconscious patient, the antidote is started at once rather than waiting for the level; patients who collapse or have reduced consciousness have a paracetamol level checked even when no history is available. Very large overdoses can cause early coma and metabolic acidosis, and may need higher antidote doses, intensive care and sometimes dialysis. State-specific modifiers (recognition delay, extra resuscitation time, share needing treatment, staff effort) are illustrative assumptions for the model, not clinical estimates.

    Optimisation decision matrix: six states × four actions

    Each cell: 8,000 simulated patients. Big number: missed windows (%). Below: liver injuries per 1,000, unneeded NAC per 1,000, staff-minutes per patient, median arrival → NAC (h:mm:ss) and total cost J. The lowest-cost action in each row is outlined; the selected state is highlighted.

    Explain this matrix

    What is shown: Rows are patient states, columns are actions. Wait for result: take the blood level (no earlier than 4 hours after ingestion) and start NAC only if it is above the line. Fast-track seams: the same, but a named coordinator cuts waiting at each seam (waits × 0.4) at the price of extra staff time. Optimised rule: at arrival, compute the slack (window left minus typical time still needed); treat now if slack is under 20 minutes or the timing cannot be trusted, fast-track if it is under 80 minutes, otherwise wait. NAC now: start the antidote at once and take bloods in parallel; stop it later if not needed.

    Total cost J = cost of a missed window × share of patients who need NAC and get it late + cost of a liver injury × expected liver injuries per patient + cost of unneeded NAC × share treated unnecessarily + cost per staff-hour × staff-hours. The liver-injury term matters for late arrivals: every action misses the window for them, but earlier NAC still lowers the risk. Change the weights on the left and the best action can change.

    What to look for: For alert, early patients, waiting is cheapest. For states where the history cannot be trusted, or the patient is late, NAC now wins by a wide margin. The optimised rule is close to the best in most rows, because it chooses per patient.

    Why it matters: No single policy is best for every patient. Matching the action to the state at the door is a rapid decision allocation, and it is cheap.

    Bottlenecks on each route

    Median time on each segment for the selected state, by action. The bottleneck (longest segment inside hospital) is outlined in red and labelled.

    Explain this map

    What is shown: One bar per route, split into segments: before arrival (grey), recognition including any resuscitation (S1), getting the blood sample including any wait for the 4-hour level (S2), the laboratory (S3), and prescribing and starting NAC (S4a). Bars end at the median antidote start.

    What to look for: The red-outlined segment. On the wait route for early arrivals it is usually S2, the wait for the 4-hour level. On the treat-now route it moves to S1, recognising that paracetamol is involved, especially in drowsy or unconscious patients, where attention goes to airway and breathing first.

    Why it matters: Improving anything other than the bottleneck saves little. Each route has its own bottleneck, so the fix depends on the state the patient arrives in.

    Trajectory: this patient through the steps

    Median time of each step after ingestion, for each action, against the 8-hour window and the liver-risk zones.

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: Each line climbs one step each time the patient passes a milestone: arrive, recognised, bloods taken, result back, NAC started. The horizontal position is hours since ingestion. Green zone: within 8 h. Amber: 8–16 h, where liver risk rises steeply. Red: after 16 h.

    What to look for: Where each line reaches "NAC started". On the NAC-now route that point comes before bloods and results; on the wait route it comes last.

    Why it matters: The trajectory shows the order of steps as well as their speed. Reordering, by starting NAC before the result, is often worth more than making every step faster.

    Do now: timed plan to the second

    Steps for the recommended action in this state. Budgets come from the model's median step times, compressed if needed so the antidote starts with at least 30 minutes of window to spare. Deadlines count from arrival (T+); once the clock is started they also show clock time.

    Process map of this plan

    The same plan as a table, with live deadlines

    Explain this plan

    What is shown: Each step, who usually does it, its time budget (h:mm:ss), its deadline from arrival, and the time since ingestion and window left at that deadline. When the clock runs, the current step counts down second by second; pressing Done records the actual time and shows whether the step was ahead of or behind budget.

    What to look for: The "window left at deadline" column. If the NAC step shows less than 30 minutes, the budgets have been compressed and every seam must move faster than usual.

    Why it matters: A plan with named deadlines turns the window into a shared, visible clock, the same idea as door-to-needle targets in stroke care. It also produces the time stamps an audit needs.

    Search hospitals
    Getting to hospital
    Design changes
    Patient and pushing

    In plain words

    The building is part of the pathway. Distance to the laboratory, where the antidote is kept, lifts, ramps, floors and crowding all add minutes, and moving patients costs staff effort and building energy.

    This tab models 29 real places on all seven continents, from overloaded public hospitals in dense megacities to purpose-designed new hospitals and a remote Antarctic clinic. Search by country, city or continent; pick one to see its layout type, its bottleneck, the effect of patient weight and pushing, and the energy and carbon each patient's pathway uses.

    How to read it

    • Each card is a hospital; the numbers are model results under its layout type, crowding and national grid. Crowding in overloaded hospitals is set from reported overload (for example 120% of beds) as a higher staff occupancy (0.88–0.91) and slower shared porters, lifts and corridors; these settings are illustrative.
    • Facts on each card are from the cited source; layouts are schematic types, not real floor plans; model parameters are illustrative.
    • Change the design, crowding or patient and pushing settings and every hospital is re-simulated.

    Hospitals on the map

    Dot colour: share of patients getting the antidote late in the model (green under 12%, amber 12–25%, red above). Ring: the hospital you have selected. Click a dot to select it; the search and filters on the left also filter the map.

    Hospitals

    Floor plan

    Explain this plan

    What is shown: A schematic, not to scale, of the hospital's layout type and the four routes the pathway uses: the patient from the entrance (blue), the blood sample to the laboratory (amber), the antidote (green) and a transfer to intensive care (purple). Each route shows its length and the minutes it adds on average for this hospital's crowding, floor and the patient settings. The dashed red route is the bottleneck.

    What to look for: In dense, overloaded hospitals the same distance costs more, because porters, lifts and corridors are shared by many more patients. In campus layouts (single-storey wards spread over a large site) the sample route dominates; in towers, lifts; in a remote clinic, the laboratory itself is missing and treatment cannot wait for a level.

    Why it matters: The bottleneck is local. A pneumatic tube helps a campus hospital far more than a hot-floor hospital, and staffing the porter service helps a crowded hospital more than adding beds.

    Getting to hospital: how long the journey takes

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: For each hospital in the search, the median time to reach it from the chosen distance, with average traffic (dark) and in the evening rush hour (light), from the city's measured travel time per 10 km. With "Ambulance", the ambulance's response time is added and the drive is a little faster; with "Motorbike", the drive is faster through traffic (illustrative). Red dots: the median time from swallowing the tablets to arriving (delay before setting off + journey).

    What to look for: The same 10 km takes about 16 minutes in Perth or Canberra and 45 minutes or more in central Dhaka, Mexico City, London or Lima in the rush hour. In dense cities, the journey alone can use a quarter of the 8-hour window's slack.

    Why it matters: Travel time is part of the pre-hospital delay A. Every minute on the road is a minute the hospital no longer has, so in congested cities treating first on arrival matters even more.

    Travel per 10 km: TomTom Traffic Index 2025 city pages where available; Dhaka from a GPS-car study (median 4.5, congested 7.9 min per km); others assumed and marked. Delay before setting off: median 90 minutes (illustrative), so that with a typical journey the median arrival is close to the paper's 2 hours.

    Add your own hospital

    Add any hospital to the model. It is simulated with the same seam model and appears in the search, cards, table and comparisons. Your additions are saved only in this browser; use Export to share them.

    Patient weight and pushing: does it matter?

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: The steady force needed to keep a patient moving, for each way of moving them, as patient weight rises, on the selected floor. Force = rolling resistance × (patient + equipment) × gravity, plus the slope on ramps. Rolling resistance is calibrated to a manufacturer push-force test: a 250 lb (113 kg) patient on a hospital bed needed about 8 lbf (36 N) to keep moving on linoleum and 23 lbf (102 N) on carpet, and about twice that to start. Dashed lines: an illustrative sustained-force limit of about 100 N per person pushing.

    What to look for: Where a line crosses the limit for the number of staff pushing. Above it, staff slow down, need help, or risk injury; a powered drive removes most of the force.

    Why it matters: Weight and equipment change how long it takes to move the patient and how much effort staff spend, but they barely change when the antidote starts, because the blood sample and the antidote move without the patient. They matter most for transfers to intensive care, and on ramps, carpets and crowded or uneven floors.

    Energy and carbon per patient pathway

    Explain these graphs

    What is shown: Top: the energy used by this hospital's pathway for one patient, split into the emergency space occupied while waiting (lighting, ventilation, cooling or heating for one cubicle), lifts, pneumatic tube sends and robots, with the carbon this causes on the national grid. Staff body energy (kcal) from walking and pushing is shown separately. Bottom: every hospital in the current search, plotted by time to antidote (across) and carbon per patient pathway (up). Hover for detail.

    What to look for: The space term is the largest: every minute a patient waits in the department is a minute of lit, ventilated, conditioned space. Faster pathways use less energy. The same pathway emits several times more carbon on a coal-heavy grid than on a hydro-powered one.

    Why it matters: Time saved at the seams is energy saved. Energy optimisation and patient safety point the same way: shorter waits, fewer trips, shorter routes.

    Energy intensities (kWh per m² per year), equipment energy and the 12 m² cubicle are illustrative assumptions; grid carbon intensities are national averages from LowCarbonPower. McMurdo uses an assumed diesel-generation intensity.

    Best vs worst in this search: where the minutes go

    Worst

    Best

    Explain this comparison

    What is shown: The hospitals with the highest and lowest missed-window rates among the current search results, side by side, with the median time at each seam. "Difference" is the minutes the worse hospital adds at that seam; the seam with the largest share is the bottleneck.

    What to look for: The remote clinic is left out because it always treats first. Search one country or continent to compare like with like, or "Dense megacity" against "City" to see what crowding does.

    Why it matters: The gap between places is mostly at one or two seams, and these are the cheapest places to act.

    Bottleneck analysis across hospitals

    For every hospital in the current search: the median time at each seam from arrival to antidote, the longest seam (red outline), the building route that adds most time, and what fixing it would do compared with treating first. Sorted by missed windows.

    Explain this analysis

    What is shown: Each bar is one hospital, split into the four seams between arrival and the antidote: S1 recognising the overdose, S2 taking the blood sample (including any wait for the 4-hour level), S3 the laboratory and getting the result to a doctor, S4a prescribing and starting the antidote. The longest seam is outlined in red: that is the seam bottleneck. The table adds the building bottleneck (the route that adds most minutes: blood sample to the laboratory, fetching the antidote, or moving the patient), then re-simulates the hospital with that route fixed (pneumatic tube or laboratory hub; antidote stocked in the ED), and again with a treat-first rule.

    What to look for: How often the same seam is the bottleneck, and whether fixing the building bottleneck closes the gap or whether only changing the decision rule does.

    Why it matters: Improving anything other than the bottleneck saves little time. Where the bottleneck is organisational (waiting for results) rather than physical, fixing the building helps only a little.

    Setting
    Distances and roads
    District hospital

    In plain words

    In the countryside the patient rarely goes straight to a large hospital. They may walk or ride to a health post, be sent on to a district hospital, and then be transferred again to a referral hospital that can measure the paracetamol level and give the antidote. Every stop is a new seam: waiting to be seen, waiting for transport, and a slower road in between.

    This tab simulates 20,000 rural patients on four routes and shows which gets the antidote in time, where the time goes, and what helps most.

    How to read it

    • Pick a setting to load typical distances, roads and services, then change anything.
    • The route map shows the four routes; the timeline shows where each route spends its hours (grey = travel, amber = waiting at a facility, blue = hospital steps).
    • Distances, speeds and waits are illustrative unless a source is named.

    Route map

    Each row is one route, drawn to scale in hours since the tablets were swallowed. Coloured lines are travel, amber is waiting, blue is hospital steps; the bar at the end marks when the antidote starts.

    Explain this map

    What is shown: A schematic of the places and roads (not to scale). Each coloured line is one route; the labels give the median time of each leg for the current settings. A, usual referral chain: home → health post → district hospital, then transfer to the referral hospital if the district cannot measure the level or give NAC. B, bypass: straight from home to the referral hospital. C, start NAC at the district: the district starts the antidote on the history alone (as poison centres advise when levels are unavailable) and transfers afterwards. D, air retrieval: remote areas, first call to hospital arrival (median 238 minutes in a study of Royal Flying Doctor Service stroke retrievals).

    What to look for: Which route's antidote dot comes first, and how much of each route is waiting rather than travel.

    Why it matters: In rural areas the longest seams are between facilities, not inside them. A decision rule at the first capable facility can matter more than a faster road.

    Local emergency plan when the hospital is far

    What the first facility (health post, nursing station or district hospital) should do while the capable hospital is hours away. An operational checklist that follows published guidance in outline; it gives no doses and does not replace the local protocol or poison-centre advice.

    From the route settings on the left (arranging the transfer + district → referral journey).

    When to act: by time since ingestion

    The row for this patient (from the slider above) is highlighted. "Act locally" means at the first facility that can do it, before the long journey.

    The same route, step by step

    Each card is one step of the route above, with who is responsible, the time since ingestion, expected signs and the window left. Press Play to walk through it, or click any card or dot.

    Explain this map

    What is shown: (Press a Play button to watch a patient move through the route on a running clock; the map scrolls to follow. "Race both" runs the two routes side by side.) Six lanes (who is responsible): the patient and family, the phone line to a poison centre or referral hospital, the first facility (health post or district hospital), transport, the referral hospital, and the liver unit. Rectangles are steps, diamonds are decisions, numbered circles R1–R5 are the referral seams where responsibility passes between places. Under each step: the typical clock time since ingestion for this patient and route. Green path: start NAC locally; blue path: transfer first.

    What to look for: Where the two paths split (decision "NAC stocked here?") and how far apart they are when NAC starts. On the transfer-first path the antidote waits for the whole journey and the referral hospital's steps.

    Why it matters: Every referral seam is a handover with no single owner. Moving the antidote before R3 (arranging transfer) removes the longest seams from the antidote's path.

    Scenario matrix: time since ingestion × travel time

    Each cell simulates patients arriving at the first facility at that time with that travel + transfer time to the capable hospital. Top: % starting NAC after 8 h if transferred first → if NAC starts locally. Colour: how much starting locally helps. Hover for liver injuries.

    Scenario matrix: setting × what the district hospital can do

    Each cell runs the full rural route simulation for that setting and district capability, and shows the best ground route with its % treated late (and the usual chain for comparison).

    Explain these matrices

    What is shown: The first matrix crosses how late the patient arrives with how far the capable hospital is. The second crosses the rural setting with what the district hospital can do: measure the level on site or not, and stock NAC or not.

    What to look for: In the first, the cells turn dark green (large benefit from starting locally) once travel exceeds 1–2 hours, and at every travel time once the patient arrives after about 4 hours. In the second, the "NAC stocked" columns are best in every setting, even without a level on site.

    Why it matters: Together they give the rule: stock NAC where the hospital is far, and start it at the first facility when a toxic dose is possible. A level on site helps much less than the antidote on site.

    When does starting locally matter? Missed windows by travel time

    Explain this plan

    What is shown: A decision for this patient (start NAC here, or transfer first), the steps for the first facility with a time budget and a deadline from arrival (to the second once the clock is started), and the red flags that mean escalate at once. The chart reruns the simulation for travel-plus-transfer times from 0 to 10 hours: the share starting the antidote after 8 hours if the facility transfers first, against starting NAC here and transferring afterwards.

    What to look for: The point where the "transfer first" line rises above the "start here" line: beyond it, every extra hour of road is an hour of liver protection lost. With this pathway's typical timings, any transfer longer than about an hour already favours starting locally when NAC is stocked.

    Why it matters: The first facility controls the most valuable minutes. Taking the history, sending bloods and starting NAC before the patient leaves turns the long journey into treatment time rather than waiting time.

    Basis: activated charcoal is considered within 1 hour of ingestion with a safe airway (RCEM); when levels are unavailable, poison centres advise starting NAC empirically if a toxic dose is possible (Ontario Poison Centre); remote nursing stations can start oral NAC before transport (Northern Ontario care pathway); rural and remote centres are advised to stock enough acetylcysteine for one full course (Queensland Poisons Information Centre); red flags for urgent liver-unit discussion include encephalopathy, INR above 4.5 at any time, creatinine above 200 µmol/L, pH below 7.3, systolic BP below 80 mmHg and hypoglycaemia (LITFL).

    Where each route spends its time

    Median minutes from swallowing the tablets to the antidote, by route. Grey: travel; amber: waiting at a facility or for transport; blue: hospital steps; red line: 8-hour window.

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: One bar per route, built from the median time of each part: the delay before setting off, each journey, each wait at a facility (to be seen, for a transfer to be arranged), and the hospital steps up to the antidote. Hover a segment for its time.

    What to look for: Whether the bar crosses the red 8-hour line, and which segment is longest: that is the route's bottleneck.

    Why it matters: Shortening the longest segment saves the most. In the usual chain that is often the transfer: arranging it and the second journey.

    Share treated late and liver risk, by route

    Explain these graphs

    What is shown: Top: the share of patients who start the antidote after 8 hours, for each route, with the expected liver injuries per 1,000 high-risk patients. Bottom: the spread of time from ingestion to antidote for each route (how many patients start at each hour).

    What to look for: Routes whose curves sit mostly left of the 8-hour line. A long right tail means some patients wait very long, usually for a transfer.

    Why it matters: The average rural patient may still be treated in time; it is the tail that misses the window, and the tail is made of transfers and bad roads.

    Sources: travel-time access (93.3% of people reach a facility within an hour by motorised transport, 58.4% on foot): Weiss et al., Nature Medicine 2020. Royal Flying Doctor Service stroke retrievals: median 238 minutes from first call to hospital (University of Melbourne). Floods can more than triple travel times (World Bank, Kampala). Rwanda ambulance journeys about one hour on average (UGHE). When levels are unavailable, poison centres advise starting NAC empirically if a toxic dose is possible (Ontario Poison Centre). Vietnam's commune health stations and district centres are the first referral points (Viet Nam News). Speeds, waits and distances are illustrative.

    Each seam is served by its own resource. Set how busy each one is; the shared crowding of the department still moves them together.
    Bottleneck analysis · theory of constraints · queueing

    Which seam limits the pathway, and what happens when you fix it?

    A bottleneck is the step whose relief saves the most patients, not simply the busiest one. Five measures are compared below; the bottleneck is then relieved step by step to show how it shifts, following the theory of constraints (identify, exploit, subordinate, elevate, repeat).

    The pathway as a pipe

    Each block is a seam. Width is the typical time spent there (work plus waiting); colour is how busy its resource is. The red outline marks the bottleneck. Hover for detail; click a block to relieve it by 0.05 in occupancy.

    Five ways to name the bottleneck

    Each measure ranks the seams; agreement across measures makes the diagnosis robust. The last column is the decision-relevant one: patients spared per 1,000 if this seam's resource were 0.05 less busy.

    Marginal value of capacity

    Patients spared per 1,000 for each 0.05 of occupancy removed at one seam (the shadow price of capacity). The tallest bar is where the next unit of effort is worth most.

    The bottleneck moves

    Relieve the current bottleneck by 0.05, recompute, and repeat. The line shows missed windows after each round; labels show which seam was the bottleneck.

    Five focusing steps for this hospital

    Any number from 100 to 20 million, e.g. 250000, 250k or 2.5m.
    Policy
    Hospital

    Changing a setting re-runs the analysis. Every what-if uses the same simulated patients (common random numbers), so differences are not noise.

    In plain words

    An operations view of the pathway: for every step, how much time is work (doing the step) and how much is waiting (at the handover before it), which step makes total times unpredictable, which step's wait is longest in the patients who miss the window, and how many missed windows each improvement would prevent.

    It runs as a big Monte Carlo: up to 10 million simulated patients, so the answers are precise to a fraction of a percentage point.

    How to read it

    • The bottleneck is the step whose waiting causes most missed windows, not simply the longest step.
    • "Halve the wait" what-ifs re-use the same patients, so every bar is directly comparable.
    • The operations table turns times into daily numbers for a hospital of your size (Little's law).

    Work and waiting at each step

    Mean minutes per patient. Dark: work within the step. Light: waiting at the seam before it. Hover for median and 90th percentile.

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: For each step S1–S4a, the average work time (dark) and waiting time (light), across all simulated patients.

    What to look for: Steps where the light part is large relative to the dark part: time is lost between teams, not in doing the work. The process cycle efficiency (work ÷ total) is in the summary above.

    Why it matters: Speeding up work rarely helps when most time is waiting; the seam has to be fixed.

    Where the unpredictability comes from

    Each step's share of the variance of total time, Cov(Xᵢ, T)/Var(T).

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: How much each step contributes to the spread of total time. Shares add to 100%. The containment ratio C compares the total spread with the sum of the steps' own spreads; above 1 means delays reinforce each other.

    Why it matters: Missed windows come from the slow tail, and the tail comes from the steps with the largest share here.

    Whose wait was longest, in patients who missed

    Share of patients treated late whose single longest wait was at each step.

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: Among patients who got the antidote after 8 hours, the step where they waited longest.

    Why it matters: This is the operational bottleneck for the outcome that matters, the step to fix first.

    Relieve each bottleneck: missed windows prevented

    Missed windows if the waiting at one step is halved (same patients), compared with today. Hover for patients spared per 1,000.

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: The share treated late if the wait at one step is cut in half, one step at a time, plus two whole-system changes: no coupling (β = 0) and treat first.

    What to look for: The tallest drop. Because the same patients are used, the difference between bars is the real effect of each change, not chance.

    Why it matters: Ranks improvements by patients spared, which is how a hospital should choose where to spend effort.

    Operations table for your hospital

    Little's law: patients waiting at a step at any moment = arrival rate × average wait. Staff time = arrivals × average work.

    Convergence of the big run

    Estimated share treated late as patients accumulate (log scale), with the 95% interval.

    Two extensions of the model. Negative coupling is compensation: staff speed up when a patient is already late, so later stages absorb delay and C falls. Load-dependent coupling lets handovers leak more when the hospital is full.

    In plain words

    Coupling asks what happens after a step runs late. Is the next step also late, so delay amplifies? Or do staff hurry to catch up, so delay is absorbed?

    The paper assumes amplification. This tab shows the other possibility too, and what happens if handovers get leakier when the hospital is full.

    How to read it

    • Left of zero (green) is catch-up: fewer misses and a lower C. C only drops clearly below 1 if catch-up outweighs the shared slowdown of a busy hospital; try lowering occupancy.
    • Right of zero is amplification: misses rise faster and faster.
    • In the lower chart, the red line lets coupling grow with how full the hospital is. The gap between the lines is the extra harm of leaky handovers at busy times.

    From compensation to amplification

    Containment ratio C and missed-window share as coupling runs from −0.5 (later stages catch up) to 0.8. The shaded side is compensation: C falls towards 1, but stays near it while a busy hospital still slows every step together.

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: Two charts with coupling β across: negative values mean staff catch up on late patients (compensation); positive values mean lateness is passed on. Left: share missing the window. Right: containment ratio C, with C = 1 dashed.

    What to look for: Both lines rise to the right. The rise in misses speeds up as β grows, a convex curve.

    Why it matters: Each extra unit of coupling costs more missed windows than the last. Cutting coupling at even one handover, for example with a treat-first rule, has a large payoff.

    Constant against load-dependent coupling

    Missed-window share across occupancy, with coupling fixed at β₀ or rising with load. The gap opens exactly where the hospital is fullest.

    Explain this graph

    What is shown: Across: mean occupancy. Up: share missing the window. Blue: coupling fixed. Red: coupling that rises as the hospital fills, β(ρ). The shaded area is the extra harm.

    What to look for: The two lines match up to about 85% occupancy and then separate, with red climbing faster.

    Why it matters: If handovers get sloppier when busy, crowding hurts twice: through slower steps and through leakier seams. The empirical study can test this with one interaction term.

    How many simulated patients are enough? (live)

    The Monte Carlo standard error of a miss rate p from n patients is √(p(1−p)/n). Move the sliders to see how precision improves with more patients.

    Sample size for the whole page: the "Sample size" control at the top multiplies every simulation on every tab (Quick ×¼, Standard ×1, Large ×5, Very large ×20). Standard runs, for example, 12,000 patients per hospital, 8,000 per decision-matrix cell, 20,000 per rural route and 100,000 in the arrival model; Very large runs 20 times as many. Errors shrink with the square root: ×5 cuts them by about 55%, ×20 by about 78%. Larger samples take longer, but every tab stays responsive while it runs.

    The idea in one paragraph

    A Monte Carlo simulation answers "how often does this go wrong?" by playing the situation out many times with random numbers, instead of solving it with a formula. Here each play is one imaginary patient moving through the pathway. Each waiting time is drawn at random from a realistic range. After hundreds of thousands of patients, the share who missed the window settles to a stable number, and that number is the answer.

    Why not just use averages?

    Averages hide the slow cases, and the slow cases are the ones that miss the window. Two hospitals with the same average time can miss very different numbers of patients. Simulation shows the whole spread, not just the middle.

    Methodology: how the simulation study is designed

    Simulation studies are reported with the ADEMP framework (Morris et al., 2019, cited in the paper) and the STRESS checklist. ADEMP stands for Aims, Data-generating mechanism, Estimands, Methods and Performance measures. Each is explained below in plain words.

    1. Aims: what the simulation is for.To show, with plausible but invented numbers, how the seams of a time-critical pathway turn delay into missed treatment windows. It illustrates the paper's propositions and prepares the real study. It does not estimate what happens in any actual hospital.
    2. Data-generating mechanism: how the fake patients are made.Each patient gets a time before arrival, a hospital occupancy at arrival, and, for each step, a work time and a waiting time. They are linked by the rules in the Model tab: waiting grows with occupancy (common shock) and with the previous step's waiting (coupling β). All settings are listed on the Model tab; they were chosen to look realistic and then checked against the paper's tables and two published hospital studies.
    3. Estimands: what is measured.The share of patients who miss the window; the containment ratio C; the median and 90th percentile of time to the antidote; and, on the uncertainty tab, the amplification effect, meaning the extra share missing when steps are linked rather than independent.
    4. Methods: which scenarios are compared.A baseline and its counterfactuals (change one thing at a time); one-way sweeps (occupancy, coupling); a probabilistic sensitivity analysis (all settings drawn at random together); and three extensions (bag changes and shift handovers, time of day, coupling that rises with load). Scenarios that are compared use the same random numbers, so the difference reflects the scenario rather than chance.
    5. Performance measures: how good the answers are.Every estimate carries Monte Carlo error, the wobble from using a finite number of patients. It is reported as a standard error and a 95% interval, shown live on the first tab. The main runs use 120,000 to 300,000 patients per scenario, which keeps the error on miss rates to about ± 0.1–0.2 percentage points.
    6. Validation: is the simulator believable?It reproduces Table 6 and the counterfactual ranking of the paper to within Monte Carlo error (Validation tab), and its infusion module reproduces published bag-change delays (Bailey et al., 2016; O'Callaghan et al., 2022) after calibration of three settings.
    7. Assumptions and limits.Times are log-normal; propagation is linear; occupancy acts through one load factor; pre-hospital time is independent of in-hospital time. Treat-first is applied to every patient as a best case. The infusion, time-of-day and load-coupling settings are the author's assumptions. Results show what the model implies under these assumptions, not findings about hospitals.
